Thus ends the twentythird sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 23

Rama’s words brought no comfort to Lakshmana. Swaying between anger and sorrow, he was a lion provoked. His rage was frightening. “What cannot a fearless chief of warriors do to control the dictates of destiny? Ill-timed is this strange behaviour of yours. The king and queen conspire to deceive you, veiling their wickedness behind a mask of virtue. You not only refuse to see it but yield to him who deluded by his passion for a woman’s wiles dismisses the most noble of his sons to languish in the wilds of Dandakaranya. How can the younger son take precedence over the elder in affairs of the state? I cannot comprehend your so-called sense of duty! How can you submit to this unjust, unpardonable command of the king who is but a puppet in Kaikeyi’s scheming hands? Why was not the story of the boons revealed before preparations for the coronation were on? The king and Kaikeyi are your enemies, masquerading as your parents. Attributing this matter to fate is whimsical, for destiny is powerless before you!

“Wait Rama! Wait and the world will not only witness destiny bow down to my might, but also assist at your coronation. A coronation that was not destined to be! I will see that those who tried to banish you to the forest, themselves inhabit it for fourteen years” stormed Lakshmana. It may befit me as a prince to sport sandal paste and ornaments on my arms but those arms meant to protect friends and dispense alms to the needy will soon let loose arrows to pierce a hundred hearts. The earth will stink with the corpses of men, horses and elephants, which piling up will prevent even the light of the Sun from reaching the earth. As I hold my unfailing bow and my dazzling sword, which among the brave will boast of their heroism? Even if the enemy were Indra, I shall slay him. Today I shall deprive the king of his powers and bestow them on you. Issue the command, Rama and I, your slave, shall subjugate the entire earth.

Wiping away Lakshmana’s welling tears, Rama quietly said, “I remain loyal to my father. His wishes are my commands and this alone is the right path”.

Thus ends the twenty fourth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 24

Beholding Rama ever in the worshipful service of his father, Kausalya held back her tears thinking, “Stranger to sorrows and hardships until this day, showering words of love on all beings, can this noble son of Dasaratha live on grain scattered on the forest floor by chance? Can he survive on the fruits and roots the forest has to offer? Who will not shudder upon hearing that the most virtuous and beloved of all in this world has been banished by the king? The gods that impel his exile must be truly powerful”. Aloud she said, “My son, the breath of your departure fans my grief, my lamentations feed it and my tears are libations to the fire it causes. I will be scorched and consumed by its intensity. Let me live Rama! Let me come with you”.

“O mother!” said Rama, “after my departure, deceived by Kaikeyi and deserted by you, the king will surely die. Do not commit the sin of abandoning your consort. So long as the king lives, submission to him is an unwritten law. Do not forsake him in his hour of need. A woman’s place is beside her husband, who is her lord and master. She may neglect even her worship and prayer, but cannot disregard her duties as a wife. Why do you sorrow, when a prince as noble as Bharata who knows no path except the path of dharma is there to serve you with the greatest devotion?”

Queen Kausalya finally gave in, coming to terms with what seemed to be the inevitable. She saw her son, unsurpassed in every virtue, rooted in dharma, standing before her with an unwavering resolution. Her eyes brimmed with tears of pride and sorrow as she blessed him with every good fortune and bade him farewell, “Go my son! Go in peace. My heart protests, but my lips urge your departure. I will wait to hear your gentle voice. O Rama! why cannot that moment of your return be now?”

Thus ends the twentyfifth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 25

Kausalya restrained her grief and resigned herself to Rama’s departure now ready to quit the coveted kingdom of Kosala to honour his father’s commitment. “Helpless to stop you, I will now wait for those dreadful fourteen years to end. Go in peace, my son. May you tread the path of your illustrious forefathers! May the dharma that you protect with such fervour in turn protect you. May all the celestials, the sages and the weapons bestowed upon you by Viswamitra be your defence! May the gods you worship every dawn shield you! May your obedience and loyalty towards your parents ensure your longevity! May all elements, the heaven, the earth and all existence protected by Brahma, protect you”. Blessing her son in every way, Kausalya propitiated the gods for the welfare of Rama, by lighting the sacred fire and performing the holy rituals. “May you come back safe, having achieved your purpose! I await that day when I will behold you, attired in royal splendour with Sita, beautiful and bejewelled by your side, seated on the golden throne.” Having completed the benedictory rites, Kausalya, her eyes full of tears, circumambulated him and embraced him tenderly while Rama paid obeisance to his mother, touching her feet repeatedly.

Rama then made his way towards the palace of his beautiful consort, Sita.

Thus ends the twenty sixth sarga *of* Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 26

Rama whose dazzling effulgence illumined the highways of Ayodhya as he passed through them arrived at the magnificent abode of Sita who waited with garlands and sandal paste to greet a king-to-be, unaware of the upheaval that had taken place. It was then that Rama’s turmoil, hitherto concealed so carefully, surfaced, clouding his face. His tormented soul vented its suffering, which manifested on his divine countenance as an expression of great desolation. Witnessing these alien signs on a face ever serene and radiant, Sita grew alarmed. With great concern she asked, “At this moment, ordained by the brahmins as auspicious for your coronation, what ails you, my Lord? Where are the royal canopy, the chariot, the horses and the elephants? Where are the royal retinue and the brahmins to perform the rituals? At this moment of sublime glory why this unhappiness?” And Rama said, “Born of a great race famed for its righteousness, you will understand my words. Listen to what has transpired. My father, the very embodiment of truth, had in the past given two boons to mother Kaikeyi and the queen has decided that now is the time to redeem them. The king bound by honour has consented to grant them. Accordingly I am to be exiled for fourteen years, while Bharata crowned king will rule Ayodhya. My dear, I have come to bid you farewell!

“May your love for me be eternal and may you with patience forgive my absence. I leave my parents to your care, give them the strength to bear the pain of my separation. To Kausalya my banishment will be unbearable and to my father the swift turn of events may be disastrous. He lived to witness my coronation, a coronation that destiny has opposed and which will drown the monarch in an endless sea of sorrow. Do serve with great reverence my noble parents worn out by grief. Serve all my mothers with the same devotion I have for them. Bharata and Satrughna are dearer to me than my life, treat them with nothing but affection. Never by your actions displease Bharata who will be the ruler and lawmaker. Tread the path of dharma. Spend your time in worship and prayer. I am going to the forest and you, my beloved, shall stay here”.

## Sarga 27

Thus ends the twenty seventh sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 27

Sita listened silently to Rama’s monologue. So immense was her love for Rama that even a moment’s separation from him was unthinkable. “What is my offence, my Lord! that you want to desert me? Our actions in our previous birth determine and dictate our suffering. Since a wife has to share the fate of her husband, your banishment is mine. You are an embodiment of dharma. Do I have to teach you that to a woman, husband is the only refuge? I cannot go against your wishes, but life for me is not possible without you”, she replied. And then her anguished heart gave way to such torrential tears that they drenched the very earth from which she was born.

Rama gently wiped Sita’s tears trying to reason with her, but his soft-spoken consort was not to be dissuaded. “I do not mean to disobey, but separation from you will kill me. For a woman the glories of the world mean nothing compared to being with her lord. My dharma says I should follow you to the very end of the earth. When you are with me, what do I have to fear? The forest where you are is heaven for me and the heaven where you are not is the intractable wilderness. Serving you and living in the enchanting exuberance of a forest alive with a myriad birds and beasts, can life be anything but bliss? A bliss enhanced by your presence.”

Neither Rama’s renowned eloquence nor dharma could shake the gentle princess from her single-minded resolve.

Thus ends the twenty eighth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 28

In anticipation of the many ordeals they would have to face in the forest Rama tried to dissuade Sita, “Sita, born of a noble race, your duty at this hour of need is to do what is righteous and not what is pleasurable. You are too delicate for the wilderness choked with vine and bush. Great storms visit those miles of greenery, plunging it in darkness even by day. Peril lies every where, birds of prey infest the skies and large, slithering snakes that twist and turn tortuously infest the land. The canopy of the forest will be our roof, the leaves of trees our bed and the fruit our food. How can a princess so fragile, so used to the painted pleasures of a palace, survive the forest?”

No hurdle mentioned daunted Sita and no plea was going to hold her back. So when Rama announced his decision, she grew defiant and got ready to fight her cause.

*cintayantim tatha tam tu nivartayitumatmavan.*

**Перевод:**

**That self-possessed scion of the Kakutstha dynasty consoled the copper-red-lipped Sita in several ways to dissuade her (from going to the forest).**

Thus ends the twenty ninth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 29

Sita gently implored, “It has been prophesied that I would have to live in the forest for a period of time. That time is now and my parents have impressed it upon me that I should always follow you. With you by my side even the gods will not dare harm me. The weak dread the jungles but what frightens you? As decreed a woman, who in this life has been given in holy matrimony to a man belongs to him even after her death. She belongs to him in prosperity and in adversity. If despite my grief, my wishes are disregarded, I shall cast myself into the fire”.

This entire anguished plea left Rama unmoved. His immense love for Sita made him reluctant to lay bare the innocence of his cherished wife to the merciless jungles.

**Summary**

Sarga 30

“My lord!” exploded Sita “my father never knew you are but a woman in the garb of a man. He will be shamed to hear you abandoned me because you are too diffident to protect me. Men in their ignorance talk of your might and its magnitude. Is that a lie?

“What fear causes this hesitation in taking me? Will you gift me to the world to be its courtesan? Why don’t you do the duties you remind me of, towards your parents, towards myself and towards Bharata? No heaven, forest or penance will I enter without you. How can I, who cannot live even for a moment away from you, survive fourteen long years of separation?” Sita finally gave vent to her torment as she fell into Rama’s arms with hot tears of anguish flowing down her face. Embracing her, Rama said, “My dear, the very heavens have no use for me, if you are not happy. Like the self-created Brahma, I am fearless. You have been created to share my life and will ever follow me, as Suvarchala follows Surya. I enter the forest not by choice, but as commanded by my father who is my god and guru. Reverence to one’s parents alone is the means to heaven, knowledge, fame, prosperity and progeny. Come, walk the path of dharma with me. Your decision brings honour to your family and mine. You have proven yourself a jewel among women. Give away all our wealth to the brahmins, to the poor and to all those who have served us”.

The glow was back on Sita’s face and rapturously she began to dispose of all that she had.

**Summary**

Sarga 31

Now it was Lakshmana’s turn. He fell at his brother’s feet and begged to let him also accompany them. Looking at Sita and then at Rama who was reputed never to abandon any who sought refuge in him, he pleaded, “Even if there is a place on this earth where there is neither old age nor death, I do not desire it. Without you, I do not want kingship of the three worlds or the heaven where you are not.” Rama said, “Lakshmana, you are not only my brother but my friend and my life. What of Kausalya and Sumitra, if you go with me? The king enticed by Kaikeyi may slight them and she with the kingdom in her hands may not do them justice. Indebted to Kaikeyi, Bharata may not spare much thought for my mothers. Stay back Lakshmana, there is no greater dharma than serving one’s parents.” Lakshmana who refused so be dissuaded said that Kausalya could look after a thousand Lakshmanas like him and so could the equally capable Sumitra. “As for Bharata, he is a noble Ikshvaku and will cherish the queens with the greatest love and reverence. Take me with you, I will be your servant.”

Moved by Lakshmana’s devotion, Rama agreed, saying “Go, bid farewell to those dear to you. Bring with you the bows, the quivers, the swords and armour”.

Lakshmana returned with Suyajna, son of Vasistha and his disciples into Rama’s presence along with other eminent brahmins so that they could pay them their worshipful image.

**Summary**

Sarga 32

Rama and Sita went forth to greet Suyajna to whom he gave him a thousand elephants, including Satrunjaya gifted to him by his uncle. Sita offered him bracelets, rings, anklets and girdle. To the priest who conducted the prayers and rituals for Kausalya, went a chariot, attendants and fine clothes. Chitraratha, Rama’s charioteer, merited a thousand cows, jewels and gems while Trijata was given a thousand cows. Forgetting none that deserved his magnanimity Rama said “May mother Kausalya be happy by witnessing all the brahmins thus bonoured.”

Rama consoled his faithful attendants whose tears he tried to check but whose desolation at his departure he could not stem.

Thus ends the thirtythird sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 33

All the wealth given away, Rama, Lakshmana and Sita set out to Dasaratha’s palace to take leave of him. None in the city were indoors. Streets thronged with people still decked in their festive finery. Some climbed trees, terraces and seven-storied buildings to catch a last glimpse of their adored prince. And then came Rama down the royal avenue neither crowned nor riding an elephant, as he should have been, but walking barefoot. Sita and Lakshmana followed him without even a canopy to protect them from the heat of the Sun. The desolate scene sent waves of shock and dismay among those who looked in disbelief while gloom and anger reigned, at the unexpected turn of events. People aired their ire, saying, “Look at the princess so delicate and shielded until now, who even the celestials had not been able to fleetingly glance at. This embodiment of beauty and grace will soon be in the forest where the rays of the Sun will scorch her, rains will drench her and the unrelenting elements will rob her of her wondrous glow.

“Rama who always rode splendid chariots of gold, drawn by the best of horses, accompanied by the four divisions of the army now walks barefoot on the sheets of Ayodhya. All this is the result of a folly committed by the king rendered witless by his evil queen. How can a son so blameless be banished? The root of the tree of humanity is Rama, and Dasaratha has severed that root without mercy.” So venting their anger, the citizens of Ayodhya decided to move out of their city. “Let Lakshmana be our ideal, let us also follow Rama. May Kaikeyi rule a ghost city where homes will lie abandoned, where fields will lie barren and where brahmins will chant no prayers, or invocations. Unkempt, unswept and uncared-for Ayodhya will fall to min. Let us make Rama’s forest our city and this city the forest. Let vultures, beasts and serpents of the jungles make Kaikeyi’s capital their home.”

Ayodhya wept for the misfortune that had befallen their master, but little was the master concerned. He strode forth unwaveringly, a picture of undisturbed serenity and did not stop until he reached his father’s doorstep guarded by Sumantra.

Thus ends the thirtyfourth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 34

In the palace lay Dasaratha devastated by the thought of separation from his son. “My Lord”, said Sumantra, “Rama is here. He wishes to bid you farewell”. Rousing himself from the depths of desolation Dasaratha asked Sumantra to bring all his wives to see Rama off. Eyes red with weeping, arrived his three hundred and fifty wives with Kausalya in their midst.

When Rama entered with palms held together followed by Lakshmana and Sita, Dasaratha rushed to embrace him but fell unconscious. Lakshmana lifted him tenderly and laid him on a couch. To Dasaratha who was still in a daze Rama said, “I seek your permission to leave for Dandakaranya. May you permit Sita and Lakshmana to accompany me.”? In a voice full of remorse Dasaratha said, “By granting boons to Kaikeyi I have been deceived. Defy me Rama! Usurp the throne of Ayodhya and be its ruler. But Rama, the very essence of dharma, convinced his father. “O father, for many long years you have been the magnanimous and mighty lord of this earth. I will not render your promises false. At the end of the fourteen- year-exile I will come back to pay you my obeisance”.

Grieving for Rama, bound by his code of honour, constrained by Kaikeyi’s demands, Dasaratha resigned himself to what was to happen. “Go in peace, my son” he said, “my feeble mind cannot fight your fearless resolve. I was deceived by a woman who hid her wickedness, as fire hides in ashes and it is you, who suffer the consequences of my imprudence.” Father,” said Rama unmoved, ‘‘I renounce this kingdom, its inhabitants and its wealth. Let it be Bharata’s. The promise you made on the battlefield to mother Kaikeyi must be fully honoured. It does not befit a mighty Ikshvaku to grieve. A father is divine, and in obeying you I obey God. Let Bharata guard the rich frontiers of this land and let your vows be implicitly fulfilled”.

Rama’s decision was Dasaratha’s final blow. With all his defenses down, he mercifully lost consciousness and his body fell in a heap. Unable to endure his master’s suffering any more Sumantra too fell unconscious and witnessing it the entire universe wept.

But away from it all stood Kaikeyi silent, unconcerned and uncaring.

**Summary**

Sarga 35

Dasaratha came out of his stupor like one emerging from dementia. His face distortedwith grief, eyes red with weeping and arms flailing restlessly, he was an epitome of sorrow. Sumantra, beholding his noble master writhing in such agony, flew into a rage. Hurling words meant to pierce her soul, he said to Kaikeyi, “Dasaratha, the Lord of all beings is also your consort and you have abandoned him. Is there no crime which you are not capable of, Kaikeyi? You will destroy Dasaratha and the great Ikshvaku dynasty. Why do you torment the noble king who is invincible like Indra, steadfast as the mountains and indomitable as the ocean? It is the tradition of this race for the first-born to ascend the throne. How can you revoke that decree? Do not hold in contempt that magnanimous soul who bears you, grants you boons and is consort to you. Bharata may be crowned king, but we go where Rama goes. Why does not the earth rive open, in the face of your atrocities, Kaikeyi?”

“As the seed, so the fruit, the king continued. You inherit the qualities of your mother who was bom under an inauspicious star. A neem tree produces no honey. Your mother did not care if it cost her consort his life, in fulfilling her wishes, realizing which your father banished her from his kingdom. You are sinfully following the same path which brought ruin upon your mother. In your arrogance you compel the king, who is so blameless, to commit a grave injustice. If Rama enters the forest a terrible curse shall befall you”.

Neither Sumantra’s plea nor Dasaratha’s incisive condemnation moved Kaikeyi. She did not display the slightest trace of fear, pity or remorse.

Thus ends the thirtysixth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 36

Dasaratha reconciling himself to the situation asked Sumantra to ready the four divisions of the army laden with wealth, to escort Rama. He also wanted chariots and hunters who knew the intricacies of the intractable forest to accompany the prince. “Let all the grains and treasures in my possession be at Rama’s disposal.” said Dasaratha. His instructions shook Kaikeyi and her voice trembled, but the arrogance in it still dominated her tone as she thundered, “Bharata will not accept a kingdom denuded of its wealth.”

Her utter disregard for decorum shocked those who heard her while shamed and disgusted Dasaratha said, “By granting you boons have I earned the infamy of exiling Rama and crowning Bharata. What other evils do you have in store to further your cause?” This enraged Kaikeyi even more, who denouncing the entire Ikshvaku race said, “An ancestor of yours, Sagara, banished his first-bom, Asamanjasa. Rama too departs in the same way. History repeats itself, my Lord!”

Dasaratha was aghast and the people were outraged at Kaikeyi’s insolence. A minister of the state, Siddhartha, stepped in to clear Kaikeyi’s insinuations as he revealed what had precipitated that exile, “Asamanjasa amused himself by mercilessly throwing children as they played on the streets of Ayodhya into the river Sarayu. When Sagara knew this he banished the guilty prince. What wrong has Rama committed to warrant his banishment? If you know of a vice that vilifies Rama, speak now, Kaikeyi and he too shall face the same justice. Stop trying to mar his purity, rather seek your own redemption from universal condemnation.”

Dasaratha in a voice frill of sorrow said “Rule Ayodhya, as you will, along with Bharata. As for me, abandoning my kingdom, my comforts and my wealth, I shall follow Rama.”

**Summary**

Sarga 37

“Father!” said Rama, “Having renounced all comforts, of what use is an escort? He, who gives away his elephant, has no use for the rope that once bound it. I desire to possess nothing. Grant me robes of bark and allow me to take a spade and a basket to serve me in my exile.” And in the presence of the entire assembly Kaikeyi had the supreme audacity to shamelessly present Rama the bark, saying, “Wear it!” Rama quietly exchanged it for his silken finery. Lakshmana followed suit. Sita, that most virtuous of women and cherished daughter of Janaka, looked with great fear at the coarse robes, as a deer would at a deer trap. Her mind in turmoil, eyes filled with tears, she stood rooted to the ground, clutching them. Unaware of how they should be worn, open to the scrutiny of a thousand eyes, Sita, bashful and sad, asked Rama as to how they should be worn and he quickly helped drape the ascetic habilimant over her silken robes. Shedding tears of distress, the women who witnessed this poignant act implored Rama to let Sita be. “The revered princess is not meant to dwell in the forest like a hermit. Grant us the favour of her presence here, in Ayodhya”.

Sita would not give up her resolve to accompany Rama. Vasistha who was witnessing this heart-rending scene finally gave way to unbridled anger. His explosive voice boomed menacingly as he berated Kaikeyi, “Your wickedness will destroy the mighty Ikshvaku dynasty. Sita need not go into exile, for she can rule in Rama’s place, as the wife of the better half of the husband. If Sita goes to the forest so will the kingdom, the treasury and the people. Bharata and Satrughna also clad in bark garments will be with Rama and alone you will rule a deserted kingdom. Obstinate woman! you were bom to destroy the earth. A kingdom where there is no Rama is no kingdom, it is now in the forest where he will dwell. Never will Bharata accept the crown that is not his nor will he, bom of Dasaratha, allow himself to live under your tutelage. Aware of the tradition of the Ikshvakus he will never accept kingship so long an heir older than he is alive. You have committed a great folly in trying to crown Bharata, the favour you think you will render him pales in the injury it will cause him. None will remain in the kingdom, even animals will follow Rama. As for Sita, she was not part of your boons, spare her. Call for chariots and attendants. She will not wear bark robes but fine silks and jewels”.

Not a word of this tirade seemed to penetrate Kaikeyi’s stubborn stance nor did it dissuade Sita from following her lord.

Thus ends the thirtyeighth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 38

Sita donned her bark robes like a woe-begone waif, though consort to the mighty Ikshvaku. “Blamed be Dasaratha!” condemned the people of Ayodhya as they wept at the injustice. Dasaratha no longer cared for his honour, his fame or his life. Sighing deeply he said, “How can a dainty princess inhabit the jungles? What harm has this virtuous daughter of a virtuous king done to warrant her banishment? Though wrested out of me against my will, the barbarous command I have issued makes me unfit to live. Kaikeyi! blind to your devious designs I granted you the boons. Now by unscrupulously exiling Rama you commit an act that will destroy you, as a bamboo bloom destroys the very bamboo out of which it was bom. Your desire to see Sita clothed in bark will cast you in hell. Sinful woman! For what fault of hers do you punish her so and what harm has Rama done?” To Dasaratha who could not control his grief, Rama said, “Father, Kausalya that virtuous queen of yours, though immersed in sorrow, does not blame you. Never has she suffered any hardships. You are her only refuge, do comfort her for she needs all your kindness and support to bear the pain of my separation. Protect her.

**Summary**

Sarga 39

Beholding Rama in the mendicant’s attire, the king and his consorts broke down; the sorrowing monarch could neither bear to look at Rama nor speak to him. “Perhaps the transgressions of my past lives haunt me now, causing me such distress. Glowing like the god of fire, he stands before me robed in the coarsest of garments. Witnessing this I should have perished, but even death heartlessly flees me. Men will accuse me, saying, is this the reward of virtue? How is it that a prince so noble is exiled by his father and mother?”

Dasaratha ordered the best of clothes and jewels to be brought for Sita. Draped in those most gorgeous of silks, her beautiful limbs aglitter with jewels, she illumined the entire palace with her celestial beauty. Kausalya, overwhelmed with love and admiration for Sita, embraced her, saying, “Many ignoble women, though cherished and pampered will desert their men should they fall from fortune. Fickle and deceitful, they remain blind to kindness received and to the bonds of affection. Only to the virtuous and the faithful the husband is shelter and salvation. Remember in prosperity and in adversity he is your master”. Sita with palms held together said “Like a chariot without wheels and a veena without strings, O mother, so is a wife without husband. I have been taught these values by my parents. How can I forget my obligations towards a consort who is my god?”

Kausalya’s tears of grief turned into tears of joy.

Rama assured Kausalya that his fourteen-year-exile would pass but like a dream. Bowing to the three hundred and fifty consorts of Dasaratha, he said, “If I had ever in my ignorance caused you any distress, do forgive me”. Those humble words saddened them even more, plunging the palace into deeper gloom.

The resonance of music and the clanging of drums were soon replaced by the wailing of many tormented souls.

Thus ends the fortieth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 40

The chariot stood waiting. Rama, Sita and Lakshmana took leave of Dasaratha, Kausalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi. Sumitra tenderly kissed Lakshmana’s forehead, saying, “Rama the custodian of this earth bom for its protection is now in exile. From now on he is your refuge and takes the place of Dasaratha. Sita, that virtuous daughter of Janaka takes my place and the forest shall be your Ayodhya. Go, my son, may you fare well!”

The resplendent chariot drawn by the most magnificent horses welcomed Sita Rama and Lakshmana. The people of Ayodhya, the old, the young and the children, milled around the speeding chariot as they beseeched Sumantra to drive slowly so that they could feast their eyes on Rama a little longer while their eyes brimmed with tears. Rama shuddered at the despairing sight of an old king bent with sorrow. Aware that people were trying to follow him, Rama hurried Sumantra, and caught between them and his master, Sumantra felt tom. The dust raised by the fleet-footed horses mingled with the tears of those thronging the streets of Ayodhya.

Rama looked back helplessly like a foal held back by the cord of dharma while Dasaratha was pulled back by the inexorable hand of fate. He stood gazing after his son who rode further and further away. It wrung his heart to see the chariot merge with and become one with the horizon. A sight so final and so frightening!

Thus ends the fortyfirst sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 41

The people of Ayodhya continued to accuse their king after Rama left. They alleged that for the destruction of the world had the foolish king had driven away Rama. “Where has he gone, the protector of the world? In whom shall we now seek refuge?” The rebuke of his people and the sobbing of his consorts made Dasaratha cower under the burden of so much reproof and remorse.

In an Ayodhya without Rama life came to a stand still. People fell into a great apathy seeking neither food nor diversion. Cows refused to let their young suckle. Elephants threw out the food they held in their trunks. Sacred fires no longer burned and no householder ever cooked food. The planets assumed a menacing stance while the Moon refused to glow and the stars hid their twinkle. The whole universe seemed troubled as all signs of joy were snuffed out. The winds ceased to blow. The Sun no longer warmed than the Moon cooled. Parents forgot children. Children forgot parents. Women heeded neither husbands nor family derserting even their loved ones to meditate upon Rama.

A city, deprived of its beloved lord, shuddered in fear exposed to every peril.

**Summary**

Sarga 42

Thus passed the fateful day of Rama’s exile the dreadful realisation of which left Dasaratha devastated. He stood rooted to the ground as he gazed longingly in the direction in which Rama had gone. So long the dust raised by the chariot was visible did the king look, and when he could no longer see Rama he fell into a dead faint. Kausalya and Kaikeyi rushed to his side. “Kaikeyi!” roared the king as he regained his senses “do not touch me! You are no longer my consort. I disown you; in your own interest you have brought my authority to naught. The holy pact of matrimony I had entered into I now renounce, in this world and the next. If Bharata is pleased with the crown of Kosala, may his funeral offerings at my obsequies not reach me! I see the hoof marks of those magnificent horses that bore my son away, but I do not see him”.

In a voice crippled by a myriad emotions Dasaratha managed to feebly ask to be taken to the palace of Kausalya. “The only place where I will find solace,” he declared. The day passed and darkness descended upon the earth. To Dasaratha who had flung himself on a couch it seemed like the night of death. Calling Kausalya, he said, “My gaze that had followed Rama far beyond the horizon refuses to return.”

Kausalya gently took his hand trying to comfort him, who pined so intensely for the son he could no longer see.

**Summary**

Sarga 43

To the royal couple, the night passed painfully and regretfully. In the dark silence Kausalya asked Dasaratha, “My lord, will Kaikeyi who has stung Rama with the poison of her deceit, now infest the palace like a snake that has cast off its slough? By depriving Rama of the crown to gratify the whims of a way ward woman you have offered him as havis to the rakshasas. What harm will not befall my children who roam the wilderness, surviving on the spartan offerings of the jungle! “When will my son return to Ayodhya with his beautiful wife? I must have separated many a calf from their mother, for I too am deprived of my child.”

Thus ends the fortyfourth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 44

Sumitra consoled Kausalya: “Noble lady, Rama is an embodiment of dharma who has abandoned the throne in order to uphold the promises of his father. He has in Lakshmana a loyal brother to follow him to the ends of the earth whose only mission in life is to serve Rama whose image and name are inscribed in his heart. Sita, beautiful as a goddess has bravely and faithfully followed Rama, disregarding the discomforts of life in the wilderness.

“What has your son, the essence of dharma, not accomplished? In which comer of the earth does his fame not pervade? Rama is divine. The Sun will caress him. The winds will waft gently bringing him the sweet scent of the woods and the Moon will lull him to sleep. Armed with the most formidable weapons given by Viswamitra, Rama is inviolable whether in the forest or in the palace. He is the splendour of fire, the root of fame, the lord of all creatures, the light of the Sun, the divinity of the gods and the manifestation of a myriad majestic qualities which will guard him, protect him, save him. Give up your grief Kausalya for soon you will see the light of your eyes and the joy of your life.”

Thus ends the fortyfifth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 45

Dasaratha bound by his duty turned back, but the people of Ayodhya followed Rama deep into the woods. Rama cajoled his tearful subjects to go back, saying “Show Bharata the same love and respect you have shown me. That virtuous prince will do everything in his power to make you happy for though young in age, he is as old as the hills in wisdom and knowledge. Gentle but valiant, he will dispel all your fears. Endowed with every sublime quality, he has all the making of a monarch. It is your duty as much as mine to obey the royal commands. If you wish to please me see that he does not miss me or grieve for me.” The more Rama tried to convince them to return home, the more stubborn they grew, unwilling to be satisfied with none other than Rama.

Soon the river Tamasa hove into sight meandering across his path seemingly reluctant to let Rama pass. Sumantra unharnessed the horses so that they could quench their thirst and graze on the green river bank.

Thus ends the forty sixth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 46

Resting on the bank of Tamasa, Rama said, “Lakshmana, the first day of our exile comes to a close, let us spend this night here. In Ayodhya our father weeps and Ayodhya weeps with him. May their incessant tears not render our parents blind! I am glad you came, I need your help to guard Sita.” Lakshmana made a bed of dry leaves and grasses on which Rama and Sita retired for the night. Even the horses seemed to rue the day they were fated to drive Rama to the forest and not to his coronation.

The Sun rose on Lakshmana and Sumantra who had a sleepless night. Rama awoke to see his faithful subjects asleep on the forest floor. “Lakshmana!” he said, “look at these citizens of Ayodhya, ready to abandon their homes, families and even their lives to be with me. Let us leave now. A king should not cause, but alleviate, the suffering of his people. Let us free them of their hardship by leaving before they come awake.”

And so they quietly sped away.Sumitra's benediction to Lakshmana 2.40.5-8

Obed ience to the elder brother is dharma.

Know that Rama is your father, ,Sita is your mother and the forest the city of Ayodhya. Or, know that Rama is Visnu, Sita is Laksmi and the forest is the abode of Visnu Or, know that Dasaratha is dead, understand that \| am living in the house of my father due to the loss of my husband. Understand Ayodhya to be a forest because all people have left with Rama. or, know Rama and Dasaratha are two types of gurus. Who is to be followed? one who can help or one who cannot? Understand Ayodhya is a forest. Which is better: enjoyment of the kingdom for worldly pleasures or obedience to the elder brother for eternal happiness?

Thus ends the fortyseventh sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 47

A rude shock awaited Rama’s faithful flock when they got up, as he was no longer with them. “Cursed be our sleep that betrayed us”, they cried. What answer will we give those in Ayodhya when they ask us where Rama is?” Giving up their futile search they even sought to end their lives by flinging themselves into fire, rather than live without Rama.

Back home they looked at Ayodhya in disbelief. Pride of Kosala and home to their lord where life once throbbed and vibrated was now veiled in a dreadful silence. A pall of gloom hung over the magnificent city which now lay bleak and barren.

*sa hi srro mahabahuh putro dasarathasya ca.*  
*pura bhavati nodrradanugacchama raghavam..2.48.16..*

**Перевод:**

**“Before that valiant, strong-armed son of Dasaratha goes too far away (from us), we should follow him.**

*padacchaya sukha bhartustadrsasya mahatmanah.*  
*sa hi natho janasyasya sa gati ssaparayanam..2.48.17..*

**Перевод:**

**“The shadow of the feet of this magnanimous lord will give us happiness. He alone is the goal and protector of all these people. He is the supreme refuge.**

*vayam paricarisyamah sitam yryam tu raghavam.*  
*iti paurastriyo bhartrn dukhartastattadabruvan..2.48.18..*

**Перевод:**

**“We will serve Sita. You will serve Rama”. Such were the words of the distressed women of the city to their husbands. (They continued).**

*yusmakam raghavo'ranye yogaksemam vidhasyati.*  
*sita nari janasyasya yogaksemam karisyati..2.48.19..*

**Перевод:**

**“In the forest, Rama will look after your well-being and Sita will ensure our, women folk’s security.**

*ko nvanena’pratitena sotkanthitajanena ca.*  
*sampriyetamanojnena vasena hrtacetasa..2.48.20..*

**Перевод:**

**“The people here are choked with grief. Who will like to stay here where life is disagreeable, cheerless, full of despondency and distress?**

*kaikeyya yadi ce drajyam syadadharmyamanathavat.*  
*na hi no jivitenarthah kutah putraih kuto dhanaih..2.48.21..*

**Перевод:**

**“If Kaikeyi rules this kingdom unethically, we do not want to live here like orphans. What is the use of our progeny or property (in such a place)?**

*yaya putrasca bharta ca tyaktavaisvaryakaranat.*  
*kam sa pariharedanyam kaikeyi kulapamsani..2.48.22..*

*upadrutamidam sarvamanalambamanayakam.*

**Перевод:**

**“The entire kingdom, for the sake of Kaikeyi, is under a great calamity. With no support or leader it will definitely go to ruin.**

*na hi pravrajite rame jivisyati mahipatih.*  
*mrte dasarathe vyaktam vilapastadanantaram..2.48.26..*

**Перевод:**

*raghavam vanugacchadhvamasrutim vapi gacchata..2.48.27..*

**Перевод:**

**“Where you are in deep trouble with merits exhausted, it is better to take poison, or follow Rama or walk into the unknown.**

*mithyapravrajito rama ssasita ssahalaksmanah.*  
*bharate sannisrstassma ssaunike pasavo yatha..2.48.28..*

**Перевод:**

**“Rama along with Sita and Lakshmana has been deceitfully exiled and all of us delivered to Bharata like beasts to a butcher (for protection!).**

*prrnacandranana ssyamo grdhajatruraxindamah.*  
*ajanubahuh padmakso ramo laksmanapirvajah..2.48.29..*

*prrvabhibhasi madhura ssatyavadi mahabalah.*  
*saumyassarvasya lokasya candravatpriyadarsanah..2.48.30..*

*nrnam purusasardrlo mattamatangavikramah.*  
*sobhayisyatyaranyani vicaran sa maharathah..2.48.31..*

**Перевод:**

**Rama, elder brother to Lakshmana is a tiger among men, a subduer of enemies, powerful like an intoxicated elephant, and a great charioteer. Blue in complexion, he has a face like the full Moon. He has lotus-like eyes, knee-long arms and fleshy clavicles. Endowed with a sweet nature, he always speaks the truth and the first to speak to others. When he roams the forest, charming like the Moon and pleasing to the whole world, he will surely make it look graceful”.**

*tastatha vilapantyastu nagare nagarastriyah.*  
*cukrusu rduhkhasantapta mrtyoriva bhayagame..2.48.32..*

**Перевод:**

**Such was the lamentation of the women of the city. Overcome with grief as if frightened at the approach of death, they wept bitterly.**

*ityevam vilapantinam strinam vesmasu raghavam.*  
*jagamastam dinakaro rajani cabhyavartata..2.48.33..*

**Перевод:**

**As the women of the city were thus lamenting over the scion of the Raghus (Rama) (sitting) at home, the sun set. Night fell.**

*nastajvalanasantapa prasantadhyayasatkatha.*  
*timirenabhilipteva sa tada nagari babhau..2.48.34..*

**Перевод:**

**With sacrificial fires extinguished and the reading of holy scriptures and sacred recitations stopped, Ayodhya looked as if besmeared with darkness.**

*upas antavanikpanya nastaharsa nirasraya.*  
*ayodhya nagari casinnastataramivambaram..2.48.35..*

**Перевод:**

**With markets closed, the city of Ayodhya cheerless and shelterless looked like the sky without stars.**

*tatha striyo ramanimittamatura*  
*yatha sute bhratari va vivasite.*  
*vilapya dina rurudurvicetasa*  
*ssrtairhi tasamadhiko hi so'bhavat..2.48.36..*

**Перевод:**

**The women grieved over Rama as if a son or a brother had been exiled. Depressed and distressed, they wept and sobbed. For them, Rama was indeed more than their sons.**

*prasantag itotsavanrttavadana*  
*vyapastaharsa pihitapanodaya.*  
*tada hyayodhya nagari babhrva sa*  
*maharnava ssanksapitodako yatha..2.48.37..*

**Перевод:**

**With the cessation of singing, celebrations, dance and music, there was no rejoicing in the city. The markets displaying merchandise were shut down. The city of Ayodhya looked like the ocean with its waters diminished.**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande astacatvarisassargah..*

Thus ends the fortyeighth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 48

“Why are you here without him?” asked the women tearfully of their men. Blessed are the rivers, streams and the lotus-lovely lakes in which Rama will bathe. Blessed are the forests he walks which will bring forth exotic fruits and flowers. Blessed are the mountains which will send their streams gurgling down their slopes where he sits.”

“Who in Ayodhya can live under a wicked woman? We are now like cows in the care of a butcher. Woe to Dasaratha who has fallen prey to a woman’s wiles! And woe to our men who have returned without Rama!”

“Take poison,” they told them, “or put as many miles as possible between you and Ayodhya.”

## Sarga 49

\[Rama crosses the frontiers of the kingdom of Kosala - crosses rivers Vedasruti and Gomati- speaks to Sumantra.\]

*ramo'pi ratrisesena tenaiva mahadantaram.*  
*jagama purusavyaghrah piturajnamanusmaran..2.49.1..*

**Перевод:**

**Recollecting his father’s command, Rama, the foremost among men, covered along distance during the remaining part of the night.**

*tathaiva gacchatastasya vyapayadrajani siva.*  
*upasya sivam sandhyam visayantam vyagahata..2.49.2..*

**Перевод:**

**While Rama was thus travelling, the auspicious night ended. With the sandhya (morning twilight), worship over, he reached the frontiers of the country.**

*gram an vikrstas imantan puspitani vanani ca.*  
*pasyannatiyayau sighram sanairiva hayottamaih..2.49.3..*

*sravan vaco manusyanam gramasamvasavasinam.*

**Перевод:**

**Watching the villages furrowed at the outskirts, forests in blossom, hearing the gossips of the people living in the midst of villages, Rama felt he was moving very slowly whereas he had actually covered a long distance with those excellent (swift) horses.**

*rajanam dhigdasaratham kamasya vasamagatam..2.49.4..*

*hanrsamsadya kaikeyi papa papanubandhini.*  
*tiksna sambhinnamaryada tiksnakarmani vartate..2.49.5..*

*ya putramidrsam rajnah pravasayati dharmikam.*  
*vanavase mahaprajnam sanukrosam jitendriyam..2.49.6..*

**Перевод:**

**(The villagers were speaking among themselves) “Fie on the king who is overtaken by passion! Alas, the heartless, sinful Kaikeyi, indulging in evil has banished into the forest this prince who is righteous and sagacious, compassionate and self-restrained. How could this cruel Kaikeyi, by breaking all limits of decorum resort to such atrocious action?**

*katham nama mahabhaga sita janakanandini.*  
*sada sukhesvabhirata duhkhanyanubhavisyati..2.49.7..*

**Перевод:**

**“How will Sita, highly fortunate daughter of Janaka and used to comforts endure these sufferings?**

*aho! dasaratho raja nisnehah svasutam priyam.*  
*prajanamanagham ramam parityaktumihecchati..2.49.8..*

**Перевод:**

**Alas, the loveless king Dasaratha now intends to abandon his own sinless son Rama who is dear to the subjects”.**

*eta vaco manusyanam gramasamvasavasinam.*  
*srnvannatiyayau virah kosalan kosalesvarah..2.49.9..*

**Перевод:**

**Such were the words of people living in villages and hamlets that Rama the valiant lord of Kosala happened to hear as he was crossing the boundaries of Kosala.**

*tato vedasrutim nama sivavarivaham nadim.*  
*uttiryabhimukhah prayadagastyadhyusitam disam..2.49.10..*

**Перевод:**

**He then crossed the river Vedasruti flowing with sacred waters and went in the southern direction where sage Agastya resided.**

*gatva tu suciram kalam tatah sitajalam nadim.*  
*gomatim goyutanrpamataratsagarangamam..2.49.11..*

**Перевод:**

*gomatim capyatikramya raghavah sighragairhayaih.*  
*maynrahamsabhirutam tatara syandikam nadim..2.49.12..*

**Перевод:**

**Gomati gone, Rama with the swift-moving horses crossed the river Syandika echoing with the cries of peacocks and swans.**

*sa mahim mamma rajna dattamiksvakave pura.*  
*sphitam rastravrtam ramo vaidehimanvadarsayat..2.49.13..*

**Перевод:**

**Rama showed Sita vast tracts of land encircled by kingdoms which were formerly bestowed upon Ikshvaku by emperor Manu.**

*srta ityeva cabhasya sarathim tamabhiksnasah.*  
*hamsamattasvarassri manuvaca purusarsabhah..2.19.14..*

**Перевод:**

**Graceful Rama, best among men with a voice resembling that of an intoxicated swan, called the charioteer again and again and said:**

*kada'ham punaragamya sarayva puspite vane.*  
*mrgayam paryatisyami matra pitra ca sangatah..2.49.15..*

**Перевод:**

**“When shall I return and reunite with my father and mother and go hunting in the blooming forest on the bank of the river Sarayu?**

*natyarthamabhikanksami mrgayam sarayrvane.*  
*ratirhyesatula loke rajarsiganasammata..2.49.16..*

**Перевод:**

**“In this world, hunting is a unique pleasure. It is regarded as a delightful sport for royal sages. But I do not have a great longing for hunting in the forest on the bank of river Sarayu.**

*kale krtam tam manujairghanvinamabhikanksitam:.2.49.17..*

*sa tamadhvanamaiksvakassrtam madhuraya gira.*  
*tam tamarthamabhipretya yayau vakyamudirayan..2.49.18..*

**Перевод:**

**The descendant of Ikshvaku related to the charioteer in a sweet voice the thoughts that came to him and went on the way (continued his journey).**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande ekdnapancasassargah..*

Thus ends the fortyninth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 49

Meanwhile Rama travelled further and further away from his father’s kingdom. The chariot raced on reaching the southern frontiers of Kosala where fields were kept ready for the sowing season. Flowering woods and cozy villages competed for Rama’s attention, as he passed homes and hamlets hearing people accuse Kaikeyi. Many miles after, he crossed the boundaries of that region and later the river Vedasruti to reach the land of Agastya.

## Sarga 50

\[Rama reaches Srngiberapura on the bank of the Ganga-Guha, chief of the nishadas welcomes Rama.\]

*visalan kosalan ramyan yatva laksmanaprrvajah.*

Thus ends the fiftieth sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 50

At the boundaries of Kosala, Rama got out of his chariot and turned towards Ayodhya to pay his obeisance to the citadel of the Ikshvakus, to wish its inhabitants to live in peace, protected by the presiding deities. Rama now crossed the borders of his beloved country, blessed, beautiful and flourishing, a land where rivers and lakes sparkled, temple bells pealed, and sacred chants echoed and re-echoed in its nooks and comers.

Many miles south of Kosala, Rama beheld the breath-taking Ganga. Her pristine waters were home to shoals of fish and her banks haven to myriad birds, beasts and bushes. Rama decided to spend that night on the broad bank of that holy river.

Meanwhile the ruler of that region Guha, chief of the nishadas whose devotion to Rama was boundless received news of his arrival. “Welcome, mighty one!” he said, looking at the divine visitor and embracing him, “the entire earth belongs to you. Blessed are we to receive you. Your very word is our command.” Guha treated them to a sumptuous feast but Rama gently declined: “I am touched by your generosity but regret my inability to accept it. Your devotion is incomparable but my vows are irrevocable. Bound by them I have come to spend a span of fourteen years to live the life of an ascetic. Hence I can enjoy neither lavish hospitality nor royal comfort.”

Content with a little water from Ganga, Rama lay down to rest. For the mighty prince hounded by fate slowly passed the long night, innumerable miles away from home. He slept on the hard crust of the earth softened by a bed of leaves and grass lovingly gathered by Lakshmana.

Thus ends the fiftyfirst sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 51

Guha greatly impressed with Lakshmana’s devotion to Rama for whose protection he had stood sentinel all night. Guha offered to continue the vigil but Lakshmana declined. His mind went back to Ayodhya, “Will the king ever survive separation from his son who was his life?” he asked Guha, “With Dasaratha’s death, mother Kausalya and Sumitra will also go his way. Ayodhya will perish. The earth will be widowed without Dasaratha. And yet if he still lives we will behold the most magnanimous of kings once again. Will that day ever come?”

**Summary**

Sarga 52

Rama looked forward to the onward journey and Guha got a sturdy boat ready to ferry the royal travellers across Ganga. “What shall I do?” asked Sumantra and Rama replied, “Return to Ayodhya and serve the king with devotion.” But Sumantra pleaded, “Rama! the world will never accept your exile. Your matchless respect for your father will be renowned in the three worlds, but what about us? We will be battered by the evil that is Kaikeyi.”

Rama met Sumantra’s outburst with soothing words “Sumantra! your devotion to the Ikshvakus is unparalleled. Do minister to my father tormented by an unbearable sorrow. The will of him who holds the sceptre shall prevail. Shield him from all evil and tell him not to brood over our life in the forest. On our behalf pay him obeisance, inform him and his queens that Bharata must be sent for and crowned king of Kosala. Tell the king he should welcome Bharata and treat our mothers with equal love.

Sumantra, unwilling to be dismissed, continued to plead, “How can I possibly go back to an Ayodhya that still grieves for you? When the heart-broken citizens ask for you, what answer shall I give them? What should I say to queen Kausalya? Should I say, Mother, do not weep! I have left your son with his maternal uncle? An untruth that may be pleasant to her but how can I tell her the bitter truth that I have abandoned Rama in the forest? It is unthinkable to go back to Ayodhya without you. Even the horses will refuse to draw the chariot. If you do not heed me I shall immolate myself, because the heaven of being with you has been denied to me, “ but Rama insisted “Sumantra, go back. Seeing you, mother Kaikeyi will rest assured that I have really gone away. I wish her to enjoy supreme authority in the name of Bharata. As ordered by my father, my exile begins now, so does my solitude and my austerities.”

They asked Guha to procure the sap of the banyan tree to get their locks matted. Robed in bark and armed with bows, the mighty Ikshvaku princes resembling resplendent priests, embarked on their journey across Ganga. Rama offered traditional worship to the holy river and Sita invoked mother Ganga for her blessings before crossing it.

Upon reaching the far bank of the river, Rama warned Lakshmana to be more vigilant with Sita. “From now on, she will experience the discomforts of the forest. A forest devoid of all human habitation, where neither grove nor garden exists, but perils and impediments abound.”

Thus ends the fiftythird sarga of Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 53

Rama, seated under a tree after his evening worship, said, “Lakshmana, the king must have spent a restless night. May Kaikeyi, in her lust for power, not make an attempt on his life. Deprived of you and me, debilitated by age, dominated by his passion for Kaikeyi, what can the king do? How can he defend himself? Which father deluded and enticed by a woman would banish a son like me? Kaikeyi seems to have entered our lives for the destruction of

Dasaratha. Hostile towards me, intoxicated with power, she may torment Kausalya and Sumitra. So return to Ayodhya. Lakshmana. Let no mother bring into this world a son like me, who causes her constant sorrow. I would face the world alone if I were the only one concerned. It is not a question of courage but a question of dharma that made me give up the crown.”

Alter days of quiet resignation, Rama finally vented the torment raging in him. Exhausted and ravaged by so much anguish and turmoil, he was like a fire extinguished. “Is it worthy of you to lament, Rama”? Lakshmana consoled, “Neither Sita nor I can live away from you.” Rama lay back peacefully resolved for all times to go through the fourteen years of banishment.

The vast forest caused no fear or distress to the noble Ikshvakus who roamed the sylvan region like lions.

**Siromani, Bharata and Satrughna at Kekaya (gacchateti) 2.1.1-4**

The events of Rama’s incarnation and his marriage, etc have been described in Balakanda. The poet now proceeds to work out Rama’s consecration as a prince regent. On father’s advice, Bharata had left for his maternal uncle’s home with Satrughna, the destroyer of enemies in the form of attraction (raga) and repulsion (dvesa).

**Tilaka, Appearance of Dasaratha 2.1.5**

Dasaratha’s four sons were like the four arms of Visnu, meaning, he appeared like lord Visnu with his four sons.

**Dharmakuta, Qualities of a king 2.1.9-39**

These verses describe the qualities of Rama by which he endeared himself to one and all. It is suggested here that only a person possessing such qualities deserves to be a king.

As dharma includes ‘rajadharma’ (science of polity), the commentator has taken here an opportunity to describe in detail qualities of an ideal king as recorded in the texts of Dharmashastra. The commentator substantiates this statement by quoting the following three authorities:

1\) Yajnyavalkya-on ideal king, 2) Rajadharma- on ideal minister, and 3) Kamandakiya Nitishastra on ideal king. When a king is equipped with such qualities as recommended in these texts he can provide the subjects with a good quality of steady rule. Only Rama and none else possessed such majestic qualities.

**Glorious virtues of Rama 2.1.9-33**

The scriptures rightly asserts: "A king shines in this world and the next, when he distributes his money for (1) dharma, (2) celebrity, (3) earning more money, (4) himself, and (5) his relatives."

That is the reason why people, of their own accord, longed for him as their king even when Dasaratha was the very best, looking after them like his progeny. The words of people later, in the second chapter substantiate the same import.

Gunas *and* Samskaras

This exhaustive description of great qualities of Rama opens a door to another discussion. An ideal king must have both gunas and samskaras (sanctifying rites). While Rama’s qualities are stated exhaustively only some and not all the samskaras are mentioned. The commentator justifies this by arguing that while all the qualities are useful and relevant for a king, samskaras ending with the sacred bath after the completion of studies in the guru’s house (avabhrilasnana) only are useful and relevant and, therefore, only those are mentioned in verses starting with:—’etc. Furthermore, Sita’s words in Yuddhakanda viz. "performed Agnistoma and such other sacrifices giving munificent gifts to brahmins" etc. stand testimony on the matter of other auspicious rites having been performed by Rama. A person not sanctified by rites ending with the sacred bath is unworthy of being entrusted with the responsibility of looking after the kingdom. He has no right to perform duties of any of the four ashramas. Therefore, sanctifying rites up to the sacred bath are essential everywhere and hence only those are stated here.

The commentator substantiates this by quoting Apastamba’s authority. He explains the import of these words, too. Thus he vindicates the stand taken by Valmiki of not mentioning all the samskaras performed to Rama and also of mentioning some as in their absence a person is not entitled to performing normal ashrama duties, too.

Importance of gunas and samskaras in dharma

This does not however mean that samskaras are less important than gunas. The commentator proceeds to establish the importance of both qualities and sanctifying rites from the point of view of dharma. They are useful for achieving the human goals not only of this world but also of the world hereafter.

*V*ital Importance of Samskaras, ending with the sacred bath on completion of studies at *the* Guru’s house:

If in the present context all samskaras are not mentioned here, it is because they are not directly useful in performing one’s duty as a king. To justify the mention of some samskaras authorities quoted are: Apastamba, Gautama, Atharvaveda.

Such is the injunction: "He who worships fire without performing darsha and paurnamasa (sacrifices performed on the new-moon and full-moon days); without performing the soma sacrifice, and without honoring guests; without offering oblations, or without performing vaishvadeva (homage paid to all the gods thrice a day by offering small portions of cooked food) and without observing the proper injunctions, destroys his seven consecutive heavenly abodes".

Bodhayana too, agrees, saying, "He who has consistently failed to observe the obligatory vows as also the incidental ones, has strayed from the righteous path and as a sinner, does not obtain heavenly abode".

So the import of the word 'ekadesha’ in the sutra is that one must perform all the rites as far as possible, without failing in the observance of those which are specifically enjoined for one’s ashrama.

Manu also advises, ‘After acquiring the Vedas as per the prescribed rites, after giving birth to sons as per the direction of dharma, after performing sacrifices as per one’s ability, one must focus one’s mind on the final emancipation’.

In the sutra stated above, only some of the great qualities like ‘compassion’ etc. are mentioned as they are common to all the four stages of life.

Vishnupurana too, says, ‘compassion towards all living beings, tolerance, absence of too much pride, truthfulness, cleanliness, spontaneous will to act, auspiciousness, agreeable speech, friendliness, absence of desire, absence of wretchedness, absence of envy’ are the virtues common to all the castes. They are also the characteristics desirable in all the four stages of life.

In the matter of taking up the responsibility of a kingdom, even more eminences are stated in verses starting with the verse sa hi rupopannashcha— etc. are desirable as per sastras on polity. Thus the mention of all the eight qualities and all the necessary rites listed up to the ceremonious bath stands to reason as through them both the protection of the kingdom here and acquiring heavenly abode hereafter are made possible.

Propriety of describing Rama’s great qualities at this stage:

A doubt may be raised here: ‘Why does the poet describe Rama’s qualities at this point while they could as well be stated after the narration of his birth’? To this the commentators reply is that the inborn qualities like having a beautiful appearance etc. could be depicted earlier but it would not be of any use at that stage of Rama’s life and it would not be possible to describe the acquired qualities like affability, reverence for the saintly and so on at that point. Since all the qualities are of great significance at the householder’s stage they are described immediately after the narration of Rama’s wedding.

In fact, the Chandogya describes the ideal qualities beginning with the study of the Vedas and goes on with the ideals of conduct and character for a householder and ends up with the words, "—attaining to Brahmaloka, never does he return (to the cycle of birth and death)". This may give rise to a doubt that the fourth (sannyasa) stage of life does not exist. To which sage Badarayana has replied ‘kritsnabhaavattu grihinopasamhaarah’ meaning that truthfulness etc. relevant to the first (brahmachari) stage, performance of agnihotra etc. relevant to the second (grihastha) stage, peacefulness etc. being relevant to the third (vanaprastha) and the fourth (Sannyasa) stage are all relevant to a householder and hence the Upanisadic passage concludes with the description of the grihastha stage and not because the fourth stage does not exist.

**Rama’s virtues 2.1.18, 26-28**

‘Aroga’ is ‘the ability to perform good deeds.’ Desakalavit, denotes, Rama possessed the conscience of the people.

Tilaka explicates Rama’s virtues saying, he knows the right place and rtght time to punish the wicked and to patronize the pious. He is conversant with the methods of tapping the sources of income. He is well-versed in collecting taxes like the honeybee which collects honey adeptly from flowers. The Mahabharata, says, ‘the expenditure of a king is met from one-half or one-fourth or three-fourths of his income’ (Sabha-V-71).

Rama enjoyed the pleasures of the senses, keeping inviolate the principles of righteousness and maintaining the soundness of his finances. Srimad Bhagavatam observes, ‘A householder spends his income on acquiring religious merit, achieving celebrity, earning more wealth, enjoying pleasures and maintaining his own people. Such a person rejoices in this as well as in the life beyond.’ (VIII.XIX-37)

**Tattvadipika, Superhuman qualities of Kama 2.1-32; 2.2.26-57**

The gods prayed Lord Visnu for the lolling of arrogant and authoritarian Ravana. Since Visnu himself appeared in the form of Rama, it is natural that Rama was a repository of all great qualities. Rama was gentle and generous, cool and composed virtues he has imbibed from men of rich experience and vast, Vedic wisdom. He has cultivated the secrets of the use of weapons, mantra and astra from experts in military science.

Rama was truthful, merciful towards the weak, and unforgiving to the wicked. Me was sweet in tongue and kind at heart. He would punish the evil and protect the good. \|n a word he respected rajadharma befitting the dynasty of the Ikshvakus.

Imbued with pratibha or intelligence, benevolence and tolerance of the Earth, Rama was simple and straightforward skilled in arguments and sincere in the discharge of duties, he acknowledged the authority of the Vedas and the dictates of dharma, for he was will-read in Nyaya, Vaisesika and Vedanta, in poetry, and poetics.

Rama knew that dharma, artha and kama had their fixed time in the day: morning, afternoon and evening, respectively, Artha has to be shared and spent on dharma reputation, investment, enjoyment and dependents. His nature never permitted association with evil persons. Grateful even for the smallest help rendered, he could read the minds of men. Rama is well-trained in riding, driving and training horses and elephants.

With a mind unperturbed and untroubled in the midst of a falling world, his war ṛõpṛditions brought him fame (Keerti), and reputation (yasas). Uninterested in meaningless disputes (japa and vitanda), he enters the war-field without fear and with a rare quickness and ability.

**Dasaratha’s proposal to make Rama his successor 2.1.39—50**

Hurricanes, circles round the Sun the Moon or the smoking horizon, earthquakes, falling of stones, oozing of blood from trees etc. are premonitions, portents Dasaratha saw. Which struck fear in him. Old age was another cause for proposing Rama’s coronation. He came to know that Rama was a remover of grief, cause of happiness, to his subjects, This was another factor.

Dasaratha did not invite Kekaya king and Janaka due to hurry as he assumed that they would hear news of Rama’s coronation later.

**Why Janaka and Kekaya were not invited 2.1.48**

Tilaka opines that in the event of the king of the Kekayas and King Janaka being invited to attend the installation ceremony, Bharata and Satrughna would have naturally accompanied their maternal grandfather. The presence of all of them would have confirmed the installation of Sri Rama and the whole course of history would have altogether changed. Sri Rama would not have proceeded to the forest and killed the demons. So the very purpose of his earthly appearance would have been defeated. In order to avert this contingency the gods changed the mind of Dasaratha and deterred him from inviting those two of his nearest relations.

**A king with a thousand eyes 2.1.50**

There is a pun on the word, sahasra-chakshu in the verse. A king is credited with a thousand eyes in the shape of a network of spies employed by him in order to ascertain the loyalty of his subjects and to detect the presence of any fifth columnists within his kingdom, as also to hunt up gangs of robbers and thieves. It is on account of these spies that a king has also been designated in works on political science as a ‘Cara-Chakshus’.

**Dasaratha seeks the approval of the assembly to consecrate Rama 2.2.1-16**

The word samnikrsta refers to the brahmins involved in personal interests. The term chatravrtananam means one who is enthroned as prince regent.

**Consent of the people 2.2.16**

Dasaratha, even after reading the mind of the subjects, wanted to confirm the same and hence asked them, why they wished Rama to be coronated, while he, too, was carrying out his kingly duties in accordance with the sacred law. To this the people recount the great qualities of Rama before him. (bahavo nripa kalyana varada tvamarhasi)

The principle of dharma (polity) that is illustrated here is of the ideal ruler is who is coronated according to the approval of the subjects. Dasaratha had a special affection for Rama but he planned the coronation only after obtaining whole-hearted consent of the people. The principle of dharma suggested here is that he who is appointed with the wholehearted and full consent of the people is an ideal king. Commentator Makhi elucidates the same by citing from "Adiparva" of the Mahabharata: People give their consent for appointing Puru as king; People approve the appointment of Yudhishthira as king; Dhritarashtra tells Duryodhana that it would not be proper to protest against Yudhisthira’s appointment as he was appointed with the consent of the people.

**Response of people’s representatives to Dasaratha’s proposal 2.2.17-22**

R ven though \[Dasaratha knew Rama’s excellence and anticipated the consent of the people, he pretended as if he did not know, and he wanted to hear from the horses mouth.

**Dasaratha seeks people’s opinion 2.2.23**

The word ajananniva means, as if not knowing. Tilaka suggests: though Dasaratha knew that Rama’s consecration was dear to everyone, he pretended as if he did not know and his query to the citizens was as if to know their opinion.

**Amrutakataka, Dasaratha acknowledges people's response and orders the coronation of Rama 2.3.1-12**

The members of the royal conclave gave concurrence to Dasaratha’s proposal. They paid obeisance with folded hands. The king acknowledged their salutations. The acknowledgement may be shown in three ways: casting a grateful glance, folding one’s own palms in respect or expressing gratitude in suitable words. This may be according to the status that one enjoys.

Modes and materials related to dharma 2.3.1

- 1\. List of materials required for the ritual of the consecration ceremony, (ritual)
- 2\. Rules and modes of greeting and reciprocating the same (customs and manners)
- 3\. Status of sons born to a king from many wives and their right to ancestral property (law)
- 4\. Father’s exhortation to his son and successor (polity)
- 5\. Necessity to control his six internal enemies like passion, anger, greed, pride, malice, infatuation (polity)
- 6\. Woman’s right to the possession of personal property (law)

**Gifts given at coronation 2.3.6-20**

These verses refer to the preparation for the coronation ceremony. Makhi corroborates the contents citing the authority of Samavidhana Brahmana. He gives a list of gifts to be given to one who performs the coronation.

**Modes of greeting 2.3.22-30**

Rama bows down at the feet of Dasaratha. Makhi explains in detail different modes of greetings prescribed by Dharmashastras. He suggests the custom of greeting one’s guru or father. It involves both gestures and words. One should approach him with folded hands announcing one’s name and the gesture as, "I am Rama offering you my salutations" and touch his feet. The Sanskrit equivalent for the words:

The person so greeted should also reciprocate it. This is called! Manu says one should not greet a person who does not know how to reciprocate it. He prescribes the mode of reciprocal greeting which is usually in the form of a blessing. The words are: May you live long, gentleman!.

Here the word saumya means one resembling Soma i.e. the moon which is cool and pleasant. When greeted properly, the elder man is delighted at the sight and conduct of the youngster who has imbibed in him good manners, as one would at the sight of the moon.

Both Manu and Yama, (Smritikara of that name) go a step ahead and say, if after receiving salutations one does not reciprocate it with blessings whatever sin that person might have committed in life is transferred to him.

Initiating conversation even before being greeted formally

To avoid this, one is advised to initiate the talk even with the low born. If one cannot think of anything else one should even say, "Drink wine (and enjoy)!"

Manu prescribes modes of purvabhi bhashana: To a brahmin one must ask,??? "How do you do?", to a kshatriya,??? "How is your health?", to a vaishya,??? "How is business?, to a sudra,??? "Are you hale and hearty", to a lady who is not a relative, depending on the age and status one should address,??? or??? Your ladyship! O Fortunate one! O Sister!,???

When not to greet.

As Manu has it, only the senior in age should be greeted.

Apastamba: Wearing boots, chappals; with head covered or with hands otherwise occupied, one must not greet. One must not greet without sincerity, half-heartedly or casually. One must not greet a person at an inauspicious time or a guru who has swerved from the right path or when he is inattentive.

Shankha: One must not greet when carrying a water pitcher, while on the job of collecting alms or while carrying red flowers or when hands are smeared with blood? or food or when in impurity, while muttering or lying down.

A brahmin must not be greeted when his hands are occupied carrying sacrificial fuel, flowers, sacred grass (kusha), ghee, mud, food, sacred rice etc. or when he is preoccupied with muttering, sacrifice and so on. A heretic, a sinner, a non-observer of rules of piety, one who has committed one of the five atrocious crimes (panchamahapatakas), a rogue, a non-believer, or an ungrateful one never deserve greeting.

One who is running, who is out of his mind, who has just urinated, who is eating or who is suffering from a disease should not be greeted on the road.

One who is vomiting, yawning, brushing teeth, has his head anointed, is bathing or one with a garland in hand, a stranger, none who is weak, an enemy or a patient, a yogi engrossed in meditation, a person younger in age must not be greeted.

Shatatapa: A woman in her courses, or who has recently delivered, or who has killed her husband, or has aborted must not be greeted.

Consideration of age, as Manu has it only the senior in age should be greeted.

Determination of seniority:

Apastamba, Gautama and Manu: An acquaintance in one’s town/city older up to ten years is a friend but beyond that is considered senior. A scholar belonging to one’s own Vedic school or, a person belonging to the class of artists) older up to five years is a friend but beyond is considered a senior. Any Vedic scholar older by three years or less is a friend but beyond is considered senior.

In a family a brother etc. is like a friend if the difference in age is very little but if the difference is considerable, he is deemed senior.

Gautama, Bodhayana, Apastamba: A woman although younger in age is considered senior, if her husband is senior. Among sacrificial priests, father-in-law, maternal and paternal uncle, those younger in age should get up and initiate conversation.

Consideration of caste

Shatatapa, Apastamba: Only a brahmin deserves greetings. A kshatriya, although older must greet a brahmin. Between a ten-year-old brahmin and a hundred-year-old kshatriya, the brahmin is like a father to the kshatriya. A brahmin must never bow down to a kshatriya (and those of other castes) although the latter is superior in knowledge, achievement and merit.

Devala: If a brahmin bows down to a sudra inadvertently, he should anoint himself and bathe and then bow down to a hundred brahmins.

Consideration of place

Visnu: Reverential salutation (by bowing down) is not done even to brahmins in an assembly of any kind, sacrificial ritual or palace. Only (namaskar) greeting with folded hands is sufficient at these places.

Salutation to Guru???

Gautama, Apastamba: Vedic scholars should, in the morning touch the feet of the guru and then start reciting the Veda after him.

Salutation at guru’s feet crossing the hands

Manu: While offering salutation to the guru, one must lay his left hand on the left and right on the right foot of the guru.

Bodhayana: Touching one’s ears, focusing his mind, one should touch the guru's feet starting from below the knees.

Visnu: It is wrong to offer salutations with a single hand. It will make all the merit accumulated from one’s birth, null and void.

Salutation to guru’s wife

Guru’s wife, if of the same caste deserves similar salutation. If of a different caste, one should show respect by standing up and initiating talk.

Manu: One should offer reverential salutation to brother’s wife every day if she is of the same caste and to other ladies who are related only when they return from journey.

Manu, Gautama: One should not offer salutation at the feet of guru’s wife after she completes twenty or becomes mature enough to discriminate between good and evil if she is young. Nor should one indulge in anointing, bathing, rubbing hands and feet, or combing the hair of guru’s wife.

Manu: One should, after telling one’s name as per rule, prostrate on the ground before the guru’s wife, if she is young. One should do this every day. One may, however, reverentially touch her feet when meeting after a journey.

Salutation to mother

This may, by implication, mean that the same rule applies to one’s mother. However, in the light of a verse, where Sumitra tells Kausalya, ‘Soon, your son will return to Ayodhya and clasp your feet with his tender hands. One can offer salutations to one’s mother by clasping her feet’.

Salutation to husband

Gautama: When a lady offers salutations to a man, no rule is prescribed about announcing the name of the man. Whatever address is proper for the respective occasion, and custom may be used for the salutation.

Reward of salutation

Manu: One who practices such salutations to the elders is rewarded with four gains: long life, sharp intellect, a healthy body and success in all undertakings.

**Taking seat offered 2.3.34-36**

Only after directed, one must take a seat in the presence of elders.

**Son is a reflection of father 2.3.37-38**

Looking at Rama, Dasaratha felt it was his own reflection in the mirror. A son is like a mirror image of his father. Shakuntala also says to Dushyanta in Kalidasa "Look at your son who is your reflection in clear water of a lake. As Ahavaniya fire originates from Garhapatya so this one originates from you and is similarly duplicated although not different from you".

**Right to ancestral property 2.3.37-39**

Makhi diverts the discussion on dharma in the sense of law. Based on the three adjectives used for Kausalya and four for Rama, Makhi first discusses here status of sons born to a king from more than one wife and their right to ancestral property. The issues discussed are: status of the queen, caste of the queen and merits of the son born to her.

Several authorities like Manu, Gautama, Yajnavalkya, Mahabharata, Trikandamandana, Katyayana, Bodhayana, Apastamba, Ashvalayana are cited on various issues and side-issues.
