The purport of Kaikeyi is, ‘even the Vedas along with their six branches guide the self born Brahma in creating the universe. So I too will guide you today.’ The scriptures say, ‘Lord Brahma, having known the elements such as earth, water, space, air etc. from the Vedas, created them.’

**Kalyanam manyamanaha 2.14.63**

There could be three alternative interpretations: Sumantra thought Dasaratha would be glad to see Rama. Or, since Dasaratha was on the verge of death he thought that it was auspicious to behold Rama. Or, he might have thought that an auspicious time has occurred to both the gods and sages.

**Rama thinks differently about Kaikeyi 2.16.16-17**

On being questioned by Dasaratha whether Rama’s consecration in the absence of Bharata was agreeable to Kaikeyi, she would certainly be highly delighted over the prospect of the installation and would hasten the king to perform the ceremony about which Bharata might come to know later on.

**Rama's influence on Kaikeyi's behaviour (suggestive sense) 2.16.16- 24**

The word lakshayitva means having targeted. The commentator suggests that Kaikeyi had targeted Ravana’s death as the goal of Rama. Having been influenced by Rama only she behaved thus, as she is the well-wisher of Rama, the gods and the world. Since it was the last period of Dasaratha’s life, Kaikeyi made him chant Rama’s name, as she wished Dasaratha well. Without considering the condition of Dasaratha and with an intention to do favour to the world and to Rama, she could tactfully utter the word of exiling Rama. Thus she hastens Dasaratha so that the purpose of Rama’s incarnation can be soon accomplished.

Dasaratha has sent Sumantra as a messenger to Rama. At that time Sumantra was in a tense mood. One can imagine the state of the assembly by seeing the mental state of its minister. Sita tells Rama that she would like to join him in the performance of the rajasuya sacrifice. This utterance implies that she too is willing to accompany Rama to the forest. Since she has never in her life performed rajasuya with Rama and she, being the goddess, is the knower of the truth, certainly wishes to accompany Rama to the forest.

When Sita and Rama as speaker and spoken are divine beings, it can be understood that there may be a special meaning attached to their speech and understanding.

**Good wishes of well wishers prior to starting 2.16.21-24**

Invited by Dasaratha on the morning, Rama gets ready to go. Sita wishes him security from every possible danger. This suggests that elders or in their absence some dear and near ones should formally express good wishes for a person starting on an important mission.

In the "Anusasanaparva" of the Mahabharata: Jambavati greets Krishna, formally on Samba's birth. In the Aranyaparva Draupadi greets Arjuna

**People praise Rama 2.16.34-38; 2.17.1-10; 13-22**

Swastikas pronounce benedictions by raising shouts of victory. Sutas are chroniclers. Magadhas glorify descent.

**Rama's popularity 2.17.10-14**

(Coronation produces direct perception of Brahman and causes the highest bliss. Nothing will be dearer than this to the people, Even when Rama is out of sight he seems to be standing in front of all due to the impressions created by the experience of seeing bis fascinating form. So no man can withdraw his mind or eyes from Rama, what to speak of women. (svatmapyenam vigarhate)’.

‘A person not seen by Rama and a person who has not seen Rama with his physical eyes when he is present and with his mind’s eye when he is absent is reproached by his own soul. He who does not see Rama in his place and he whom Rama does not find in his country is reproached by one and all on the ground that he could not have the luclc of experiencing the supreme Brahman appearing in the form of Rama. He misses the opportunity of obtaining emancipation by viewing the Brahman, the liberator, directly and so will never be able to cross the ocean of worldly existence.

**Fruits obtained by seeing Rama's face 2.17.10, 11, 14**

If the people see Rama coming out of the palace of king Dasaratha, they would certainly obtain both pleasure and moksha, the final liberation. The intention of using ‘if’ in the verse suggests that ‘if’ they do not see Rama, the result may be opposite. Nothing else will be dearer to the citizens than the installation of Sri Rama on the throne, because they will gain real happiness with the reign of a good king.

There can be various reasons behind this attachment. One who does not behold Rama as his own self or as omnipresent or as a human being by the name Rama, wearing a particular dress and living in a particular place and one whom Sri Rama does not notice will not obtain the subject attached to the knowledge. This implies that one who beholds Rama will certainly obtain the subject attached to the knowledge. If one could not notice Rama as a human being, wearing a particular dress and living in a particular place, then he would certainly be despised in the eyes of the world. His self would reproach him that he is unfit to have the divine knowledge as he is devoid of Rama.

The poet uses Vinokti as the figure of speech. Thus he who possesses the knowledge of the lord is blessed. Since Rama is virtuous, he bestows kindness on all people, irrespective of their caste and age. Hence the entire world was devoted to him in thought, word and deed. The word chaturnam refers to both the four varnas i.e. the four castes and four ashramas.

**Paying homage 2.17.17**

Rama on his way to meet Dasaratha reverentially performed pradaxina at all the temples, road-crossings, and other places of worship. Gautama, Manu, and Vyasa in "Anusasanaparva" recommend homage even to cow, trees on the way.

**Obedience to king 2.18.1**

Father's order must be obeyed at any cost that does not involve harm to others. Visnu Puranam stresses implicit obedience to (father, mother, preceptor and) king: "All gods reside in a king and disobeying god is sacrilegious". In the "Adiparva" of the Mahabharata, Vidura tells Dhritarashtra: "Bhishma has advised you keeping your interest and welfare in mind. So follow it".

In the present context Dasaratha is father, preceptor, well-wisher and king,- all four in one. So his order has to be obeyed.

**Rama’s inquiry of Dasaratha’s state and Kaikeyi’s reply 2.18.9-26**

Rama cannot live even fora moment without serving the Icing’s pleasure and without obeying his order. For he was the cause of his birth and, therefore, a visible god Thus he turned to Kaikeyi and asked if she had said anything harsh due to anger or pride? Kaikeyi with no sense of shame (sunirlajja) asked Kama to go to the forest which will facilitate her son’s coronation.

**Kaikeyi’s opinion on truth 2.18.24**

Kaikeyi says to Rama, truth is the root of dharma. So he should see that his father does not do anything out of anger other than truth. By doing this he would rescue his father from adharma. It indicates that it is a great virtue for a son to oblige his father’s orders.

**Reason for Rama’s grief 2.18.27**

Like Dasaratha, Rama too knows that the boons of Kaikeyi were horrendous. But being a courageous person, he assures Kaikeyi. Rama’s grief is because Kaikeyi suspected him that he may violate the elders’ orders.

**Rama accepts to carry out his father’s promise 2.19.1-12**

Rama’s grief, if any, was because of the grief of those near and dear to him. His self-control knew no agony for, he was pure consciousness.

**Rama’s indifference to wealth that contradicts dharma 2.19.4-8**

Rama concedes to Kaikeyi's wish. Rama says to her, "I have no greed for money". A doubt may arise here that one has to pursue only dharma in life and that 'artha' (money) serves no purpose. Rut this is wrong. Money is necessary for pursuing dharma. Brihadaranyaka: "If I have to perform religious rituals, I have to have money"; In "Yuddhakanda" Lakshmana blames Rama for renouncing the throne as that leads to uprooting dharma. ???

Visnu Purama: Soma, sacrifice and food are all dependent on money. So one must earn money.

In the "Aranyaparva" of the Mahabharata Bhishma tells Yudhishthira,"charity, sacrifice, honouring saints and so on are enjoined by the shastras as the most important dharma which cannot be pursued without money.

Thus money is the important means of dharma. How did Rama then express indifference to it? The answer is, Rama is indifferent to the wealth that contradicts the principles of dharma. Manu says: ??? Pursuit of artha and êṁḍṁ which is likely to run contrary to the principles of dharma must be abandoned. Visnu Purana states: ??? One must earn money only in a way as would not contradict the principles of his dharma. Apastamba observes: ??? People detest him who pursues artha at the cost of everything else. Even those given to the pursuit of êṁḍṁ dislike them.

Makhi, therefore, concludes Rama’s renouncing the throne stands to reason.

**Rama’s vow 2.19.20-13**

Even though Dasaratha has not said it himself, what is not contradicted is accepted. Rama would walk into the forest. You are superior to me and \| am obedient to you’.

I won't delay. Only permit to stay till I bid farewell to my mother and console my wife, Sita\`, says Rama to Kaikeyi.

**Rama’s virtues 2.19.20-23**

‘I am not interested in material gains. I am devoted to immaculate righteousness.’ This statement of Rama shows that to remain balanced in happiness and sorrow and to remain in the path of salvation is quite natural to him.

One should obey his step-mother’s order. It is equal to his father’s. It is also equal to his own mothers. And if it is the orders of his parents then no question should be raised.

**Reason for Rama’s steadiness, control and agony 2.19.31-40**

Rama circumambulated the vessel in which the requisites for the projected consecration are kept. Because, it contained the sacred material like the holy water of Ganges etc.’ ‘Rama moved slowly without casting his eyes on the vessel. Tilaka expounds various reasons for Rama’s steadiness in doing so. He would have set his eyes on his journey to the forest. Or, like an actor who covers his own form while acting, Rama, too, keen on comforting the world and to be blessed by the world would have set his eyes on the vessel. Hence, he left the palace slowly.

Rama controlled his senses by concealing his inner sorrow. Having controlled his senses he did not reveal even an iota of the expression of sorrow and has borne the news of his departure to the forest. By keeping the world in his mind, he became neutral and did not reveal the news of losing the kingship even in his expressions.

Some opine that, if there was any pain in Rama, it was only because the news might bring scandal to Kaikeyi. According to Tilaka, the word ‘suhrujjanasya’ should be understood as Dasaratha and Kausalya. Rama was annoyed because it may bring disaster and end the life of both Dasaratha and Kausalya.

**Rama’s Virtue 2.20.1-4**

Rama is neither the object nor the agent of anger.

Discussion on Rama’s age at the time of exile

Dasaratha tells Viswamitra in Balakanda that Rama is less than sixteen. Sita tells Anasuya later that she lived in the palace of the \|kshvakus for twelve years, before proceeding to the forest. Therefore, Rama should be twenty eight at the time of leaving for the forest. How does Kausalya say that she waited for seventeen years? She might be right because here the second birth of Rama viz., during his Upanayana is intended. A kshatriya has his Upanayana at the age of eleven. The first birth from mother’s womb is not counted here. The second birth for the twice-born is. The second birth begins with the tying of ‘manju’ grass at the time of the thread ceremony when goddess Savitri is mother and the Acharya is father. That is why brahmanas, kshatriyas and vaisyas are called twice-born.

Mothers feel relieved after the son’s Upanayana because he attains maturity. When did Rama’s Upanayana take place? \|n the commentary on the Sutra, the ninth, tenth and eleventh years from the date of conception have been taken to be the meaning of ekadasesa which is plural. \|n Kama’s case, Upanayana was conducted in the eighth year and after Upanayana, seventeen years passed. Rama went into the forest in his twenty fifth year.

Dasaratha tells Viswamitra that Rama was Unasodasavarsa i.e. twelve years. Maricha tells Ravana in Aranyakanda, 'Rama is a twelve-year-old and has not been trained in martial arts’. So Rama was only twelve at the time of his marriage. Sita tells Ravana who appears in the guise of a mendicant, ‘I resided at the palace of the Ikshvakus for twelve years’, Again, ‘\|n the thirteenth year of our married life, the king sent for Rama in order to tell him about Kaikeyi's boons.’ She also says referring to the beginning of life in the forest, ‘My husband who is shining with valour is twenty five’. Hence Rama was twenty five at the time of entering the forest.

**Kausalya’s reaction to Rama's announcement of his exile 2.20.9-23.**

Smelling the head and forehead of a child is said to be a mark of pure affection.

Rama said to Kausalya, ‘What I am going to reveal will cause untold agony to you, no less than to Sita and Lakshmana’. (However, it does not grieve me as I am pure consciousness).

**Rama seeks Kausalya’s blessings 2.20.13-34**

Rama said that he was worthy of vistara or a seat made of twenty-five blades of darbha grass. The royal seat did not fascinate him. The inhabitants of the forest Dandaka, are threatened by rakshasas. "Now, I must go to the forest to free them of their fright. I pray my departure would not cause sorrow to you, to Vaidehi, and Lakshmana. Abandoning amisa or the objects of royal enjoyment, I will dwell in the forest leading the life of an ascetic, said Rama.

The commentator notes that the word amisa here does not refer to meat. This is used in the sense of an object of enjoyment.

**Rama reveals his decision to leave Ayodhya 2.20.28-31**

"I am now leaving Ayodhya to proceed to the Dandaka forest. Time has come that I should use a mat of kusha grass - vistara (a mat meant for those who perform penance and it is made of twenty-five blades of kusha grass)."

**Definition of the word Vistara 2.20.28**

The word vistara means a kind of seat used by the ascetics. Tilaka quotes the smruti text and explains the term vistara as a mat made of twenty-five blades of kusa grass.

**Kausalya’s grief 2.20.32-55**

It is believed that when a woman gives birth to a son, she enjoys a double advantage: One, her husband would be pleased to oblige her. Second, there is that joy of looking at the growing son. But I am undone by the order of the monarch. My grief is endless. It is beyond description."

**Kausalya’s grief 2.20.38**

Kausalya says she was always destined to suffer. She has neither the love and affection of her husband nor the royal jewels and dresses. She was waiting for her son placed in power to make up the loss.

There can be no worse misery to a woman than hearing words of scorn from a co-wife.

**Age of Sri Rama 2.20.45**

From the word ‘jatasya’ Tilaka interprets Rama’s age. A reference to (I- 20-2) of the Valmiki Ramayana would reveal that according to King Dasaratha himself Sri Rama was less than sixteen years i.e. fifteen years of age when he accompanied the sage Viswamitra and was eventually married with Sita. Tilaka further mentions a sloka from Padmapurana, which reveals that he had spent twelve years of his married life before the emperor proclaimed his intention of installing him on the throne as Prince Regent. (Uttara..ccl.xix. 181-183). Sri Rama’s age could not, therefore, be only seventeen years at the time of his exile. Hence the word ‘jatasya’ in the verse (45) has been taken in the sense of ‘born for a second time'. It indicates the investiture with the sacred thread. This must have presumably taken place at the age of ten in as much as it is laid down in the smritis that a kshatriya boy must be invested with the sacred thread at the age of ten to eleven years: ekadase va rajanyam. Hence Sri Rama could be seventeen plus ten or twentyseven years of age at the time of leaving for the forest.’

Since Rama has completed seventeen years of age after his birth for the second time in the form of investiture with the sacred thread, Kausalya hoped she could live happily after Sri Rama’s consecration. And now that his installation has been cancelled, how could she see Kaikeyi’s face?

According to Panini’s sutra, igyanaha samprasaranam (1.1.45), Rama’s age can be calculated as double ten and add seven which comes to twentyseven.

Kausalya mentions Rama’s age as seventeen years because of her distressed condition or an emotional expression of the great poet Valmiki.

**Lakshmana’s anger 2.21.1-29**

Lakshmana vows to annihilate the enemies in the palace. But Rama declares his unexceptional faith in dharma and especially in truth. Which brings out his mental fortitude even in worst adversity. Lakshmana says, our father has grown too old and has lost the sense of right and wrong and has been prevailed upon to take this wrong decision by his pet wife. When so pressed, in his love for her, he is apt to take inappropriate decisions, not one or two, but hundreds. Hence, I declare that his orders need not be accepted or respected."

Asamanja was banished to the forest by his father for his lawless acts. But what offence has Rama committed that he should be ordered to go to the forest? I will slay my father who has become a slave to his lust. Even the worst sinner cannot complain against Rama. Rama is god-like, self-controlled, kindly even to enemies like Kaikeyi. He is, in truth, dharma incarnate. When it is so, which father, excepting Dasaratha could think of abandoning a righteous son like Rama who is free from any guilt? A loving father forgives his son. But our father finds fault with his exceptionally faultless son.

Which son will heed the words of a king who has slipped into a second childhood? Even before things go beyond your hands, get, as announced already, the consecration done. Take up the reins of administration. I will stand by you. While I hold my bow and arrow and stand by you, who will be able to wag his tail? If any one, whoever he may be, comes in the way of your kingship, I will wipe him out with my sharp shafts." If that father of ours, prevailed upon by that evil-hearted Kaikeyi, becomes inimical to your interest, I will end him or send him to prison. What right has he got to give away the royal glory according to his whims and fancies? He has no such powers."

**Rama reiterates his devotion to dharma 2.21.1**

Rama reiterates his devotion to dharma in following father's words. Implicit obedience to father is dharma says "Anusasanaparva" of the Mahabharata Rama also advises Lakshmana to give up his natural reaction as a kshatriya and follow the dictates of dharma. He reminds Kausalya of her duty as a wife (pativrata): Wife must stay with her husband throughout his life and after his death with the son. Manu says the same thing:

**Kausalya’s justification in dissuading Rama 2.2 1.1-28**

Kausalya told Rama that the kingdom had come to him according to the rules of dharma, and it could be controlled by them (Rama and Kausalya). On what grounds did the king want to give it to Kaikeyi? When the objection of how could one disobey his father was raised by Rama, Kausalya said that those were not his father’s words but the words of her co-wife. Further, she told him about Kasyapa who reached heaven by rendering service to his mother. "\| shall not permit you to go. I shall vow not to take food or water if I am separated from you" tells Kausalya.

**Interpretation of Lakshmana’s reaction 2.21.11-12**

The word pakshyaha means ‘maternal uncle.’ Lakshmana says this is not the time for soft approach. If pleased with Kaikeyi and instigated by her, the king becomes their enemy then let him be made captive or let him be killed. This harshness can be explained with reference to the time. It was the transition between two yugas i.e. Treta and Dwapara, the influence of adharma made Lakshmana say so. Tilaka applies the same reason to Kaikeyi’s behaviour and the fraudulent killing of Vali by Rama. According to scriptures one can punish even the elders, if one commits a mistake. So Lakshmana cannot be faulted. The words of Kausalya, however, reveal her disapproval of Lakshmana’s reaction.

**Myth of the ocean 2.21.28**

Once the ocean, the spouse of deities presiding over the rivers, underwent hellish torture as a result of Brahmanicide through unrighteousness in the form of inflicting suffering on his own mother.

**Rama's rejoinder 2.21.29-53**

"I have no strength to break the promise of my father. Your words are also to be respected and obeyed. But father’s words came first and so they have greater power. Both cannot be obeyed together. So my father’s order should be carried out first. Since father’s orders have greater authority, great people of yore have performed such acts as killing of cow and mother" said Rama.

By referring to the sons of Sagara who met with death, it is indicated that one should obey the father’s order even at the cost of one’s life. And spendingjust a few years in the forest is not at all a big thing. Parasurama slaughtered his mother with his own hands. "\| am doing what has been done earlier by people. \| shall obey my father’s word even if it brings grief to my mother," Rama observed.

Turning to Lakshmana and Kausalya, Rama said, "I am following truth even though it causes you some grief. You grieve because you know not the secret of truth and because of your love for me. "Dharma is the greatest among purusarthas (goals of life). Truth is established in dharma. It is the best reason. \| shall see that my father’s words are firmly fixed in dharma. \| take a vow to do so. Since I have vowed, \| shall not transgress. Give up this idea of occupying the kingdom, killing father, if necessary. My decision, which is bent on implementing my father’s orders, should be supported by you". Like an elephant driven out by people waving burning faggots at night enters into darkness roaring, Kausalya’s pitiable sobbing and lament only augmented Rama’s anguish.

It is said that Dharmasastra is a bigger authority than Arthasastra. Dasaratha was not only father but also guru to Rama as he taught him archery. So Rama says he cannot but fulfil the king’s promise. "Since Dasaratha is your husband" Rama tells Kausalya, "he is your resort and not me and your fate is the same as that of Dasaratha".

**Importance of obeying father’s orders 2.21.41**

To Rama the command of his father is supreme as it is based on righteousness. It means the command of his father leads to righteousness in the form of penance and service to the ascetics in the forest. The word uttama means ‘it brings pleasure to all the three worlds.’

Rama speaks to Kausalya and Lakshmana the philosophy of life 2.21.56-64

Valmiki appreciates Rama’s righteousness. Even in such a critical situation, the way he respects dharma is exceptional. He himself is the embodiment of dharma. He is the supreme Brahman.

One should restrain oneself from unrighteous acts and pursue the established path of dharma for he who hankers after worldly prosperity divorced from righteousness, becomes hateful.

**Importance of dharma 2.21.57**

According to Rama, artha and kama i.e., material gain and worldly pleasures, follow dharma or righteousness just as one’s wife, being obedient, becomes helpful in the discharge of one’s religious obligations such as hospitality to guests, in giving worldly pleasures and in promoting prosperity in the other world by procreating a son. Hence dharma alone is important and it should be protected.

**Dictates of destiny 2.22.3-30**

Rama advises Lakshmana not to entertain ill feelings towards Kaikeyi, for it is all the dictate of destiny. Sita later echoes these words to Anasuya. In the "Vanaparva" of the Mahabharata Yudhishthira tells Yaksha that he loves both Kunti and Madri equally and hence Yaksha must revive his step-brother Nakula, too. One must never blame one’s misfortune on others but should consider it a result of his own past deeds.

Aranyaka says: When difficulties befall even the wise blame the god, for they do not know their own previous deeds. In the "Yuddhakanda" Sita advises Hanuman not to kill the female demons in the Ashokavana as her own deeds in the past were responsible for her misfortune.

**Providence 2.22.4; 15-19**

Rama denies the instrumentality of Kaikeyi in his banishment and lays the entire blame on his own fate. Since Rama is the supreme Lord, it can be understood that all that has happened was on account of his decision.

Rama says, ‘Providence alone is responsible for my banishment’. In order to remove the misery of the gods Rama’s consecration had to be cancelled. It cannot be his misfortune as it is not applicable to the supreme Lord.

Kaikeyi, being a princess of gentle disposition and possessing virtuous qualities, would not speak such harsh words before her husband, unless she is influenced by providence.

**It is Fate that has led Kaikeyi to decide otherwise 2.22.15-30**

Rama says fate is the cause of change in Kaikeyi’s attitude. "She is generous by nature until this moment and we have experienced her kindness and her love. Not only Kaikeyi, I am also under the control of fate says Rama, "That which cannot be imagined, that which cannot be altered by people is an act of fate. Reverse has happened (Viparyayah Praptah) in my case as well as in Kaikeyi’s. In my case it is the loss of kingdom which was on the palm of my hand. In the case of Kaikeyi, it is the disappearance of the motherly love she had for me."

"How to accept the power of fate? What proof is there in the existence of fate? questions Lakshmana. Kama replies" Who can fight with fate whose acts are not seen except in the results. Who can stop that fate? "The meaning is, fate can only be inferred, not interfered with, because it is seen only in results. It cannot be fought with and hence it is power. Inference is the means to know its existence. So fate is powerful and human effort is incidental. Bondage and liberation are the act of fate.

This confirms the higher strength of fate. Viswamira and other risis who strictly adhered to rules of conduct were defeated by desire and anger.

When what has been begun is abandoned and an unintended action is taken up without any visible cause, that is definitely an act of fate.

"The kingdom is a means of dharma through just governance of the people. Dwelling in the forest (Vanavasa Mahodaya) is a help to austerities. But, between these two, there is a difference. Since there will be no worry about right and wrong actions to be taken and also since it will help me observe austerities and obey father’s orders, dwelling in the forest is the most desirable thing" observed Rama.

"I am hit by fate", said Rama conclusively.

**Providence is supreme 2.23.1-4**

Rama is unalloyed sattva (i.e. unmixed goodness). Lakshmana has rajas combined with sattva. He argues that man’s efforts should score over providence. It is human weakness to declare providence pre-eminent in all matters.

The Amrita Kataka of Madhavayogin states that like Balarama, Lakshmana was the incarnation of Shesha-Shabda-Brahma during the avatara of Visnu. There is, however, one difference: While both were Suddhabrahman (pure consciousness), lord Krishna displayed his power of illusion (maya), while the divine Rama appeared in flesh and blood.

Pondering over the exhortation of Rama with his head bent down, Lakshmana was oscillating, as it were, between dejection and happiness, dejection, because Rama’s consecration was cancelled and happiness, because Rama with steadfastness upheld righteousness (dharma) even at that juncture. Rama was by no means weak, even when he declared that providence is supreme. Lakshmana felt astonished and angry. This brings out Lakshmana’s inner nature i.e. a combination of sattva and rajas. Madhavayogin quotes the Bhagavadgita: ‘Even one who know the self acts in conformity with his inner nature’ (111.33).

When Lakshmana remembers Rama’s exhortation of Buddhiyoga and the supremacy of providence, Lakshmana is happy. But when he is a victim of his inner nature, he gets disturbed and feels anguish out of anger. His inner nature getting the better of himself, he knits his eyebrows and hisses like an enraged mighty cobra in its hole.

**Lakshmana’s angry reaction 2.23.1-39**

Lakshmana was in the midst of joy and sorrow, joy to see the fortitude of his elder brother, but sorrow to see him abandon the kingdom (dukha harsayor madhyam jagama). Lakshmana moved his hands and his head up and across due to excessive anger. He was looking across through the corners of his eyes.

Lest people should ask, how can this Kama protect us when he does not even obey his father’s order? Rama decides to walk the path of dharma, he decides to accept the dictates of destiny.

But Lakshmana reacts differently. "How could a paragon of kshatriyas like you extol fate like a rustic? Are you not sinning against dharma by obeying the two sinners, Kaikeyi and Dasaratha? "There are people who use performance of dharma as a guise. Clever people conceal their sins under cover of religious behaviour in this world. How is it that you do not understand their clever ploy to stop your coronation? If Dasaratha and Kaikeyi had not planned to rob your kingdom earlier, the boon should have been granted and realized long ago. Why now? This is malafide and malicious. Therefore, I do not think that the story of boon is true" Lakshmana observed.

"Is it dharma to coronate the younger brother ignoring the rightful claims of the elder? Why should you think sin might fall on you, if you disobey your father? Is it not a fact that this act was planned with ulterior motives?

Lakshmana wants to take law into his hands while Rama sticks to the rules of dharma.

**Lakshmana, the incarnation of adisesha 2.23.1**

Since Lakshmana was the incarnation of Adisesha, the serpent-king, he was endowed with ‘tamoguna’ i.e. ignorance. Whice Rama was full of satvaguna: The word iva suggests the tamasik nature of Lakshmana.

Lakshmana pondered with his head bent low while Sri Rama spoke to him. This indicates Lakshmana’s acceptance of Rama’s opinion.

**Lakshmana discredits fatalistic attitude of Rama 2.23.5-39**

"Look here, brother, this attitude has appeared at a wrong time. I think there are two thoughts overcoming you. One, there should not be any diversion from the path of dharma: two, we should not set a bad example. You are agitated lest people should think a prince who is disloyal to his own aged father is not expected to rule his subjects righteously. It is an utter delusion in your mind.

"O, mighty brother, for a strong man it is possible to overpower providence. Why do you say nothing can be done against Fate?"

Lakshmana now takes up the question of dharma. "They are seeking, through fraud, their selfish ends. Why did the giver of the boon and the receiver keep quiet so far? Even before the preparations were made for the installation, they could have thought over it. They have hatched a big fraud. You are the worst victim. You are righteous while they are pretenders of righteousness.

I cannot brook the installation of any one other than you, for you are the eldest among the princes, and the best in virtue. You accepted the office of the crown prince first and now you reject it. It is not your devotion to dharma but your aquiscence to infatuation. Had it not been so, how are you going to redeem the pledge of the king, which according to me is untrue and unreal? You can do, undo and outdo by your valour-anything. But you are now subdued by Kaikeyi. Interruption to your installation has no righteousness in it. It is sheer machination, silently evolved by the king and Kaikeyi.

"Granting that father’s boon to Kaikeyi is true and his pledge to fulfil it is also true, you believe that this is also caused by providence. I have no faith, whatsoever, in such a decree of Fate. Who has an upper hand - Fate or human effort? I am prepared to display my valour and let those people who foiled your coronation know that fate can be fought. Neither the guardians of the quarters nor the denizens of all the three worlds can block your installation today. How can our father do?

"I promise I shall guard you as well as the kingdom, even as the shores guard the security of the seas. Let me not get into the Hall of Fame meant for the valiant in heaven, if I fail to do so.

"With my sharp arrows shining like a flash of lightning, I am prepared to face my enemy, even if it should be Indra, the wielder of the thunder-bolt. If there should be a war, the earth will be thickly set with dead elephants, horses and soldiers of my enemies. When I enter the war-field well-equipped to fight, how can any one among the enemies remain proud of his fighting ability? Today, I will show the effectiveness of my arrows. I will stop all those who try to interrupt your consecration. O, my dear brother, tell me how to proceed to bring the globe under your benign control. I am at your beck and call."

**Superiority of valour over destiny 2.23.6-40**

Lakshmana advocates superiority of valour over destiny. The Mahabharata says, one obtains everything by valour and not by luck. Rama stresses importance of destiny while Lakshmana that of Valour. But there is no inherent contradiction here as destiny without human effort or human effort without destiny is equally futile. The two are interdependent. The Mahabharata writes, there can be no fruit without seed and no seed without fruit. Similarly human effort and fortune are interdependent.

Makhi, however, is of the opinion that destiny is superior to human effort. He quotes Visnu Parana has it, everybody aspires for kingdom and for wealth. But only those favoured by fortune achieve it.

The Mahabharata observes, human effort should be directed to turn destiny in one's favour.

**Lakshmana’s comments on fate 2.23.5-13**

Lest people should think that a prince who is disloyal to his father cannot rule his subjects righteously and also if he violated his father’s words, they may also violate theirs, he decided to go on exile. This is what Lakshmana tells Rama. Being foremost among the kshatriyas, Rama should not give importance to fate which is indeed ineffectual, and impotent.

The story of the boons, Lakshmana suspects, is mere fabrication and its purpose is only to deceive Rama. If the story were true, it would have been granted much before the preparations for the installation had taken place.

The act of consecrating the younger son and banishing the eldest is against dharma. Lakshmana asks Rama to forgive him his audacity for saying this. Rama inclined to accept the office of Prince Regent and later foregoing it is repellent to him. Of all persons only Rama can fulfil the wishes of those who call themselves parents but are really enemies. Manasapi which means ‘even in thought’. Leave aside implementing their desire, Lakshmana suggests, drop the idea of going into exile. What he means is, kings certainly go and reside in the forest, but not before they commit the subjects to the care of their sons or successors.

**Lakshmana desires Rama to counter his fate 2.23.16-41**

"Ravana has hindered your consecration which your parents strive for. I will crush him. I am strong enough to repulse the attack by the monster king. Get consecrated. I will bring the world under your control,"

Rule the kingdom for thousands of years. When the term of your kingship is over, you may leave for the forest in conformity with the tradition of our lineage. Thereafter, your sons will protect the subjects without interruption," says Soumitri.

**Lakshmana’s view on Rama’s exile 2.23.25**

(1) Dasaratha’s mind is averse to the life of Vanaprastha on account of passionate attachment to his wife. (2) Rama's intention to go to the forest is due to the fear that violation of the king’s words might result in political turmoil. (3) If dharma is the foremost consideration, Rama should rule the kingdom, not give it up.

**Rama’s reply to Lakshmana 2.23.41**

The word satpathah means ‘the path trodden by the righteous.’ A son qualifies to be one by following three obligations: One, by obeying his father’s order, two, by offering sraddha, and three, by offering pinda i.e. lump of cooked rice offered to the manes at the obsequies at Gaya'.

The word nibodha means ‘to know’, know by remembering the extra¬ordinary events that follow at the time of incarnation.

**Rama makes Kausalya understand righteousness alone wins 2.24.1-9**

It is only righteousness that wins - never unrighteousness: First, Kausalya felt sad that Rama should live in the forest on roots and fruits, while ministers and servants partook excellent food living in the palace.

She says the fire of grief is burning up her emaciated body, the fire fanned by the wind of Rama’s impending absence and fed by the fuel of anguish, nourished by tears, covered with the smoke of sighs.

**Superiority of mother’s order over that of father 2.24.2**

Kausalya bemoans her fate and Rama consoles her reminding her once again that it is her first and foremost duty to take care of Dasaratha. Dharma demands this from him as well as from her. Kausalya tells him to act as per her wish since carrying out mother's order is also dharma. This creates a contradiction.

In the "Vanaparva" and "Anusasanaparva" it is said that one should carry out the orders of parents and preceptors even though they contradict dharma. Manu writes: ??? And Bharata ??? Gautama and Apastamba ??? also support this view.

Superiority of father's order:

· Visnu Purana: Father is recognized as the guru of all gurus.

· Purana Samucchaya: Between father and mother the former is superior as seed is more important than soil.

· Bharata (Mokshadharma): Father is the highest idol for humans even compared to mother.

In the present case however, while both father and mother are gurus, the former is self-dependent while the latter is not so as is obvious from Manu's words, ??? Hence obedience to mother is not justifiable especially when her order contradicts that of father. Statements asserting importance of mother have significance only in the context of service and protection. Bharata writes: ??? Thus here father's order must be given preference over mother's wish.

Rama's words, ??? convey the same import. Bharata: ‘Father's orders must be obeyed without question. It washes away even the sins of the son’.

Thus it is imperative to look after the mother but it is equally essential to obey the father even if that means killing the mother. It is the import of the story of Chirakarika (one who procrastinates) in Mokshadharma. Ordered by his father to kill the mother who had violated rules of conduct Chirakarika keeps thinking, being baffled by the contradiction in the two principles of dharma-one that sought implicit obedience to father and the other, cites the mother: He finally concludes that in the matter of obedience father must be given preference.

All this justifies Rama’s obedience to Dasaratha even though meant disobedience to mother.

When Kausalya did not give up, Rama binds her by oath in the name of his life and asks her to do the swastyayana, the formal ceremony of wishing well to the dear and near one when he is about to start on an important mission.

**Rama exhorts Kausalya on the duties of a devoted wife 2.24.10-17**

"I consider it a cruelty on the part of a wife to desert her husband, especially in his old age. If you desert your husband, you will not be happy either here or hereafter. You should serve him by all means until he is alive. He is the king for us, to you the husband and an eminent model of truthfulness to the world. Hence, both you and I should obey his words. I have served my father well. After my return from the forest, I will serve you also with devotion.

"With Bharata attending on you, Kaikeyi’s anger will not be effective. I pray, look after my father tenderly in my absence. He is old and he cannot bear this terrible agony of my separation brought on him.

"By serving one’s husband, a wife secures the highest heaven. Just as Gayatri is most sacred to a man, service to husband is most sacred to a woman. A wife may forget to meditate on God or worship the family god but, if she forgets to serve her husband, there is no heaven for her. This is righteousness in the case of a married woman.

**Rama’s suggestion to Kausalya 2.24.26**

Rama suggests Kausalya to serve her husband. As a brahmin’s duty is to chant Gayatri mantra, so a woman should serve her husband. Except by serving her husband, a woman cannot expiate her sins, even though she practices spiritual observances.

**Kausalya’s reactions at Rama’s departure 2.24.38**

Kausalya realized that Rama was following dharma and his incarnation was intended for protecting gods and sages.

**Rites of benediction before departure 2.25.1-47**

"May the presiding deities of the seasons, measures of time like kala (equivalent to one minute) and kastha i.e. 1 /30thof a kala (two seconds) grant you happiness!

"May your pathways (agamas) be propitious and may your truthfulness never fail.

**Emotional identity of Valmiki 2.25.39-40**

The verbs uvacha and avadat used in these two verses give the same meaning ‘said’. Tilaka says the reason for repetition of the words with the same meaning is due to an emotional identity of the poet with the situation.

**Reason for Rama’s distress 2.26.7**

Rama behaved like a subdued person because of the presence of Sita who was the incarnation of prakriti or ‘primordial nature’ which is called maya. The commentator poses a question here, ‘If Rama was God why should he appear pale due to sorrow?’ And he answers, Rama looks sorrowful out of sympathy for the distressed. So he appeared as if he was distressed but was not really so.

With the first boon Rama was ordered to go to the forest and with the second, Bharata was to be installed as a Prince Regent. If implies that Bharata would be installed by Rama as it cannot happen without his consent, he being the elder.

Sita should not think Kausalya would not be honoured in the absence of Rama, for it is dharma that rules.

**Sita's surprise 2.26.9-19**

"How is it that the Pushya-Ratha, the lovely gold chariot drawn by the four dainty horses is not seen? (A Pushya-Ratha is an elegant small chariot made of gold and a symbol of royal glory and paraphernalia of the king. It moves in front of the royal procession heralding the royal chariot. It is not used in a war.) How is it that the majestic royal elephant resembling a huge dark cloud and caparisoned with finery is absent? How is it there is no Bhadrasana carrier in front of you? (Bhadrasana is an auspicious seat. It is a royal symbol and an official of the palace carries it in front of the royal procession.)"

**Rama tells Sita about his father’s command 2.26.19-27**

"My dear, you may describe my virtues to Bharata without emphasis on my exile. My virtues will lessen his stress on my separation. Further, do not praise his excellence exceedingly. He may not brook his glorification, as he has attained greatness by virtue of me."

**Wife’s dharma when husband is away 2.26.29**

While the husband is away, the wife should pass her days by performing religious deeds, vows and fasting etc. Shandali and Draupadi say the same words in the "Anusasanaparva".

**Justification of Sita to follow Rama into the forest 2.27.1-23**

Valmiki says that Sita’s love for her husband is not marred by any dislike or disgust. It is heightened when she says. "O prince, you are the best among men, yet you tender this commonplace advice? Your exhortation belittles my stature. I am amused to hear them. They are a big joke."

**Sita's justification to accompany Rama 2.27.3-23; 2.29. 1-18**

A father enjoys the fruits of his own deeds, not the deeds of his son. But the wife, considered half her husband, has to enjoy the fruits of the deeds of her husband, because they share the responsibilities of each other’s actions. "Therefore", observes Sita, "the order given to you applies to me also".

The second argument is, the husband is the last resort for a wife and not father or mother.

Third, "There is no sin in me which makes you abandon me" says Sita.

Fourth, she should not be left behind because she is eternally related to him. Whether the husband is in a palace or in the skies, his wife follows him like a shadow.

"At the time of my marriage my father said to you, "This is my daughter Sita. She will be your companion in doing dharma. She will always follow you like your shadow" pleaded Sita.

Long ago I had heard in my father’s residence palmists and astrologers (laksanibhyah) say that I would have to live in a forest". This was Sita’s fifth argument.

Sixth, I know that there are difficulties in forest life, but they are insurmountable only for the weak who have not their senses under control and who crave for pleasures. These are not difficulties for people like you and me", observed Sita.

Seventh, "I have a strong desire to visit the hermitages on the banks of Ganga. Eighth," I like to serve you when you are in the forest" and last but not least, I will also be purified by following you because husband is my god (suddhatman), argued Sita. A woman given in marriage belongs to the husband here and hereafter.

**Wife’s dharma 2.27.4**

Sita tells Rama that she will not stay back as according to dharma wife must always stay with the husband. In the "Vanaparva" Damayanti stays with Nala deprived of his kingdom, wealth and everything else including his clothes.

**Casting away envy 2.27.8**

Rama should not envy Sita’s courage in voluntarily offering to accompany him to the forest. Though much younger, she displays enviable courage.

**Rama dissuades Sita 2.28.3**

Rama tries to dissuade Sita by describing the hardships of forest life fit for Vanaprastha. Manu, Apastamba, Gautama, Kurma Purana: A doubt may arise here, how being a householder Rama has to follow the duties of a Vanaprasthi. When Rama departs for the forest Kaikeyi gives him tree-barks etc. due to which he is required to follow only some and not all of the duties of a Vanaprasthin. Otherwise eating animal flesh, living with wife Sita, returning to Ayodhya and resuming charge as a king would not stand to reason.

**Sita’s reply to Rama 2.29.7-10**

Sita tells Rama, ‘when you asked me to adjust to Bharata’s reign, it is understood that a woman cannot survive in the absence of her husband.’

The second version is ‘though you have explained the difficulties of forest life I need not hesitate to accompany you to the forest as I am prabala bhartruka’, i.e. ‘the one who possesses a heroic husband’.

Since Sita already knew that she has to live in the forest, as foretold by the astrologer before her marriage, she can live in the forest without any hesitation. The prediction of the astrologer doesn’t become otherwise. Since it was by Rama’s order (he being omnipresent) the astrologers have predicted Sita’s future.

Not only the astrologer’s prediction but the incident of cancellation of the installation which happened only the night before occurred only because of Rama’s order. The purport of the commentator is to emphasize Rama’s omnipresent nature.

**Hidden meaning in Sita’s reply 2.29.11-12**

Sita says, ‘let the prediction of the astrologer or the brahmins come true.’ The word dvijaha i.e. ‘a brahmin’ refers to Ravana, since in Swetadipika Ravana has predicted that he would be killed because of Lakshmi, and in that sense Sita says ‘let his (Ravana’s) words become true’. No doubt forest life is fearful, but those who have no control over their minds panic. The inner sense is ‘Rama should not be concerned over the hardships of forest life for Sita as he has self-control.

The first meaning is ‘Sita is happy at the prospect of serving Rama during his exile’.The second meaning:‘Sita is delighted imagining the deeds of Rama i.e. killing the demons in the forest.’

**The purpose of Sita accompanying Rama 2.29.16**

Sita tells Rama, ‘by accompanying you to the forest with loving devotion, I shall surely be absolved from all guilt. ’The intention is, ‘she would be freed from the scandals of the world, if she accompanies Rama.’

**Sita’s sorrow 2.29.23; 2.30.34**

Tilaka opines that Sita was not really sorrowful. The word ‘sthapayanti iva ’ confirms the view. It means, she was moistening the earth, as it was burning, with tears dropped from her eyes. According to the commentator, ‘as the word batha itself indicates extreme sorrow, there is no poetic defect in using a few words to reveal the sorrow of Sita.

The word pavi means ‘the fearful world’ and tra means ‘to protect’. Hence, by joining the two, ‘pavitram’ gives the meaning ‘that which protects us from the fearful world.’ Further, it is applicable to the inhabitants of the earth, not to those of the other two worlds.

**Ingenious interpretation of Sita's words 2.30.1-47**

In order to obtain permission to live in the forest Sita said "O Rama, had my father known you are really a woman in a man’s body be would not have given me to you in marriage. In the Visnupurana it is said: sa eva vasudevoyam saksat purusauoyate striprayṁm itarat sarvam jagadbrahmapurassaram. Which means, ‘only that Vasudeva is the real Man. All others in the world starting with Brahma are only feminine’. So the meaning is, ‘my father, king of Videha, obtained you as his son-in-law and considered every one other than you a woman in the guise of man. Why did he do so? Sinse you are so timid, my father was under an illusion to think so. Or, if the words are separated thus, ramaja, amataram prapya purusa, vigraham he ramaja, one who is born to make the world happy, Amataram striyam, the woman in the form of a step-mother, He Purusa, O supreme man, Prapya, keeping in mind as the target, Vigraham quarrel. The idea is Sita’s father Janaka did not know that the controversy would be raised by Kaikeyi. Sita persists Rama should not even then go to the forest, leaving her. Or, ramajamataram is one word. Purusavigraham is one who takes up the devotees specially for granting his grace. Ramajamataram, a son-in-law who is the very embodiment of bliss. This is substantiated by the Sruti: ramante yogino nanate etc. The idea is, "Did my father, Janaka, think that women, sons, friends etc., and the heaven as true? No, he knew all this to be void and became full of bliss. Thus, being the cause of bliss of all beings, how and why do you cause me anguish", questioned Sita.

"This world says there is brilliance of the burning Sun in Rama. But the world does not know it is not there and it is not at all seen." Or, Sita is afraid she scolded Rama out of ignorance. So she rectifies her mistake by saying that the world says so. The world is ignorant and so it says that there is no splendour in Rama like in the shining Sun or the world is telling a lie. "I cannot tolerate this" said Sita.

Sita tells Ramṁ, "Your anger is equal to the fire of the final annihilation; why are you afraid about my following you into the forest? There is no reason for leaving me alone".

"I am like Savitri a devoted wife of Satyavan, Dyumatsena’s son. Therefore, I will come with you." And even then when Rama does not relent, Sita says "Like an actor who lives on the earnings of his wife you want to give me to others. Or, why do you want to give away this ancestral kingdom to Bharata and others like an actor? This is most improper for you."

Reacting to Rama’s earlier statement, she says Rama may become an obedient follower and helper of Bharata, because he speaks what is congenial for his younger brother to whose coronation he is bound. But she is not going to act according to Bharata’s whims and fancies. She will be obedient to Rama only. "I will not be weary in the forest path and it will be just like strolling in gardens that are soft like cotton and wool" said Sita.

"There is no such happiness even when I sit on a silky mats, or a beautiful bed as I have when sitting on grasslands with you on which kusumbha flowers are strewn." Wherever she be with Rama it will be heaven and without him it will be hell.

"What you have decided now is like that of one who has an unperturbed mind, a yogin. Your accompanying me is dharma. Dharma, was the duty of wives who followed the sage-kings into the forest. Follow me as Suvarcala follows the Sun", said Rama.

Rama observes that his departure for the forest was a foregone decision. "I will surely go at any cost. The king’s word, reinforced by his promise, sends me into the forest. I am bent on obeying my father’s order. I cannot transgress dharma which lays down that one should obey one’s father. Where there is the trio of mother, father and teacher, there are the three worlds. The idea is that by the service rendered to the mother, father and teacher, one obtains the fruit of the worship of all gods in the three worlds. So there is nothing holier than these three". Or, the word pavitram means ‘one which saves a person from samsara which is extremely fearsome.

\[The commentator gives far-fetched explanations to some words in this sarga, because he does not find it palatable when Sita scolds Rama. The interpretation may be ingenious, but it does not appear to be what Valmiki wanted to say.\]

**Sita's loyalty 2.30.3-6**

One must not find fault with Sita for speaking such harsh words to Rama. It is out of her love for Rama and not with the intention of insulting him that she speaks here harshly. Sita wants Rama to compare her with Savitri following Satyavan even when Yama was taking away his body. Why in spite of there being many other devoted wives Savitri alone is cited as a model of loyalty to husband. The reason is that she drew the entire family out of misery and raised their status by her devotion to husband. Makhi has quoted here the story in detail because it illustrates pativrata dharma most effectively.

The Mahabharata contains the well-known Savitryupakhyana: It tells the story how Savitri brings back her husband Satyavan from the clutches of the god of death Yama.

Savitri follows Yama who was taking away the subtle body of her dead husband arguing, ("???") Wherever my husband is being taken or is himself going, there I must go. That is the teaching of the everlasting dharma". She debates cleverly with Yama and impresses him by her learning, wisdom and devotion to the husband. Yama grants her boons one after the other and Savitri asks for so many favours for her parents-in-law, brother, herself and finally wins back her husband alive.

**Rama appreciates Sita's decision 2.30.27-44**

Rama is the self-born Brahman. He has no fear. Fear comes only when there is a second. Brahman has enveloped everything and everyone. How can there be any fear to the Supreme being, when there is none outside him?

Follow me just as Suvarchala (Samjna) does the Sun-god. (Suvarchala is another name for Surya’s wife, Samjna.)

**Parents are perceptible gods 2.30.33**

Rama tells Sita, (sloka 33) "I could not disobey the order of father, mother and preceptor. They are the gods perceptible to us and who can be made favourable to us through service and worship. If I could not succeed in this, how can I possibly win the favour of the imperceptible Fate and God?"

One reason for this could be to reaffirm Rama’s belief that father, mother and preceptor are visible gods, a thought he had expressed in the presence of Dasaratha and Kaikeyi. When he reaffirms it in their absence it is further strengthened. Yet another doubt may arise here. It is stated earlier that men must never confide in women. How could Rama confide in Sita?

Makhi explains: Even Rama is of the opinion that women entertain husbands when happily placed and quit them when they are in difficulties. But here he wanted to know Sita’s mind and therefore describes to her the risks involved in exile. When Sita still asserts that in his company any place is heaven and without him any place is hell, Rama is convinced about her love and trust in him and then confides in her the secret of dharma regarding pleasing the invisible god by obeying the visible ones, in this case, father. Hence Rama’s confiding the secret of dharma in Sita, his loving and trustful wife stands to reason.

Regarding Rama’s patience and tolerance with Lakshmana and Sita even when provoked by harsh words, Makhi quotes Vyasa and Manu: One must never argue with a priest, a domestic chaplain, a preceptor, maternal uncle, guest, patrons, old people, children, patients, doctors, relatives, parents, female relatives, brothers, sons, wife, daughter, and servants. When provoked by them one must not get worked up and bear it with patience.

**Rama’s message to Sita 2.30.40; 2.31.27**

Sahadharmachari Bhava means ‘be my companion while performing dharma’. The commentator suggests, ‘it would be impossible for Rama to discharge his duties as a forest-dweller and in killing demons, in the absence of Sita’ Rama tells Sita to be his companion while performing her dharma.

The word ‘svapatascha’ means ‘foregoing his sleep’.

**Lakshmana's appeal to Rama 2.31.1-33**

The eldest brother is equal to the father. By serving him, he will become a fulfilled soul.By the phrase svapatasca te, it is indicated that Lakshmana did not sleep at night.

**Lakshmana pleads with Rama 2.31.3-5**

You said to Sita, ‘Bharata and Satrughna should be looked after as your own brothers and sons.’ You did not include my name (among those who should remain in Ayodhya). That was how you have already permitted me to be in your company in the forest. (2.26.33) Again you said to me, ‘Do not worry yourself about my proceeding to the forest. Get ready and call off all the proceedings of my coronation.’ I am ready to go to the forest.

**Dharma of younger brother 2.31.3-5**

Lakshmana wants to accompany Rama on his exile. It is suggested hereby that others too should follow the example and follow the elder brother even in the face of hardships sacrificing their comforts and pleasures. Manu says "The eldest son must look after the younger brothers like his children and the younger ones must respect him like a father". Puranasara: In "Bhishmaparva" as Yudhishthira gets down from the chariot and offers his respects to Bhishma, Arjuna, follows suit.

In "Mahaprasthana", as Yudhishthira decides to depart all the younger brothers and Draupadi, follow him.

Granted that an elder brother should be served like father only after father’s death, how does Lakshmana want to serve Rama even when Dasaratha is alive. Besides, service to mother is imperative. How could he follow the elder brother forgetting his duty to the mothers?

To such misgivings Makhi’s reply is: There is nothing wrong in serving the elder brother with the consent of the parents. In "Yuddhakanda"; Dasaratha says to Lakshmana- ‘It is a great pleasure to me that by serving Rama and Sita you have made me very happy and have obtained for yourself merit. Sumitra tells Lakshmana: ‘Consider Rama to be Dasaratha and Sita to be myself’.

**Lakshmana convinces Rama 2.31.18-27**

I shall wait on you both whether you are walking and sleeping. (This suggests that he would not sleep even during nights.)

**On Valmiki's way 2.31.30**

Varuna gave bows to both of us in the sacrifice conducted by Janaka, tells Rama to Lakshmana. They are well-preserved at the residence of Vasistha. How is it that it has never been mentioned earlier that such a gift was given? This is Valmiki’s way. When he is engrossed in the description of a certain event, he does not say everything there. He keeps it for other places. The episode of Kakasura (demon in the form of a crow) which should have been narrated in the Ayodhyakanda, finds a place subsequently in the Sundarakanda with slokas like sa pitra ca partiyaktah suraisca samaharsibhih. The tying of a gem figures not in the Balakanda, but in the Sundarakanda: maniratnam idam dattam vaidchyah svasurena me etc.,

This is Valmiki’s flashback technique.

**Rights over father’s property 2.31.33-34**

The contents of these verses show that Rama gave away wealth in charity- even as Dasaratha was alive. This gives rise to doubts regarding some legal issues of inheritance and right to property. Makhi discusses the quoting several passages on different aspects of the subject from several authorities. The discussion can be summarized as follows:

Manu: Brothers inherit father’s property only after the death of the parents but till that time they have no right over it. Wife, sons and servants have no right to possess any property independently Whatever they might gain also belongs to whomever they belong.

Gautama and Yajnavalkya: also hold similar opinion.

This is refuted. Rama had the right over father’s property by virtue of his birth. This by implication means that right to property is not determined by shastras alone. It is also determined by the ways of the world. It is a worldly practice to recognize the right of the newborn baby on father’s property.

Vijnaneshvara says, property is acquired by all four castes by four means: inherited from father after his death (rikta), purchasing something (kraya), brothers distribute common property among themselves (samvibhaga), acquiring trees, wood, water, grass etc. from forest which belongs to no one, before others do so (parigraha). Besides, brahmins can acquire additional wealth through performing sacrifices for others, teaching etc. (adhikya). kshatriyas can acquire additional wealth by valour. (vijita) and vaisyas can do so by cultivating land and sudras by service (both called nirvishta). Right to property in these cases can be determined through common practice and is recognized by birth.

Ancestral property cannot be given or sold away without agreement between father and sons. Even right to dispose movable property is restricted to one that is self-earned. Regarding ancestral movable property a collective agreement is necessary Yajnavalkya, Manu, and Vyasa are authorities quoted. In the end Makhi concludes that Rama did have wealth that belonged to him exclusively and had a right to give it away in charity.

**Rama’s charity to brahmins 2.31.34; 2.32.12; 2.34.56**

Before going to the forest, Rama decides to give away his wealth to the brahmins, who are firmly devoted to their preceptors. It is said that ‘the selection of the brahmins for giving charity indicates his devotion to those who have great knowledge.’

Brahmeva tridasesvaram points at the superior and inferior lordship between the assignor and the assigned. The interpretation of the phrase ‘seemasu anusaasthu’ is ‘while ruling the kingdom Bharata should neither enjoy the sovereignty nor feel proud of it.’ Rama’s words indicate the Nandigrama life of Bharata.

**Offering presents to Brahmins 2.32.44-45**

The word ‘yatharha’ (as befitting) is used in the text. The presents are to be made worshipfully. This has to be done in keeping with the relation and status of the person concerned. Makhi adds, ‘A person with high status must be offered the best worship and th e one with lower status must be offered worship of a low order. The status is to be determined by caste, character, and education. Gautama supports this.

Manu also says, in matters of offering seat, providing bed and resting place, accompanying at departure and attention, the status of the person should be taken into consideration.

Rama gave gifts to brahmins. Examples from Mahabharata are also cited.

**Citizens’ remarks on Rama’s state 2.33.6-25**

How could the king inflict banishment on Rama, the ocean of virtue and the foremost of men endowed with six excellences namely, harmlessness, kindliness, learning, amiable disposition, self-control and peace of mind. Rama is the very root of the tree of humanity.

(Note: In the last verse of the previous sarga, Rama had told Sumantra to announce to the king his presence at the door. It is repeated here to hasten him as probably he could not go.)

**Propriety in Rama seeking Dasaratha’s permission to take Sita and Lakshmana 2.34.23**

Rama prays Dasaratha to permit all the three of them to depart for the forest. A doubt arises here. Rama and Lakshmana being dependent on the father must seek his permission but Sita is dependent on her husband and does not need Dasaratha’s permission for her departure. Makhi clarifies the point. Rama himself being dependent on father it was necessary to seek his permission to take Sita along with him. Manu also states that anything done with regard to anybody, though with their consent, must be reported to the parents. In Vipulopakhyana, "Anushasanaparva" a disciple looking after the wife of his guru as per his order was considered guilty for not reporting to him the way he looked after her.

**Dasaratha speaks of future to Rama 2.34.30-38**

Dasaratha is destined to leave for the other world after Rama’s departure. The final union of both father and son would take place in the world of Saketa. However, prior to the end of exile, Rama would bow to the king’s sacred sandals.

"My dear son, go and destroy your enemy. That may bring benevolence to the onlookers also. Bestow the kingdom (of Lanka) upon someone else, and return happily. "

"Rama, Kaikeyi is brilliant like spark of fire covered with ashes. Endowed with guileless behaviour befitting the Manu-lineage, she has reminded me of the Brahman’s appeal to you. She has inspired me to induce you to go into exile. Of course, your separation torments me" says the king.

**Rama permits Bharata to rule 2.34.55-56**

Rama says to Kaikeyi, "May Bharata rule the kingdom the claim on which I have withdrawn."

The point raised here is, ‘is there any propriety in Rama ‘permitting’ Bharata to rule the kingdom? Doesn’t Dasaratha have the right to pass on the throne to Bharata’? Makhi defends the poet and asserts the correctness in Rama permitting Bharata to rule the kingdom. Since even the father can dispose of immovable property only with the consent of the son, Dasaratha got this formal consent from Rama with these words. He is also relieved of the guilt of breaking the tradition of passing on the kingdom to the eldest son when the latter has himself renounced it. Besides the sin of breaking his promise to Rama of consecrating him will not accrue to him due to these words of Rama.

**Interpretation of 'najivitam tvam' 2.34.58**

Rama was determined to fulfil his father’s boons. To achieve this, he says Dasaratha may die but he would not stop going to the forest. Because untruthfulness may destroy the fame in the other worlds which is worse than death. Rama will be affected by neither his father’s death nor any sin because he is bound by the truthfulness.

**Patighni 2.35.6**

Kaikeyi is not stirred by Sumantra’s advice or threats. Sumantra addresses Kaikeyi as ‘'patighni’ (killer of husband). Kaikeyi is not stirred by Sumantra’s advice or threats. ‘When she has not killed Dasaratha, how could Sumantra call her so’?

Makhi defends the use of that adjective. Harsh condemnation of husband who is like a guru is equivalent to killing him. While in Yriddha Manu-??? ‘Husband alone is the guru for women’, in "the Karnaparva" Srikrishna says to Arjuna??? ‘Insult of a guru is called ‘murder’ of the guru’.

‘No brahmin will hereafter stay in your house’, says Sumantra to Kaikeyi. This suggests that a house in which there is an admixture of the four castes is not good for dwelling for a brahmin or anyone who desires wellbeing. " Mokshadharma" in the Mahabharata observes ‘A house in which people are bridged between castes or left dangling due to greed, must be discarded like a garment that has caught fire at its end’.

**The sport of hunting 2.49.13-17**

Hunting provides for the gratification of kings. Accompanied by expert bowmen in summer they would march into the jungles and enjoy hunting. The word ‘hi’ in verse 15 suggests this meaning. How does this fit in with the enjoyment of hunting? The answer is: these seven weaknesses trouble the addicts and not the sthitaprajnas. For those who are committed to righteous rule and welfare of the subjects, this is not a sin when done within limits.

**Justification of occasional hunting by the kings 2.49.16-17**

Is hunting, considered one of the seven sins like gambling and womanizing, acceptable to the cultured? The sport of hunting is for the pleasure of great kings at the appropriate time, i.e., at the time of sraddha (rituals performed for the satisfaction of the dead) by people who follow the right conduct or when desired by archers for using their skills in striking the target.

**Ancestors of the nishada king 2.50.33-34**

There lived a nishada king, Guha. He was the intimate friend of Rama and king Dasaratha. Here the question should not arise as to how the righteous king Dasaratha bom in an illustrious family had friendship with a person of low caste. Nishadas originally belonged to the kshatriya caste. They sprang from the body of king Vena, father of king Prthu, when the brahmins churned it. Further, scriptures like the Mimamsa authorized the nishada king to perform vedic sacrifices.

However, the Dharmasastra texts condemned the friendship of a higher caste with a low-caste, considering it upapataka or secondary sin. While listing the low- caste persons, they mention nishada. Here, the word nishada refers to the one who is ‘born in reverse order’. That is, ‘the one born of a mother belonging to a higher caste than the father’s. Of course, the issue of an outcaste is irrelevant here.
