They killed a spotted deer and a black deer, as they were very hungry. They just roasted it in fire and ate it. They were not brahmins and so, were not prohibited. Besides, they offered it first to the gods before they ate the flesh.

**Sita offers prayers to Ganga 2.52.82-91**

Doubt arises here, how a river can be addressed with adjectives and phrases which superimpose on her the characteristics of living beings like capacity to protect, marriage with ocean, position of a divine being worthy of offering worship with praises and salutations, worthiness of being propitiated and so on. Even the holy places on her bank are stated to be worthy of worship. It is only the divinities which are believed to be endowed with divine spirit who are addressed in prayers and worship in this manner.

Makhi sets this objection at rest in his commentary with very lengthy discussion. They relate primarily to the theological aspects. Deifying Ganga raises the fundamental point of belief in idol-worship. Vedic religion based on sacrificial rituals was gradually replaced by worship of Hindu idols due to various socioreligious and socio-historical circumstances. The Purva Mimamsa school of Indian philosophy believed only in the authority of the Vedas and the rituals prescribed in the four Vedas and Brahmanas which commented on them. Dharma according to this school consists in performing sacrificial rituals correctly following the instructions regarding them in the Vedic texts. It concentrated chiefly on the correct interpretation of the Vedic texts. The school was against idol-worship but dharma being the main focus of Makhi’s commentary and idol-worship being an important aspect of Hindu religion, he has taken this opportunity to present the views of the Mimamsa School on this topic in order to refute them one by one finally justifying idol worship, the very foundation of dharma and through it the deification of Ganga. Several authorities are quoted on both sides. The commentary on this portion is summarized below.

Mantra, Itihasa, Purana prove that Indra and other gods are endowed with spirit. Vigraha (idol) is a visible form through which the spirit of the deity can be invoked. Similarly on the same basis deification of rivers like Ganga can be understood. Acceptance of oblations on the part of deities like Indra and others stands to reason on the strength of Vedic Mantras, Arthavada (eulogy and explanation of precepts) and Itihasa (descriptions which depict their deeds as facts).Several examples of Mantra, Arthavada and Itihasa are cited from the Vedic texts. Deification of Ganga is similarly proved by citing Vedic Mantras and so on. Mantras:??? or???

Adiparva: Itihasa (The story of Shantanu) is narrated in brief. Shantanu met a beautiful woman on the banks of the Ganga who was none else but the deity appearing in a lovely human form as if his fortune impelled her to appear before him as his wife.

These passages prove that the spirit of Ganga too, can be invoked through an idol and prayers can be offered to her.

It may be said here that the idol-worship of Ganga is based on the analogy of idol-worship of Indra and other gods but the idol form of Indra and other gods itself is not proved on the basis of mantra etc. Mantras express the sense of rituals to he performed and not idols as qualifying the gods. Arthavada also contains praise auxiliary to the ritual and does not prove the idol form. Hence Mantra and Arthavada cannot be understood as indicating the sense of idol. This stand is finally refuted on the basis of scriptural passages to establish the five attributes of Ganga which are questioned: being represented as idol, ability to protect devotees, possibility of being a spouse, worthiness of being prayed, merit of being propitiated.

Other points discussed in the context are: Can gods actually arrive at the place of sacrifice where they are invoked?, Do gods actually consume oblations offered to them through sacrificial fire?, Do forefathers appear in the form of the brahmins when food is offered to them on Shraddha (death anniversary)?, Does the fruit accrue directly from the ritualistic deed itself or later from the supreme God?, Can Indra and other gods then be said to be the givers of fruit?, Are Indra and other gods essentially different from the Supreme Lord?

At the end of this debate Makhi establishes the concept of idols by quoting authorities and citing several scriptural texts, This proves that worship of Ganga stands to reason. Although no word is used in the passage denoting ‘idol’, the word ‘Ganga itself can denote not just the stream of water but also the superintending deity of that water-stream. Makhi further adds that in the text of the Ramayana, there are many examples where rivers, ocean, cities, mountains, trees, aerial vehicle and so on are directly invoked for prayer, praise, propitiation and help. All these passages must be understood as these objects being conceived as idols through which the respective superintending deities respond to the invocation and favour the devotees.

Examples from Ramayana:

· Sita similarly prays river Yamuna.

· In "Balakanda" Himalaya is described as a living entity.

· In "Sundarakanda" Mainaka Mountain is said to have emerged from the sea to congratulate Hanuman.

· Sita prays Nyagrodha tree for helping her to complete her vow.

· In "Yuddhakanda" Rama permits the aerial car to go.

· In "Uttarakanda" Rama hears words of ‘Pushpaka’ the aerial vehicle.

· In Balakanda the Sun approaches Rama in divine form with the blessings of Viswamitra.

Other examples:

· Chandogya: When one branch of the tree is abandoned by ‘Jiva’ it dries up and dies. One after the other the branches dry up and die. The tree dies because ‘Jiva’ abandons it. Jiva itself does not die.

· Taittiriyaka: Trees get a boon that they will grow again after being cut and that although placed in the vacuity of ground, they will grow again.

· Manu: Trees, creepers etc. have life.???

· Bharata: River Yamuna appears in a female form when Balarama drags her with his plough.

· Bharata (Mokshadharma): Brahma listens to the prayers of trees etc. and grants them a boon giving them relief from cutting and destroying during certain auspicious periods cursing those who harm them during those times.

· Kalidasa: Superintending deity appears before Kusha.

· Harivansha: Sudharma the assembly hall is described as 'Kamarupini’ (Capable of assuming any form at will).

· Bharata: Savitri (Gayatri) appears in a visible form before Asvapati.

· Brihadaranyaka:??? Atman living spirit resides in earth, water, fire, intermediary space, wind, space, Sun, quarters, Moon and stars, sky, darkness, fiery energy, as adhidaivata divine substratum; in all the gross elements as adhibhuta (material substratum), and in breath, speech, eyes, ears, mind, skin, knowledge and seminal fluid as adhyatma (spiritual substratum).

· Bhagavadgita:??? I am the inner essence of all elements??? There is nothing in the universe of which I am not the essence.

· Maha, (Mokshadharma) The dialogue between Bhrigu and Bharadwaja contains in detail the description of trees as having the essence of five elements and of divine spirit. They can even ‘feel’ happiness and sorrow. The Supreme Lord manifests Himself in all the three substrata which proves.

His omnipresence. Objects known to be non-living according to worldly standards also have manifestation of god in them. This justifies the concept of idols, their invocation, prayer, praises and propitiation.

**Rama speaks on values of life (Purusarthas) 2.53.2-27**

"Over three values of life on purusharthas in this world, the value of desire (kama) holds sway. What an irony that the father, in his lust for a woman, throws away an illustrious son! - a thing even a layman will not do. That our father who is wise, learned in all branches of knowledge, who is an emperor, sufficiently aged committed this unbecoming act proves sufficiently strongly that between righteousness of dharma and desire or kama, it is kama (gratification of earthly desires) that holds sway." Rama tells Lakshmana.

If one should ask how Rama levels such a charge when he knows that the bonds of truth fettered the king?, the answer is "Which man, even though ignorant, would actually abandon, for the sake of a woman, an illustrious son as our father has done?"

**Kama 2.53.9-13**

The contents suggest that one must not pursue kama to the exclusion of dharma and artha.

Vanaparva: Bhishma advises Yudhishthira: He, who pursues even dharma only in the interest of kama and nothing else, loses both dharma and artha and like fish without water being addicted to pleasures of kama alone, meets his end.

Hence the wise never err in matters of dharma and artha.

Rama’s statements here imply that Dasaratha sent him away due to his excessive love for Kaikeyi, which is not justifiable. Dasaratha explained his stand saying that his hands were tied up by the dictates of dharma and Rama himself has stated, ‘I want to see that father’s truthfulness is upheld’. Besides, having given boons to Kaikeyi in the past, it is dharma that expects him to fulfil his promise. Hence Rama’s words that Dasaratha was prompted by kama in sending him on exile, do not stand to reason.

Makhi’s reply to this is affirmative, to begin with. But refuting it finally he argues that taking Kaikeyi along to the field of battle unable to bear her separation is itself prompted by kama. Hence, giving her boons and then trying to keep his promise are all indirectly prompted by kama and so Rama’s statements are above criticism.

The contents of these (v 24-26) verses suggest that one should never act against the principles of dharma even though one has the capability to do so. Markandeya observes: Great kings like Nabhaga and Bhagiratha who conquered the earth and extended it up to the ocean by valour could conquer the divine regions hereafter only due to truthfulness. One must never transgress the limits of dharma just because one has strength.

**Rama’s compassion 2.55.27-25**

Rama’s face was filled with tears because be could not endure the misery of his dear ones and not because of his own grief.

**Summary**

Sarga 54

Travelling deeper into the forest, the exiles beheld the unsurpassed beauty of nature, which was mesmeric. At sunset Rama Lakshmana and Sita reached the confluence of the rivers Ganga and Yamuna, where at a distance rose a column of smoke. There gleamed the hermitage of Bharadwaja and walking towards it, they saw the sage finishing his evening worship. “We two are the sons of Dasaratha, Rama and Lakshmana, and this, my consort Sita. I am here banished from Ayodhya, commanded by my father to lead the life of an ascetic.” Rama introduced himself to the sage.

Bharadwaja welcomed them. He said the place was most suitable for their ascetic pursuits. “But this wonderful place is too close to Ayodhya and my people will be tempted to visit us often so I wish to move on to a region less accessible” intervened Rama The sage then suggested ten miles from his hermitage, the mountain Chitrakuta where innumerable ascetics had performed rigorous penance and attained heaven with their mortal bodies.

Rama gratefully thanked Bharadwaja for the information and rested there for the night.

**Summary**

Sarga 55

At daybreak like a fond father Bharadwaja bade farewell to his royal visitors, asking them to follow the river Kalindi flowing westward. Across the river stood a magnificent banyan tree known as Shyama. A mile from there starts the path which leads to Chitrakuta. With their meagre belongings on the boat, they ferried across the river, to the banyan tree where Sita offered her worship for their safe return from exile. Late that evening, they chose a great fig tree for shelter.

**Summary**

Sarga 56

The Sun rose and so did Rama to the many sounds of birds and beasts that emanated from the forest. “Come, listen to the caroling of birds, Lakshmana!” said Rama as he sat listening in rapture to the winged wonders. The three of them continued their journey passing through arrestingly beautiful tracts of land. Sita looked ravishing with her lotus-like eyes wide open in wonder and joy at nature in all its glory. Their journey ended with the splendid slopes of the Chitrakuta and Rama said, “This mountain with its limpid pools and trees laden with fruits and flowers shall be our home”.

They then went to pay their homage to sage Valmiki.

Lakshmana gathered logs of wood and bundles of grass to build a cottage. Rama performed the ritual of ‘ Vastu Shanti and propitiated the gods, Rudra, Visnu and the Visvadevas by offering them worship. Enticed by its charm, bewitched by the grandeur of its mountain peaks, rivers and lakes Rama happily settled down on mount Chitrakuta. The sparkling waters of the river Mayavati, meandering along mountain paths, plains and valleys fascinated Rama who at that moment did not want to be anywhere else. Even his banishment from Kosala no longer distressed him.

**Simmary**

Sarga 57

Meanwhile in Ayodhya, Sumantra was taken aback at the eerie silence that prevailed in the once bustling streets. A pall of gloom hung over the entire city. As soon as the fleet-footed horses drew the chariot into the city, people by the hundreds and thousands spilled out of their homes, looking askance at Sumantra. When he told them that in spite of his most impassioned pleas, Rama had crossed the Ganga, it brought fresh tears to the listeners who feared for their safety. Even as Sumantra felt the palpabe silence, he wondered “What has happened to the horses, elephants, the people and the king? Did they all fall victims to the fire of their anguish over Rama's exile?” More poured out on to the streets clamouring for news of Rama. Heartbroken to see the chariot vacant they lamented, “Where is he who shared our joy and sorrow, who was an unfailing presence at our festivals and funerals? Where is he? Can Kausalya survive this devastation?” The questions were endless but there were no answers.

While Sumantra was going to see Dasaratha, women, eyes streaming with tears, came down from heir mansions to hear news of Rama while in the palace was heard the weeping of the queens. All pitied Kausalya, who was able to neither endure her separation, nor die in peace. When Sumantra conveyed Rama’s message to Dasaratha to the king whose mind was mangled with grief it proved the last straw and he slipped into a merciful faint. Alarmed, his consorts wept aloud and Kausalya raising Dasaratha from the floor said, “You banished Rama against every code of honour. Shamed by that act you now refuse to even ask of him. Afraid of Kaikeyi who is not even here you refuse to speak to Sumantra.”

Dasaratha’s exhausted mind gave up its battle, once again triggering unrest and melancholy which spread over the entire city.

**Summary**

Sarga 58

Dasaratha, like an elephant trapped, saw Sumantra tearful and dust-laden. In a voice gentle and fragile he asked, “O charioteer! tell me how Rama, that son of mine and lord of the earth sleeps on the hard floor of the forest? Which tree gives him shelter and what food does he eat? How does that orphan live in the wilderness infested with cobras and carnivores?

How do Sita’s dainty feet tread thorny wooded pathways?” Dasartha’s curiosity of how Rama, Lakshmana and Sita fared and how they inhabited the formidable forest was insatiable. Prodded by his love that defied description for a son who was his world and his life, Dasaratha kept pestering, “Tell me! tell me, Sumantra so that I may live a while longer.”

In a tremulous voice choked with emotion Sumantra relayed Rama’s messages he had been committed to deliver: “Sumantra, tell the king, my father, that I place my head at his august feet in profound obeisance. I pay homage to all those women in the inner apartments of the palace and request mother Kausalya to tend the sacrificial fires and serve the king as unto a god. May you mother, not let your ego come in the way of other queens. Bestow equal grace on Dasaratha and Kaikeyi! Give Bharata his due as sovereign. Though not the eldest of the king’s sons it is his royal prerogative. Bharata the coronated king of Kosala should obey the commands of the monarch, his father. May Bharata enjoy his sovereignty, but not oppose or depose Dasaratha”.

Lakshmana’s message was not so gentle. Beholding Rama’s distress he had burst out ma fiery tirade lashing out at Dasaratha without mercy: To me “Dasaratha, the great monarch, is no father. To me, Rama is brother, father and master. How can Rama, beloved prince of Ayodhya. ever in the service of his people, be banished? It is unrighteous and unpardonable.”

Of Sita, Sumantra spoke sadly: “Born a princess, unacquainted with hardships Sita had no comments even in the face of the terrible misfortune that had befallen her. Though grieving at the fate of her consort, not a word of blame did she let loose against Kaikeyi. So noble was her silence. Looking at Rama sorrowfully she noticed my departure and the tears she had been fighting to hold back, spilled from her beautiful eyes as did from Rama’s who stood by her side. My last vision of Sita was a piteous picture of woe as she stood gazing after me in wistful silence.”

**Перевод:**

**Wailing, Dasaratha fell unconscious. He was doubly grieved due to his yearning for Rama. Rama's mother was seized with fear hearing those lamentations.**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande ekonasastitamassargah..*

Thus ends the fiftyninth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 59

Sumantra went on with his nan-ation of events that had taken place after he left Rama. He said that even the horses shedding tears were reluctant to part with Rama and how he had tarried with Guha in the hope of Rama sending for him. “Rama’s exile is beyond description” he said, “and so are its effects on nature. A shroud of gloom hangs over the entire earth where trees have no green leaves, flowers have no scent, rivers and lakes run dry, limpid pools turn turbid and forests where no beasts roam are soundless. Weighed down with grief, the petals of the lotus have drowned, groves and gardens have lost their charm and birds no longer chirp. People behold my chariot in disappointment, for they see no Rama there.”

As he listened to Sumantra, Dasaratha was a picture of abject misery. Wearied of deceptions, deprived of a dutiful son and denounced by his people, he was haunted by grief that bore him down. “Enticed by Kaikeyi, whose mind is an abode of evil, I have committed an unforgivable folly, which will now destroy my dynasty. Sumantra! If ever I have done you a good turn bring back that mighty-armed son of mine or take me to him, as I am about to die. While alive, I can feast my eyes on my son with Sita and Lakshmana by his side. To Kausalya he said, “The ocean of grief in which I am drowning is boundless. It has Rama’s misfortune as its currents and Sita’s banishment as its utmost borne. My sighs are the waves whose foaming waters are polluted by my tears. My flailing arms are like the fish, my wailing the sound of crashing waves and in its depth dwells the dreadful volcanic fire, called Kaikeyi, who is bom out of my copious tears. This ocean is infested with monstrous crocodiles, which are the words of the hunch-back. Its fathomless waters are like the wicked boons of Kaikeyi and its distant shores are Rama’s exile, caused by that vile woman! Without my Rama, how can I cross this ocean of sorrow? And it will be a great calamity if in spite of my longing I cannot ever behold my Rama and Lakshmana.”

Thus ends the sixtieth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 60

Kausalya wept inconsolably asking Sumantra to take her to Rama as she could no longer live away from him. And Sumantra said, “O mother! dispel your grief. Rama is served by no less than Lakshmana who is a noble brother, aware of every dharma and master of all his senses. He serves Rama with a devotion that makes him worthy of heaven. As for Sita, though living in the wilderness, ever meditating on Rama, she lives as fearlessly as she would in the palace. I see no trace of self-pity in her, whose radiant face is ever serene as she follows Rama revelling under the green canopies. Since Rama is her very life, without him Ayodhya would be the most dreaded of forests for her. Fascinated by the glories of nature she minds neither the heat of the sun, the fear of the forest, or the unbridled forces of the winds. She remains dainty as a lotus, luminous as the moon and her feet though devoid of vermilion continue to be as supple and tender as the lotus buds. Her anklets tinkle as she traipses alongside Rama, fearing neither elephant nor tiger; she takes refuge in the arms of her consort”.

“The famed story of a son’s submission to his father’s commands will forever find pride of place in the history of this world. Abandoning all sorrow they walk the path of the great rishis, with uncompromising resolution. So there is no reason to grieve for Rama, or for the king.”

Despite Sumantra’s reassurance of Rama’s safety and welfare, Kausalya refused to give up her lament.

Thus ends the sixtyfirst sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 61

Kausalya in her sorrow blamed Dasaratha for the woes of her children. She asked how a king so righteous, renowned and compassionate could bear the thought of their suffering. “How can Sita exposed to the elements, living on forest fare and listening to the fearful roar of animals in place of melodious music survive? When will I behold my Rama enjoying the comforts of the palace? The princes who once had the luxuries of a kingdom are now victims of your ruthless command. Should Rama return at the end of his fourteen-year exile, he will not accept the kingdom from Bharata. To him, it will be like the food offered at a shraddha ceremony. Rama will not suffer the ignominy of receiving a kingdom passed on to him after being enjoyed by a brother younger than he.

“Rama, whom the united forces of the devas and danavas cannot vanquish, has been destroyed by you. The first refuge for a woman is her husband, the second her son, the third her relatives. The fourth is independence, which does not exist for me in this world. Enslaved to Kaikeyi, you are no longer mine and as you are nothing to me, you are no longer my refuge. My second refuge Rama is in the forests where I cannot go, because I am married to you. As for my family it is far away and beyond my reach, so in every way you have destroyed me, ruined yourself, the kingdom and the ministers. You have no crown, kingdom, kinsmen or counselors. You have brought nothing but disaster. Ruined are the inhabitants of Ayodhya, my son and I. Bharata and Kaikeyi alone are happy!”

Listening to Kausalya’s accusations, Dasaratha’s battered mind writhing with remorse and anguish refused to function.

## Sarga 62

\[Sudden flash of a thought in the mind of Dasaratha about an evil act done by him in the past — Dasaratha attributes present misfortune to the past action — seeks forgiveness of Kausalya.\]

**"O Kausalya! I entreat you with folded palms. Be merciful. Forever affectionate, you are not cruel even towards your enemies.**

*sa mrrdhnibadhva rudati rajnah padmamivanjalim.*

**Перевод:**

**Frightened Kausalya, weeping and raising her palms folded like lotus on to her head, and charged with emotions said with stumbling syllables:**

**Summary**

Sarga 62

Dasaratha sank into a deep melancholy as he brooded over events beyond his control. Slowly in his mind surfaced the memory of an incident that had occurred many years ago. He remembered an unforgivable sin that he had committed as a young prince while indulging in his favorite pastime of hunting. He had unwittingly released an arrow towards what he thought was a sound made by an animal only to find out that his target was an ascetic. It now dawned on Dasaratha that his present suffering was the consequence of that act, which had ended in a great calamity. The memory shook him, and bowing to Kausalya with palms together, he said, “Do forgive me, Kausalya. You are a woman of great compassion even to your enemies. Plunged in a great sorrow, I beg you to curb your temper, for I cannot bear such anger.”

Listening to a king as mighty as Dasaratha, begging for mercy and forgiveness, Kausalya was distressed. Holding his hands, she said, “I prostrate to you, my lord, I am a sinner. I made you beg of me. A woman, who compels her husband to seek her pardon, loses her place in this world and the world after. My grief perhaps betrays my discretion, for there is no greater enemy than grief. Rama’s five days of exile seem like five years to me and the more I think of him the more I grieve.”

The Sun set on one more day and the great monarch lulled and consoled by his consort fell into blissful sleep.

**Summary**

Sarga 63

Coming awake hours before dawn, thoughts that had tormented Dasaratha the day before assailed him. Wishing to share them with Kausalya on the sixth day of Rama’s exile Dasaratha remorsefully recollected at midnight the misdeed he had committed unwittingly in his youth. “O Kausalya, man has to reap the fruit of all his deeds, be they good or evil. Only the foolish do not consider the consequences of their acts. A good act gains man merit but an evil act brings suffering. A wrong act committed thoughtlessly may be regretted but its outcome can never be stemmed. In my youth, I had mastered ‘shabdavedi’, the great skill of shooting at any target by its sound. This mastery that brought me great renown as an archer was also the cause of my sin. Its consequences make me suffer not in the next world, but here in this world and now.”

“As a young prince hunting was my favorite sport and armed with the knowledge of ‘shabdavedi’, it was even more thrilling. On a beautiful evening I went on to the shores of the

Sarayu. The Sun was westward bound. The heat had abated. Birds sang. Frogs croaked in delight. And I was ecstatic. As thick clouds scudded across the skies, and twilight gently embraced the earth, at that moment I heard a gurgling sound. Unable to see clearly, mistaking it for an elephant drinking water, I aimed my arrow towards the sound which struck an ascetic and not an elephant. The noise I had heard was that of an ascetic filling his pot with water. My target fell into the Sarayu. To my horror, I heard a voice which said, ‘How can weapons fall on me? Who shot this arrow and why? I do not rue my destruction, but what of my parents? How can they survive after death claims me? Who is that ignoble one who killed us all with a single arrow?’ Petrified with shock, feeling drained, my bow slipped to the ground.

“I rushed towards the sound and to my dismay beheld a young hermit, whose body was covered with blood and dust. A broken pot lay by his side bearing mute witness to my sin. As I stood quivering with fear, he looked at me like one who wanted to immolate me in the blaze of his anger and said bitterly, ‘To fetch a pot of water for my parents I had come here, but now that I am struck, my parents too will perish. ’ He then asked me to quickly take some water to his old parents but warned me to pacify his father first so as to avert any curses he may pronounce upon me. He also asked me to remove the arrow still in his body as the pain was unbearable. As I stood rooted to the ground, miserable and horrified, beholding my sorrow, he said gently, ‘My mind grows peaceful. I no longer grieve and I will soon be dead. And you will not be guilty of killing a brahmin, for I am no brahmin, but born of a Sudra mother and a Vaisya father’. I then pulled out the arrow and he shuddered with pain until death released him from his suffering. An innocent life was lost and I was to blame.

“Though unintentional, it was still a sin irreversible and inexcusable.”

**Summary**

Sarga 64

Dasaratha continued with his harrowing tale, “By slaying an ascetic, I committed a crime that no man ever should. Alone, shattered by a disaster beyond description and afraid of its consequences, I stood stunned. Finally, taking some water I wended my way to the cottage where I beheld an old couple who were blind. With none to help them they were like birds whose wings had been severed. They sat talking of their son, not knowing he would no more fetch them water. My grief doubled at the thought. Hearing my footsteps, the old father said, ‘ Why the delay, my son? Your mother waits for you impatiently. Give us the water. To us you are our eyes and our very life. We have no refuge other than you. Speak, my child, why are you silent?’As I looked at him my heart filled with dread, my voice felt strangled and my words came garbled, but I managed to say, ‘I am a kshatriya. Dasaratha is my name. I am not your son but the cause of a great calamity. Noble sire, as I stood on the sands of the Sarayu I shot an arrow at what I thought was an elephant, only to discover to my horror that my arrow had not struck an elephant but had fatally wounded your son. ’

‘Grieving for you who would no longer have any refuge, he breathed his last asking me to tend to your needs. My sin, though unpardonable was unintended. I implore you to forgive me.’ Shocked at the news of his son’s death, the sage’s eyes streamed with tears. Sighing, he said, ‘In your ignorance you have transgressed. Had you not confessed you would not be alive; your head would have shattered into a thousand pieces. The race of the Ikshvakus will also now continue, which would otherwise have been extinguished.’ Crying piteously for the son who was everything to them, they wailed, ‘Who will now protect us, feed us and look after us. We too will soon follow you and there I will ask Yama to give you back to us and the righteous lord will surely grant my wish.’

“The old couple tearfully performed the funeral rites of their son, who by merit of his penance and service to his parents immediately ascended the heaven. He then came back to console them, assuring them they would soon be with him”.

The sage now turned towards me, as I stood trembling to say ‘Kill me now with the same arrow you snuffed out my son’s life with! What can surpass that pain? May the grief, which now consumes me, befall you, too, causing your death, as it now causes mine! Since you sinned unwittingly, instead of reducing you to ashes here and now, I curse you to die like me, grieving for a son. ’

Musing over those past events, Dasaratha said, “Sorrowing for my son, I too will die now and the curse of the sage will come to pass. Banishing Rama was an injustice and does not befit me. No greater grief can befall me than that of not seeing him. It was my destiny to exile Rama as dictated by Kaikeyi. If only he can touch me once, or appear before me, I may still live. Once a person goes to the land of the dead, he can no longer see any one. Kausalya! I cannot see you, my faculties are deserting me, and the messengers of death hurry me. My life flickers as a flame in a lamp whose oil is soon to be over and my body feels like the banks of a river being washed away by the force of its flood.” As death approached and drove away his hopes of ever seeing Rama, a cry of torment escaped Dasaratha “O Rama! Where are you. my son, my protector, my life? Kausalya! Sumitra! Where are you? Kaikeyi! My enemy, destroyer of my race! ” Anguished beyond endurance at Rama’s separation, the noble Ikshvaku fated to die, away from Rama, gave up the ghost a little after midnight.

Thus ends the sixtyfifth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 65

The fateful night which had witnessed the end of Dasaratha’s grief, remorse and his very life, ended. A new dawn brought with it the usual early morning visitors to the palace. There came the ministers, bards, musicians and others, all singing praise of the king. The king’s attendants were busy filling the golden pitchers with aromatic waters for the royal ablutions, while beautiful women saw to the procurement of unguents, oil, mirrors and combs. The Sun rose higher and the king still slumbered. The ladies in attendance grew anxious and approached the couch but the king did not move nor did he seem to breathe. Fearing for his life they shook like reeds caught in the river currents and a closer look confirmed their worst fears had come true. The palace was soon to discover that the mighty king who had ruled

Ayodhya gloriously had passed away. Noble and renowned, the very embodiment of kshatriya dharma, Dasaratha had at last succumbed to the accusations of Lakshmana, to the silent tears of Sita and to the greatest blow of his life, his separation from Rama. The air of doom that had hung over Ayodhya seemed to have descended to claim the life of its king. For Kausalya and Sumitra, their hour of waking had come and gone, but they slept deeply. Exhausted with grief, their tear-stained faces were dull, as was Dasaratha’s in death.

Waking up to the terrible wailing of the women of the palace realizing that Dasaratha was no more, all the queens, overcome with grief, fell in a faint, mourning the loss of their protector.

Thus ends the sixtysixth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 66

Kausalya, plunged in sorrow, felt a great emptiness like the sea with its waters drained. Cradling Dasaratha’s head in her lap, looking at Kaikeyi, she said, “With Rama banished and Dasaratha dead, the kingdom is now yours to enjoy. Which woman having lost her husband will want to live except you who has abandoned her dharma? Your treachery has rendered Dasaratha lifeless and Rama homeless. Rama does not know I am now a widow and shelterless. As a devoted wife, I will enter the blaze of the funeral pyre.”

Kausalya’s laments were heart-rending as those in charge of the royal funeral tried to extricate the king’s body from her embrace. In the aftermath of the tragic events that had come to pass, the sorrowing population of Ayodhya questioned themselves, “Death has deprived us of Dasaratha and fate has deprived us of Rama. How can we survive the evil Kaikeyi who has even killed her consort?”

The king mourning for a son lay dead. Grieving for that king, his consorts lay stricken on the palace floor and the Sun, as if averse to witnessing such tragedy, dipped into the western horizon letting the darkness of night invade the earth.

Thus ends the sixtyseventh sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 67

The Sun finally set on an unforgettable day of untold miseries. At dawn the next day, sages of great renown, Markandeya, Moudgalya, Vamadeva, Kasyapa, Katyayana, Goutama and Jabali assembled to counsel with Vasistha. They said that since Dasaratha was no more and Rama was in exile, it was imperative that one among the Ikshvakus should be proclaimed king. “Many are the maladies of a land without a ruler. In a kingdom without protection of a king, thieves and dacoits flourish. Merchants cannot conduct their business as lawlessness and fear will grip people. Where there is no wealth, the country cannot maintain an army and without soldiers anarchy will prevail. Without the presence of a king, even the god of rain will not send his cool showers and no grain will grow. The brahmins will no longer chant the mantras and the wealthy will no longer be able to sleep in peace, for lack of safety. No flowers or sweets will be offered in temples and no alms will be given. A king who is the essence of truth and righteousness is family to those who have no family and is father and mother to those who have none. Yama judges. Kubera gives. Indra rules. Varuna disciplines. But a king surpasses them all, as he performs all these duties himself.”

The final decision of the sages was to redeem Ayodhya from the possible darkness of anarchy by crowning an Ikshvaku as king of Kosala.

Thus ends the sixtyeighth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 68

Vasistha sent for Siddhartha, Vijaya, Jambavanta, Ashoka and Nandana messengers to bring Bharata and Satrughna from Kekaya. They were not to reveal the exile of Rama or the passing away of Dasaratha but tell Bharata that his immediate presence in Ayodhya was imperative. “Take gifts of fine clothes and ornaments to the king of Kekaya and his son,” he added.

Mounted on swift-footed horses, the messengers set out on their mission traveling north of the Pralamba Mountains, passing Apartala along the shores of the river Malini. At Hastinapura, they crossed Ganga and from there westward bound, arrived at Panchala, by way of Kurujanga after which they crossed the Sarabanda river. Many miles later they reached the mountain of Bodhibhavan and the river Ikshumati venerated by the Ikshvaku dynasty. They passed many regions dotted with lakes, streams, step-wells and limpid pools, where tigers, lions, elephants and deer freely roamed. They sped past the lovely city of Girivraja and galloped on and on till they touched Rajagriha by nightfall.

Thus ends the sixtyninth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki

**Summary**

Sarga 69

The night the messengers arrived from Ayodhya, Bharata had a terrible dream. As he got up at dawn, troubled memories of that dream flooded back into his mind and a great melancholy that defied reason engulfed him. Friends of the prince tried to cheer him, but Bharata said, “In my dream last night I saw my father whose body was soiled and hair disheveled as he fell from the peak of a mountain into a pit of dung! It seemed like he was wallowing in it and drinking oil with his cupped palms. I also beheld the moon cast itself on to the earth and the oceans dry up. The universe was plunged in darkness and the elephant that carried Dasaratha had only one tusk. An eerie feeling that a blazing fire which had just been extinguished came over me. And I saw the king, my father, ride a chariot drawn by donkeys, robed in black, daubed with red sandal paste as a woman whose skin was black and yellow derided him. To my horror I then saw a demon, clad in red, laughing loudly, beating and dragging him away.

“My night was full of inauspicious dreams. Surely Dasaratha, Rama or I will soon die. He, who is seen riding a chariot drawn by donkeys, will soon reach his funeral pyre to go up in smoke. Memories of that frightful dream make me uneasy. I suffer from the dread of the unknown, a dread that is painful and which I cannot shake off. My throat dries, my voice trembles and I seem to loathe myself and I do not know the reason why!”

**Summary**

Sarga 70

As Bharata was desolately recollecting his dream, the messengers from Ayodhya arrived. Presenting themselves to Bharata, they conveyed Vasistha’s message. “Vasistha offers you his salutations. He wishes your immediate return to Ayodhya as an urgent matter requires your attention.” Bharata enquired of the welfare of Dasaratha, Rama and Lakshmana. “Howfares noble mother Kausalya?” Bharata wanted to know, “and what of Sumitra, an equally virtuous mother and that irascible, selfish lady, my mother?”

The messengers .assured Bharata that all was well and that they should set out for Ayodhya. The king of Kekaya tenderly kissed Bharata on his brow, blessed him and bade him an affectionate farewell. He also bestowed on his grandson a part of all that he possessed. He gave well-bred elephants, thoroughbred dogs raised with care in the palace which were as ferocious as tigers. Gold nuggets, woollens, fine clothes, antelope skins, sixteen thousand horses and the elephants, Airavata and Indrasra, presented by Yudhaj it. Distinguished counselors were to accompany Bharata as a mark of respect and honour but nothing of this pomp or the generous display of his grandfather’s love for him cheered Bharata.

An inexplicable gloom that had settled on him refused to be dispelled.

Thus ends the seventyfirst sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 71

Leaving Rajagriha, Bharata travelled eastward, crossing the rivers Hladini, Satadru and Salyakarsana. Riding past mount Mahasaila, Chaitraratha forest, cities and villages till they touched the confluence of Ganga and Saraswati where they entered the Bharunda forest. Except for stops when men or animals wearied or they needed to replenish supplies, the royal retinue tarried nowhere. They passed through picturesque countries where lush forest and majestic mountains lent their charm to the landscape. Magnificent rivers flowed with their waters shimmering as they snaked their way through mountains, plains and valleys that enhanced the beauty of their surroundings.

Bharata with a far-away look in his eyes did not seem to notice much, for a premonition of some great ill haunted him to distraction. Close to Ayodhya, at Ujjihanagar, Bharata ordered the fastest horses to be harnessed to his chariot and sped towards Ayodhya, like the god of the winds passing through space. Even the horses seemed to feel the restless urgency of their master. After travelling seven days and seven nights they reached the outer bounds of Kosala and at dawn of the eighth day, Bharata beheld the golden turrets of Ayodhya, magnificent capital of the Ikshvakus built by lord Manu.

Bharata’s heart leaped up for a moment, at the sight of his beloved city, Ayodhya, with the green of its gardens and groves, its white sands, the wealth of its knowledge and riches which made it more beautiful than Indra’s Amaravati. But as he entered, he was puzzled at the unusual quiet of the city and said, “Charioteer, tell me why a city renowned for its wealth, learning and beauty, where Vedic priests abound, where yagnas and yagas are always performed should look so joyless. Why do I not hear the clamour of people, the wheels of chariots or the bustle on the streets? The gardens are so quiet: Homes look deserted and yards unclean. The drooping trees in the gardens seem to shed tears and not leaves. I see neither beasts nor birds. The air is no longer filled with the fragrance of incense and sandal. Why do the drums not boom and why is there no music? The stillness frightens me, charioteer! Is it possible that all is not well with my kinsfolk? I see many inauspicious omens and I hear the howls of vixens that bode ill.”

When Bharata entered Ayodhya an eerie silence seemed to grip him. His heart throbbed, His body trembled. He stopped dead on the track. “Charioteer”, he said, “tell me why you brought me here in such haste? The streets are empty, houses joyless and even the temple bells are silent!”

Overwhelmed by the gloom that had engulfed Ayodhya, the troubled prince, head bowed and heart anguished, entered the palace of his father.

**Summary**

Sarga 72

To Bharata, homecoming proved joyless. Oppressed by an inexplicable feeling of doom, he went in search of the king, but in vain. When he went to meet his mother, she embraced him and kissed him tenderly on his brow asking him of the welfare of his grandfather and uncle. “All are well”, said Bharata, “My grandfather sends his greetings to you and my father. The gifts he has given me will soon arrive. Hurried by the messengers from Ayodhya, I have reached earlier. Tell me, mother, why is father not on this golden couch and why is everything so desolate? I do long to see him and pay him my obeisance.”

Deluded by the love for her son and her greed for the kingdom, Kaikeyi, in her ignorance, revealed the staggering truth deeming it delightful, “The king, a great soul, has attained that state which all beings should one day attain!” The suddenness of the announcement, and its cold, precise delivery sent waves of shock through Bharata. Reeling at the blow which was almost physical, he fell down on the floor like one struck. Kaikeyi saw him sobbing inconsolably and stroking him tenderly said, “Rise, my son. This show of sorrow in public does not become a prince.” Choking with grief Bharata demanded, “Assuming I was summoned either for the coronation of Rama or for the king’s yagna I traveled to Ayodhya only to find my father no longer alive. What disease claimed his life, mother? Blessed is Rama and blessed are those who performed his funeral rites. Where is the hand that guided me, wiped my tears and would have now dusted my clothes and stroked me lovingly? Where is Rama? Is not an elder brother like a father? I long to offer myself at his feet. Where is the most virtuous, and the most venerable of my brothers who is now my father and my solace?”

Bharata wanted to know if the king had any message for him and what his last words were. Kaikeyi said, “Crying out for Rama, Sita and Lakshmana, his last words were that all those who would one day behold them return to Ayodhya are indeed fortunate!” “Where is Rama?” repeated Bharata. And it was Kaikeyi’s moment of triumph for which she had been waiting so long. Sure Rama’s exile would be Bharata’s joy! She said, “Rama, clad in bark, has gone to live in the Dandakaranya along with Sita and Lakshmana.” Bharata stood puzzled and pained. He wondered what transgression warranted his exile. “Did Rama steal from a brahmin? Did he torment the innocent of Ayodhya or did he covet the wife of a subject? Why did the king banish Rama like a criminal who had slain a Vedic brahmin?” asked Bharata.

Kaikeyi now proudly laid bare the intricacies of her diabolic plan: “My son, Rama has committed no crime. The moment I heard of his coronation, I demanded that the king grant me the crown of Kosala and the banishment of Rama. Bound by his commitment made long ago Dasaratha agreed and exiled Rama. Sita and Lakshmana followed him. Do not grieve any more, my son! I have achieved all this for you.”

Basking in the glory of her achievement, Kaikeyi exulted: “Get ready to rule Kosala, its golden throne awaits you!”

Thus ends the seventythird sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 73

Bharata tried to shut out Kaikeyi’s dreadful words, as they echoed and re-echoed in his mind. Grieving for an expired father and an exiled brother, he said, “Deprived of a father and a brother, of what use is this kingdom? You have rendered Dasaratha dead and Rama an ascetic condemned to the wildernesses of Dandakaranya. Like salt upon a raw wound you cause me sorrow upon sorrow. You are here for the destruction of the Ikshvaku dynasty like the night of death and deluge. Dasaratha’s marriage to you has brought him death! Why mother, why did you kill my father and banish Rama? What made you clothe Rama in bark garments? Did it not horrify you to see him so, the noblest son of Dasaratha who looked upon you with such love and respect? Kausalya who was to you a sister, did she deserve this? What have you achieved? Trying to bestow on me the crown, you have brought upon yourself a great calamity. Now, relying on whose strength do I rule this country? If only Rama had not looked upon you as his own mother, I would have abandoned you without any qualms. What made you deviate from the path of justice and fall to this state, which will surely be condemned by all our ancestors?

“Tradition and kshatriya dharma decree that the first-born alone will inherit the throne. How can you, bom of a race that values the same traditions, deviate from them? How did these lowly, contemptible thoughts occur to you? I will bring Rama back to Ayodhya and be his slave”.

Though his grief was uncontrollable, it did not hold him back from letting loose a barrage of abusive accusations against the queen.

**Summary**

Sarga 74

As Kaikeyi’s injustices came back to his mind again and again, Bharata continued reviling her. “You should be cast out of the country, Kaikeyi! The harm you caused Dasaratha has sent him to his death. Dharma has abandoned you, wicked woman! Do not sorrow for a consort whom you have killed. Consider me dead and grieve forever. Languish in hell. You have brought me disgrace!

“Your infamy will also be mine, for I too will be blamed for Rama’s banishment and Dasaratha’s death. Do not speak to me! How much must be the grief of Kausalya and Sumitra for having to share this palace with you? For depriving Kausalya of both husband and son, to which loka will you go now? If Kamadhenu, the noble cow worshipped by the three worlds, could weep to see a pair of oxen on earth faint in the mid-day Sun out of thousands of her breed, how can Kausalya live without her only son? Why don’t you throw yourself into fire, or enter Dandakaranya, or hang yourself with a noose around your neck? You have no other salvation. I will be rid of my sins only after Rama sets foot in Ayodhya.”

Bharata’s sighs were like the hisses of an angry serpent. Red-eyed with rage and tears, clothes and ornaments in disarray, he fell to the ground.

**Summary**

Sarga 75

Bharata, physically weary and emotionally drained, slowly sat up, his eyes still brimming with tears. He wanted Sumantra and the ministers to know what had happened and said, “Never have I coveted the kingdom of Ayodhya nor talked of it to my mother. I was miles away and unaware of both my proposed coronation and Rama’s banishment. I do not wish to profit by my mother’s efforts, which should have been stemmed at the very beginning.”

Meanwhile hearing of Bharata’s arrival Kausalya wanted to see that ‘wicked Kaikeyi’s son’. Unmindful of her filthy clothes and floating hair, she was going to Bharata, when he, accompanied by Satrughna appeared at her doorstep.

Seeing Kausalya who was a picture of utter grief and desolation, the two princes embraced her with loving concern. She pounced upon Bharata saying, “Did you not crave the crown of Ayodhya, my son? By banishing Rama, Kaikeyi’s ruthless hand has taken hold of what you so longed for. What did Kaikeyi get by driving away my son to the jungles, clothed in bark garments? Let Kaikeyi send me to Rama or with Dasaratha’s body and the sacrificial fire he once worshipped I shall go to Dandakaranya.” What Kausalya meant was, Rama could then perform the funeral rites of the king who had once in his anger forbidden Bharata to do.

As Kausalya went on, Bharata who was waiting to prove his innocence fell at her feet, saying, “Worshipful mother, unaware of my love for Rama you accuse me of transgressions that I am not guilty of. May all the merit earned by those with whose consent Rama now lives in exile, perish! May the sons, slaves and servants guilty of Rama’s banishment given to women, wine and gambling, perish. I was neither aware of nor had control over what eventuated here during my absence, so how can this blame befall me? Rama, mighty prince of Ayodhya, whose religion is truth, is exiled and I am not and never will be party to my mother’s deeds against dharma. If I am, then may all the sins visit me and render me a beggar!”Bharata’s impassioned denials of the deceit that he was accused of calmed Kausalya. Regretting her outburst, she said, “My son, distracted by grief beyond endurance, I accused you. Your duty to your honour which makes you want to follow your brother is commendable. Blessed are you!”

Kausalya tenderly embraced Bharata, but the prince would not be consoled as he deeply grieved for a father who was dead and a brother who was banished.

**Summary**

Sarga 76

Vasistha said to Bharata who was still in a state of shock, “Enough of grieving Bharata, let us think of the funeral rites of the king.” Dasaratha’s body was taken out of the casket of preserving oils, to lay in state on a couch studded with every possible gem. As he lay like one in a deep slumber, Bharata wept for him whose love he had lost forever and whose embrace which would no longer gather him into its protective warmth. He wept for an Ayodhya that was orphaned and an earth that was widowed.

Citizens of Ayodhya lined its thoroughfares to catch a glimpse of their beloved monarch who was about to set out on his last journey upon the earth. They showered flowers made of gold and silver on the body. Priests, brahmins, the queens along with Bharata and Satrughna circumambulated the pyre. Bharata then touched it with the sacrificial fire and lit it.

Thus ends the seventyseventh sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 77

In Ayodhya life passed slowly. Nothing was normal any more. Twelve days after the cremation, the 'shraddha' ceremony took place when the brahmins were bestowed with gifts of gold, silver, gems, food and fine clothes along with hundreds of cows and goats. Mansions and servants too were part of the charity. On the morning of the thirteenth day, Bharata, collecting his father’s ashes, lamented, “Father, I have lost my brother to the jungles and you to death! Who will be my refuge now? Beholding a mighty monarch reduced to a fistful of ashes and a handful of bones, Bharata sobbed hopelessly, abandoning all restraint.

Satrughna battling with his own sorrow and overwhelmed with Bharata’s grief, wailed. “Father, when you, the very essence of dharma, departed why did not the earth shatter? I will never enter an Ayodhya which is not graced by Rama.” Consoling the prince, Vasishta gently reminded him of his duties yet to be done. He said that every man born was subject to the inescapable dualities of nature such as hunger and thirst, grief and delusion, age and death. The wise do not grieve over the inevitable and the inescapable. Life is an eternal war between these dualities and death is the ultimate event of every life. So why lament?”

**Summary**

Sarga 78

Like the dance of death leaped the flames, hissing and spewing sparks, as the merlal remains of Dasaratha were reduced to ashes. Back in the palace, Bharata sat dolefully, wondering how he might meet Rama while Satrughna questioned the injustice of Rama’s exile: “How could Rama, the refuge of all be cast away into the jungles by a mere woman? Was not there a strong and valiant son of Dasaratha called Lakshmana? Why did he not restrain the king deluded by his passion for a woman? Why did he not prevent and protect Rama from the indignity and injustice of exile?

Just then, Manthara the infamous hunchback came in and her arrival added fuel to the fire of Bharata’s anger. She was decked from the crown of her crooked head to the tips of her crooked toes, in a vulgar display of her ill-gotten’ wealth. Smeared with red sandal paste, draped in the finest of silks, wearing row upon row of gold and pearl chains, with strange glittering objects stuck all over, she looked like a monkey bound with ropes. Manthara, whom the world had condemned for its woes, sauntered in. The ludicrous woman was pounced upon with great glee by the guards as she shrieked, more in shock than in pain. They took her to Bharata, saying, “Here is the cause of Rama’s exile and Dasaratha’s death. Punish this bane of Kosala as you wish”.

In a fury frightening to behold, Bharata caught hold of Manthara. Impaled by his fierce looks, the hapless woman quailed with terror and shrieked again, as her friends fled the place to seek refuge in Kausalya. Hissing like an angry serpent, Satrughna struck Manthara’s ugly form. As he dragged her, all her ornaments broke and lay scattered while the pearls, the chains and the other baubles supposed to enhance her beauty lent their brilliance to the royal abode. The palace echoed with the howls of the mortally afraid woman who feared for her very life.

Satrughna dealt harshly with Manthara, in defiance of Kaikeyi. Even as the maid shuddered with fright witnessing his unleashed fury, Kaikeyi quickly hid behind Bharata. Bharata tried to quell his raging brother. “Though a sinner, a woman must not be killed. So escaped my first victim, this wicked Kaikeyi! Fear of Rama also holds me back, for he who is the very personification of dharma will never pardon us for defiling our hands by killing this wretched hunchback”. Manthara, saved by the dharma that the Ikshvakus lived by, was relieved.

She, whose counsel had benefited neither the counsellor nor the counselled, fell battered and bruised, at the feet of her saviour, Kaikeyi, who led her away.

Thus ends the seventyninth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

Summary

Sarga 79

All those concerned with the proclamation of Bharata as king assembled at the palace. They told their prince that, since Dasaratha was no more, and Rama along with Lakshmana was away, he was now their sovereign. “Though without a king, this country has not yet fallen prey to anarchy by the grace of god. The ministers, priests and the citizens of Ayodhya look forward to your coronation. Do accept the throne of Kosala.” Bharata, ever conscious of his duties and his dharma, circumambulated all that had been procured for his coronation and said, “Aware of the traditions of the Ikshvaku dynasty, does it befit you to crown me? Rama will be king and I will live in Dandakaranya, serving his fourteen-year-term. Let the four divisions of the army, chariots, horses, elephants and infantry march forth, carrying with them all that has been gathered here for the coronation. I will crown Rama who is the rightful heir to this throne and worshipfully bring him to Ayodhya like the holy fire borne to the sacrifice. Never will I lend myself to Kaikeyi’s scheming mind, who is mother to me only in name.” Those who had earlier misread Bharata’s intentions now lauded and blessed him for his magnanimity. Bharata also told the ministers to make all paths to Dandaka and back fordable and smooth for Rama’s homecoming.

Commending his noble thoughts, people left the palace with tears of joy in their eyes.

**Summary**

Sarga 80

As commanded by Bharata hordes of people moved towards Dandakaranya to meet Rama. Men skilled in clearing jungles led that mass of humanity which resembled a heaving,

blustering sea at full moon. Ahead of them went those adepts at filling ditches, bridging rivers and digging wells. Cooks, basket-weavers, boat-makers, sculptors and innumerable skilled and unskilled labourers along with their masters marched on. It was a labour of love.

Some chopped trees and some transplanted them. Some raised the ground while others levelled it. Paths and roads created were hardened with lime and mortar. Resorts surrounded by natural and man-made lakes and pools for the weary travellers sprung overnight. Lush trees bearing fruit and flower were hosts to myriad birds. The camping grounds of the royals on which stood the temporary mansions for Bharata and the other dignitaries were gorgeous like carefully crafted jewels.

The pathway dotted with temples added sanctity to the ambiance. Magnificent roads appeared from nowhere and on them travelled the endless sea of humanity. Soon they arrived on the banks of one of the most beautiful rivers on the face of the earth. Its crystalline waters bubbling, gushing and spraying mist coursed through hills, valleys and dales. Breath-taking from the top of its foam-crested waves to its cool depths, Ganga pulsating with life and beauty, hastened in turbulent joy to be one with the vast boundless ocean.

**Summary**

Sarga 81

The Sun set on the first day of Bharata's mammoth effort to lead Rama back to

Ayodhya. The small hours of dawn the next day saw the arrival of bards and minstrels, who sang praise of Bharata, which only reminded him of Rama. Commanding their silence, he

complained to Satrughna: Do you see how Kaikeyi has deluded the people? A kingdom rooted in righteousness is in peril. It drifts like a rudderless ship in a pathless ocean.

Meanwhile, Vasistha walked into the splendor of the golden hall inlaid with precious gems whose brilliance had not given way to the gloom that prevailed in the palace. He then ordered all the generals, ministers, brahmins and kshatriyas to assemble.

**Summary**

Sarga 82

In the middle of the elite assembly Vasistha addressed Bharata, "My son, placing this earth in your care, the king has departed and Rama who rivals Dasaratha in truth and dharmahas removed himself to the forest to redeem his father’s pledge. Your father and brother have given you custody of this land of which you are now the lord. May you soon be its crowned king.” Bharata found Vasistha’s advice opposed to the code of honour that he knew. “Rama,” he protested, “has not only acquired profound knowledge of the Vedas, but is also an ardent follower of dharma mentioned in every Veda. How can a son of Dasaratha bound by the scriptures steal the kingdom from his brother? Tell me what is righteous?"

Comparable to king Nahusha and Dilipa, Rama the first-born, alone is fit to be king. What the wise would not contemplate upon and what is opposed to the heavens is sin. It will bring infamy to foe noble race of the Ikshvaku. I condemn my mother’s transgressions and offer my homage to Rama who, deprived of his legitimate right, dwells in the forest. In the presence of all those assembled here, I vow to bring Rama back to Ayodhya failing which I shall stay there, like Lakshmana”.

Ayodhya rejoiced at Bharata’s nobility and his unswerving devotion to Rama.

When Bharata asked Sumantra to order the march of the armies, there arose a great clamour in the city of Ayodhya. In every home every wife demanded she be taken. People poured out of homes, mounted on every possible mode of transport. Brahmins, kshatriyas, vaisyas and sudras waited with bated breath, as did their horses, elephants, camels and donkeys.

As soon as Bharata’s magnificent chariot moved, the massive columns surged forward.

Thus ends the eightythitf sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki

**Summary**

Sarga 83

Bharata’s entourage of sixty thousand chariots filled with valiant men, carrying gleaming weapons was followed by skilled archers and soldiers, as well as a hundred thousand horses mounted by armed riders. The forward line consisted of the queens, Kausalya, Sumitra and Kaikeyi, their faces aglow at the prospect of soon beholding Rama. Citizens of Ayodhya came in hordes, anxious not to be left out of what seemed to be like a holy pilgrimage. Bharata’s retinue followed by priests and ministers was awesome and the nine thousand elephants that trundled along were royally bedecked from head to tail. Thousands forged towards Dandaka in bullock carts. There were merchants, potters, jewellers, hunters, goldsmiths, tailors, shepherds, jugglers, masons, distillers and carpenters. Along with them came cord-weavers, ivory-makers, confectioners and many more of diverse professions who, unwilling to be left behind, came in droves. But the one common cause of their travel, the only desire that made every one’s heart palpitate with excitement, was Rama. The very thought that they would soon be with him lent wings to their feet.

At Srngaberapura, a region under the rule of Guha, Bharata ordered the armies to disband for the night.

**Summary**

Sarga 84

Guha, the nishada chief, saw Bharata’s entourage spread out like a vast sea of humanity. Wondering and wary of its sheer size, unable to discern where it began and where it ended as part of it seemed to merge with the horizon, he told his people, “See that formidable army, the flag with the Kovidara emblem on the chariot means the presence of an Ikshvaku and I believe it belongs to evil-minded Bharata”. Frowning at what he thought was Bharata’s expedition against Rama, Guha grew anxious. He commanded his army to position themselves on the bank of the Ganga and keep strict vigil. He ordered five hundred boats, each manned with a hundred men ready to fight. If Bharata’s intentions were honourable, his armies were to safely cross the river. Having made his instructions clear, Guha went to meet Bharata, carrying gifts of fish, meat and honey.

Sumantra, happy to see Guha, counselled Bharata to receive the king who had thousands of kin familiar with the terrain of Dandaka. Moreover he was a dear friend of Rama and would tell them which part of the fearful forest had the good fortune of his graceful presence.

Guha approached Bharata and paid him homage, offering him and his people a bounteous feast of roots, fruits, and meat, dried and fresh.

Thus ends the eightyfifth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 85

Bharata said to Guha “Friend of Rama! we accept your generous hospitality” and the nishada chief, with doubts hovering in his mind, prodded, “Are you going without any evil intent to that embodiment of mercy, Rama, who harms none? Your large army makes me cautious and suspicious.” Tranquil as the blue sky, Bharata quietly replied, “Rama is more a father than a brother to me, Guha! Believe it, I’m now going to escort him back to Ayodhya”.

Guha’s frown gave way to a large smile. Relieved, he said, “Bless you and your magnanimity which makes you renounce a kingdom. May your fame be eternal” As they spoke, the Sun dipped down the western horizon and the brothers along with the army retired for the night.

Though Bharata lay down, the bliss of sleep evaded him and the night passed in a sadness he could not define.

Thus ends the eightysixth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 86

When Guha met Bharata, he beheld in the prince an unsurpassed devotion and a resolve that was unshakable. In him he saw a love whose burning intensity knew no release until Rama was crowned king. To lessen that agony, Guha told him of Lakshmana’s unparalleled servitude towards his brother. He elaborated on how meticulously and personally, Lakshmana oversaw all of Rama’s needs and comforts: “When Rama stopped here for a night, he stood guard with no thought of either rest or sleep. When I volunteered to keep vigil, would you know what he said? ‘ Seeing the son of Dasaratha sleep on the ground with Sita resting by his side, and still be alive is in itself impossible? How can I even think of sleep? And how can I be comfortable and happy? Look Guha, look at Rama, the most heroic of men whom the combined forces of the devas and danavas cannot vanquish! See him, who is the divine manifestation of his father! Dasaratha, Kausalya and Sumitra will not survive this separation from Rama beyond this night and the earth will be widowed with the death of the king. Sumitra may survive because of Satrughna, but Kausalya will not. Fortunate are Bharata and Satrughna who will perform the obsequies of my father. Only the blessed will inherit Ayodhya, a splendid city teeming with handsome people, horses, chariots and elephants.’”

Guha concluded his narration, saying that he had ferried the exiles across the Ganga from where they had entered the forest to begin the first day of their fourteen years exile.

**Summary**

Sarga 87

As he heard Guha, Bharata’s face clouded and he slipped into an anguished silence. Like an elephant goaded, he dropped to the ground as if to escape the agony of his mind. The queens rushed to him and Kausalya, embracing Bharata, gently said, “Is anything ailing you, my son? Is everything well with Rama and Lakshmana? With Dasaratha no more, you are our only refuge and solace”. Consoling Kausalya, Bharata asked Guha, “Tell me Guha, where did my brother sleep in this wilderness and what did he eat?” And Guha said, “Rama would not accept anything. Turning down even the food I repeatedly offered, the three of them fasted that night. Here at the foot of the ingudi tree rested Rama and Sita on a bed of grass made by Lakshmana, who guarded them, bow in hand, the entire night, trusting none else to perform that duty.”

**Summary**

Sarga 88

Bharata, showing the queens the tree under which Rama had slept, said, “How could this be! Did the precious body of Rama rest here on the harsh floor of the forest? Alas, mother! there is no power as irrevocable as destiny. How could a prince and his consort, used to the spledour of the palace, sleep here?

“If Sita did not mind the discomfort of this bed of grass, it was because she is a devout wife who would find anything acceptable so long she is with her consort. Lotus-eyed Rama, beloved of the worlds and handsome as a god roams this wilderness like an orphan and I am the cause! I bow my head in shame. Fortunate is Lakshmana and blessed is Sita for accompanying Rama while we, the unfortunate, live in fear that Rama may reject our services as we have abandoned him. Devoid of Dasaratha and deprived of Rama, the earth has lost its lustre. From now on, I too shall sleep on the floor, wear matted hair, put on robes of bark and live on roots and fruits. I will crown Rama as king of Ayodhya, where he shall stay with Lakshmana, protecting and gracing that most wonderful of cities. May the gods grant my desire.”

Thus ends the eighty ninth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 89

Guha arranged to ferry Bharata and his men across the river in five hundred boats. The one meant for the royals was ornate, embellished with gold and firmly put together with large nails of steel. Guha himself took charge of this resplendent boat on which sailed Bharata, Satrughna, priests, preceptors, brahmins and the queens. The clamour of embarkation reached a crescendo as the enthusiastic multitudes, splashed and jostled. Boats carrying chariots, carts and various animals followed while elephants goaded by mahouts crossed the river, appearing like mountains in motion. Some went by boat and raft, some rode elephants while some swam. Purified and blessed by the celestial waters of the Ganga, the army with its princes soon reached the other bank. Disembarking in the magnificent woods of Prayaga, Bharata commanded the army to rest, while he went along with Vasistha to pay homage to sage Bharadwaja.

**Summary**

Sarga 90

A league away from the hermitage Bharata stripping himself of his jewels and other royal trappings walked barefoot. Beholding them, Bharadwaja rose quickly, asking his disciples to get ready to welcome his honored guests. After greeting each other, Bharadwaja said, “Tell me Bharata, I know you rule Ayodhya, but Rama, the most renowned of men, has been banished by a father who has fallen prey to the wiles of his queen. Wishing to rid your kingdom of all enemies, have you come to slay that sinless Rama?” Bharadwaja’s words stunned Bharata as tears streamed down his face. In a voice that shook with untold anguish he said, “If you think I am to blame, consider me dead. How can you, with your knowledge of the past, present and future, accuse me of such an atrocity? I do not deserve your reproach nor am I responsible for what had happened during my absence from Ayodhya. I do not condone my mother’s actions, nor was I ever a party to her treachery. I am here to take Rama back to Ayodhya. Now sir, can you tell me where Rama may be found?”

Appeasing Bharata, Bharadwaja said, “To you, born of the race of the Ikshvakus, the qualities of responsibility, nobility, self-control and courage are natural. Bharata, I know the purpose of your visit. I questioned you only to enhance your renown as a faithful brother. Rama now lives on the Chitrakuta Mountain. Stay for the night. You may travel tomorrow.”

*ityevam ramamananam devanamiva nandane.*  
*bharadvajasrame ramye sa ratrirvyatyavartata..2.91.82..*

**Перевод:**

**As they were enjoying themselves in Bharadwaja's hermitage like the gods in the garden of Indra the night wore off.**

*pratijagmusca ta nadyo gandharvasca yathagatam.*  
*bharadvajamanujnapya tasca sarva varanganah..2.91.83..*

**Перевод:**

**Those rivers, the gandharvas and all those lovely women took leave of sage Bharadwaja and returned to where they had come from.**

*tathaiva matta madirotkata nara-*  
*stathaiva divyagarucandanoksitah.*  
*tathaiva divya vividhassraguttamah*  
*prthakprakirna manujaih pramarditah..2.91.84..*

**Перевод:**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavya ayodhyakande ekanavatitamassargah..*

Thus ends the ninety first sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 91

Bharadwaja requested Bharata to extend his stay by another day. He even asked the army into the hermitage against the wishes of Bharata who said that kings or princes should always spare hermitages from desecration as spirited horses and intoxicated elephants could damage plants and cottages. But the sage insisted. He invoked the powers that be to offer the best to his guests: “May Visvakarma, the architect of the world, create spacious shelters for my guests. May Indra, Varuna, Yama and Kubera provide sumptuous food and the rivers diverted here to bring waves of the best of wines. I invite Rambha, Menaka and Urvasi along with Thumbura to hasten along with their musical instruments to entertain our honored guests”.

In an instant celestial clouds showered flowers to the reverberations of divine drums and gongs, while the earth and sky hummed a melody. And then appeared a veritable paradise invoked by Bharadwaja and created by the gods. Its unparalleled beauty rivalled the very heavens.

For five yojanas on each side lay carpet-like grasslands lined with luxuriant trees of gooseberry, mango, jackfruit and more. Magnificent mansions had sprung all over. Even the animals had their ample resting places filled with cool lakes and green foliage. A lofty palace dazzling with turrets seemed to pierce the clouds. Furnished with rich carpets, filled with celestial scents, it was stocked with delectable food and ambrosial drinks of every kind. Bharata entered the gem-encrusted palace, followed by his bedazzled counselors. There they saw in an enclosure, a golden throne meant for Bharata who circumambulated it, as if Rama were already seated. He then took a seat meant for the ministers, worshipfully avoiding the throne intended for him.

Into that divine dazzle arrived twenty thousand apsaras sent by Bramha and bewitchingly beautiful women sent by Kubera. Thumbura and the gandharvas sang for Bharata while the celestials Allsmbusa, Punderika, Misrakesi and Vamana danced. Commanded by the sage, even the maredu trees played the drums, the Thandra rang the cymbals and the Bodhi trees danced. Mesmerized by the apsaras they swore never to return to Ayodhya nor enter the Dandaka. “Let Bharata live here and Rama be happy where he is” they declared. Eating, drinking and making merry, the soldiers wore garlands, danced and sang to their heart’s content. Cows poured out streams of milk and trees dripped honey. An unbelievable array of unguents, perfumes, mirrors and combs were provided. People bathed in shimmering lakes bright with lotus and lily and partook the wine called Maireya.

This day of feasting and festivity finally came to an end and Bharata took reverential leave of Bharadwaja.

Thus ends the ninety second sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 92

Bharata thanked Bharadwaja profusely for his lavish hospitality, which would forever remain a cherished memory in the minds of all of them. To Bharata pining to see Rama the sage said, “A few miles from here, where no men dwell other than the rishis, is the mountain known as Chitrakuta and to the north of it flows the river Mandakini. Between the river and the mountain is a cottage where Rama, Lakshmana and Sita dwell. Travel south from here and you will soon reach your destination.”

Then came the queens to pay their respects to the sage and Bharata introduced them: “The one who is emaciated with grief is Kausalya, foremost among the queens who bore a divine son, like Aditi bore Visnu. She who stands to the left plunged in sorrow is Sumitra, who holds middle place among the queens and mother to the celestially handsome and noble brothers Lakshmana and Satrughna.” The last was Kaikeyi of whom with utter disdain Bharata said, “This is the woman who sent the most virtuous among men to the wilderness and the noblest among kings to his death. An arrogantly ambitious woman who in her vanity believes herself the most beautiful and intelligent has imperiled the very world with her greed. She stands stripped of all respect whose virtuous facade belies her sinful nature. This is my mother, a ruthless woman full of evil and the cause of my misery.”

Bharata’s impassioned tirade was broken by his frustrated sobs. The red in his eyes matched the fire of his anger and the anger in his sighs matched the hissing of an angry serpent. Pacifying him, Bharadwaja in his wisdom said, “Do not deem Rama’s banishment to be Kaikeyi’s fault for in times to come it will prove a great boon for the devas, danavas and the rishis."

The night of revelry disappeared with the light of dawn. The apsarasas and gandharvas left, but the armies from Ayodhya still inebriated were in a dream-like state. Their crushed garlands bore testimony to a glorious night of song, dance and festivity.

Bharata was out on his journey, followed by an army that moved like a large cloud spreading over the entire southern region.

Thus ends the ninety third sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 93

Beholding the intimidating numbers invade their territory, the denizens of the forest scattered in fright. Elephants fled in terror, as dappled deer, bear and antelope ran helter- skelter. Reaching Chitrakuta, Bharata said “See these trees with their dark foliage crowned with fragrant flowers! The peacock tries to hide its spectacular plumage behind a rock! How enchanting! Is this the holy retreat of the rishis? It is like the threshold of heaven.”

Though spell-bound by the gorgeous display of nature’s beauty, not for a moment did Bharata’s mind lose track of Rama. Just then they saw a plume of smoke rise above the tree- tops. Was it the abode of Rama or of an ascetic who would guide them to him? A wave of happiness passed through the masses.

Bharata raced ahead with Vasistha and Sumantra, while the rest blissfully waited to see their beloved lord.
