**Summary**

Sarga 94

Sita had for a long time wanted to share the joys of nature with Rama. To make her happy and to revel in that happiness, Rama one day showed her the Chitrakuta Mountain, a mammoth heap of rock and forest. True to its name, Chitrakuta was a treasure-trove of nature’s wonders. Rama said, “Beholding this ravishing mountain, lost in this paradise, neither the loss of friends nor of the kingdom distresses me any more. In this splendor prevails a charm that mesmerizes even fearful beasts. The serene presence of the ascetics seems to have rendered them docile. The mango, gooseberry, neem, jackfruit, and bilva are among the hundreds that have the privilege of having Chitrakuta as their home. A playground of the celestials, this mountain seems to have shot out of the very depths of the earth. I can live here forever, for this mountain holds me a prisoner of its charms. Even my exile seems a blessing. My father cannot blame me for dereliction of duty and Bharata can rule in peace. At night the medicinal herbs on these majestic mountains show up their light, glowing like fire. O Sita! do you not wish to lose yourself in the song of the nightingale and be caressed by the cool breeze?

In this tranquillity and beauty will pass the fourteen years of my exile with you by my side. Treading the path of truth and following the kshatriya dharma of my race, I shall enjoy the life of a king.”

**Summary**

Sarga 95

Sita’s ever-serene face, luminous like the Moon, never ceased to enchant Rama. Every time he beheld her, his eyes opened wide in wonder at her breathtaking beauty. Revelling in her company, aware of her intense love of nature, he led Sita on to the banks of the river Mandakini. Its crystal-clear waters filled with lotus were vibrant with colour and the call of heron and swan.

Rama said, “The river seems to beckon me to bathe in it. The charm of this place rivals Kubera’s Saugandhika lake. Sita, come, bathe with me among the lotuses whose beauty will pale into insignificance in your divine presence. Vanquished, they will perhaps submerge themselves into the flow of Mandakini. From now on, think of the beasts of the forest as the citizens of Ayodhya, this river as Sarayu and Chitrakuta as the city we have left behind. Going through the ritual baths with you three times a day, living on honey and fruits, I desire neither kingdom nor kinsmen. No man seeing these elephants, lions and monkeys will tire of this forest, nor fail to wonder at the gorgeous display of nature’s best blooms, birds and all its bounties”.

**Summary**

Sarga 96

Having shown Sita the river that meandered at the foot of Chitrakuta, Rama sat with her on the hillside regaling her with his culinary skills. It was a blissful scene but bliss short-lived as Bharata would soon invade this sylvan paradise with his troops. Rama saw the dust kicked by Bharata’s vast army and heard its clamour. Rivalling the din of the approaching army, rose the thunder of alarmed animals racing away from a danger they could not define. Even mighty elephants turned tail and lumbered away as fast as their large legs could carry them. ”What are these sounds, Lakshmana? Has a king on a hunt frightened the denizens of the forest? See what causes this great terror” said Rama.

Lakshmana quickly clambered up a tree to scan the horizon. Towards the north, vast armies loomed clear and large with their horses, elephants, chariots, infantry and fluttering banners! Lakshmana called out to Rama, “Brother! I see troops. Put out the fire, hide Sita in the cave. Ready your bow, your arrows and your shield.” “Under which banner does the army march?” Rama asked, and replied Lakshmana: “I see the emblem of the Kovidara on the chariot. It is Bharata. The ruthless son of a ruthless mother. Not content with what he possesses, he perhaps comes to eliminate his enemies, you and me. Should we go up the mountain or remain here? Bharata shall pay for our misfortune. Kill him, Rama, and rule the earth. May Kaikeyi grieve, beholding her son destroyed like a tree felled by an elephant! I shall fight the army and slay Kaikeyi and the hunchback Manthara, ridding the world of a great taint.”

Lakshmana threatened to let

**Summary**

Sarga 97

As Lakshmana declared war on Bharata, Rama gently intervened, “Bharata, a virtuous archer, never takes arms unless occasion demands. Of what use are our bows and arrows when he himself comes here? What do I want with a kingdom gained by breaking a father’s promise and claiming a brother’s life? Akingdom begotten by the slaying of friends or relatives is poisoned food. If ever I desire anything, be they gems, jewels or the very world it is for the happiness of all my brothers. This sea-bound earth is not inviolable to me but if dharma does not allow it, I will not lay siege even if it were the throne of Indra. Having arrived in Ayodhya, Bharata must have been told of what had taken place during his absence. Honouring the Ikshvaku tradition, which decrees the crowning of the first-born, and distressed at my banishment, Bharata is here for the love of me. He is here to offer me the kingdom of Kosala. Lakshmana! what makes you suspect Bharata? Is it fear or injury done in the past? In no circumstances will a son kill a father. Nor will a brother kill a brother. You do not comprehend Bharata’s magnanimity. A word from me and he will crown you king of Kosala.” Subdued, Lakshmana came down the tree and stood beside Rama.

Meanwhile, Bharata’s armies came to a halt around Chitrakuta, forbidden by him to enter the sacred enclosure of the ascetics.

**Summary**

Sarga 98

While Lakshmana was suspecting Bharata of treachery and Rama was allaying those suspicions, Bharata was organizing his men. Guha was to take a thousand of his well-armed kin to carry on the search while he would walk with his gurus, his ministers and citizens. Satrughna was to lead the search with the hill people. Unable to endure Rama’s absence any longer, Bharata burst out, “Peace eludes me. So long as my brother and Sita are not found will my anguish continue. The unrest that rages in me will only be quelled the day Rama is crowned king of Kosala. Blessed is Lakshmana who always beholds Rama and blessed is Sita who for ever follows that lord of the earth. As Kubera brings splendor to Nandanavana, so does Rama to Chitrakuta”.

Striding hurriedly through clumps of trees towards the wisps of smoke, Bharata felt the thrill of a drowning man reaching the shores of a mighty ocean.

**Summary**

Sarga 99

Bharata’s excitement mounted as he neared the abode of Rama. Requesting Vasistha to bring the queens, he strode ahead. Beholding what seemed to be the leafy cottage of Rama, Bharata saw a pile of chopped wood and flowers gathered for worship. Dried dung of deer and buffalo lay piled to be burnt on a cold night. Strips of bark and pieces of reed were tied to trees and bushes as signs of different pathways. Bharata told Satrughna the smoke they had seen rose from the perpetual fires that the ascetics maintained in the forest for their worship. “Here I will surely behold my brother who inhabits these fearsome forests because of me. I will now absolve myself by falling at the feet of Rama, Sita and Lakshmana to regain their grace,” lamented Bharata.

What Bharata sought the moment he had heard the dreadful news of Rama’s exile, he now saw. An aura of profound sanctity prevailed around the cottage glowing with the effulgence of a sacrificial altar. There, gold-plated bows and formidable arrows sparkled and radiated light, like the rays of the sun. Razor-sharp swords rested snugly in scabbards of gold and shields of chased silver studded with yellow nails of gold twinkled like stars. Gauntlets and finger guards of deerskin embellished with burnished gold hung around, enhancing the magnificence of the awesome array of weapons.

Thus came into sight the most beautiful and sacred home of Rama, impregnable as a fortress and inviolable to the enemy. Neither man nor beast dared to tread its hallowed ground. Just as deer keep away from a lion’s lair, so did all keep away from the hermitage of that mighty prince of Ayodhya. Bharata’s roving gaze suddenly stilled. He stood transfixed as his eyes riveted on an image to behold which his soul had pined endlessly and his mind had

agonized relentlessly. He beheld Rama his brother and his very life, a life more precious than the one he recognized as his own. Mighty and broad-shouldered, with eyes like limpid pools, sat the lord of the ocean-bound earth on a pile of kusa grass, effulgent as the eternal Brahma and inviolable as Agni. By his side sat Sita and Lakshmana.

Bharata stood like one hypnotized as he looked unbelievingly. Snapping out of his trance, he broke down at the sight of Rama clad in ascetic garb. Choking with grief, he said, “An emperor who should be holding court with the most exalted of men that inhabit the earth, now sits, garbed in deer skin, attended by beasts that inhabit the wild. A body perfumed with rare unguents, caressed by the finest and most expensive of silks is now robed in coarse bark. How can Rama ever bear the weight of his matted locks?” Cursed be my existence that caused pain to all, they blame me for my cruelty and they blame me for depriving Rama of the luxuries of the palace”. Distraught, overwhelmed and unable to say even another word beyond ‘Arya’, he fell at Rama’s feet as did Satrughna.

Rama tenderly gathered them into his embrace even as his tears mingled with those of his brothers.

Thus ends the hundredth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 100

As Bharata lay on the floor, his grief was too terrible to behold. Rama could hardly recognize him whose body was emaciated and whose mind was ravaged by a great sorrow. Picking him up tenderly and kissing him on the forehead, Rama asked Bharata the reason why he was at Chitrakuta and not in Ayodhya, serving his father. “Has your inexperience imperilled Kosala? Why do you wander this wilderness, forfeiting that vast empire? How is our father? He would have never let you go if he were alive. He has not succumbed to his grief, has he? Does the renowned Guru of the Ikshvakus, Vasishta still command the respect of the people? Are Kausalya and Sumitra well and does Kaikeyi enjoy the kingdom she gained?

“A man of modesty and wisdom free from envy and of noble birth should be your preceptor. I do hope you continue worshipping the gods, pay homage to our ancestors, gums, ministers and relatives who are equals of our father. Do you honour Sudhanva, master of state craft and sciences, who is equipped with the most formidable arrows and mantra- propelled weapons? Have you ordained into your services men of honour who are skilled in the art of interpreting the motives of others by their behavior. Take counsel of those ministers who are your equals in virtue and who will not yield to bribery.

“Do not discuss affairs of the state late into the night. Decisions of importance should be made in the early hours of the morning and guarded well. Let not your plans or those of your ministers become public knowledge. Abandon a thousand fools but heed one wise man who can avert or handle calamities, for one wise man can render service that ten thousand fools cannot. A single minister who is discreet, brave and skilful can bring about great prosperity to kings.

“Do not embark on unworthy charities. Earning wealth by overtaxing your subjects, you will incur their scorn. Aking who cannot suppress the cunning and the greedy will instigate those who serve him to rebel, to injure or usurp the kingdom. Is the chief of your armies a man of good lineage, loyal, honest and wise who keeps enemies at bay?

“Do you honour and commend those soldiers who have served you beyond their call of duty? Skilled warriors and heroes should be recognized, praised and rewarded. Is the army paid on time and are all their needs implicitly taken care of? If not, they turn hostile. The men of the army should be of good stock and ready to give up their lives for you and your cause. An envoy chosen by you should be from Kosala, who can quickly grasp the intent of others, who can rise to any occasion and be adept at repeating as well as receiving messages. Keep watch over enemies whom you have vanquished and never underestimate them. Do not entertain foolish brahmins who have big ambitions and little knowledge. They bring disaster by indulging in futile talk, and contradict the laws of dharma. Ignoramus that they are, they pretend to be wise.

“Is Ayodhya, true to its name, impregnable and are you guarding it well? Protect the women of the palace, treat them with chivalry, but do not divulge any secrets to them. Discourage them from conversing with strange men. Are all forts well-equipped with men, food and weapons? Your expenditure should not exceed your revenue. All matters whether they pertain to the rich or the poor should be looked into with equal interest. The sons and the cattle of a king will soon perish by the tears of a man falsely accused by the king. For the sake of pleasure do not ever forsake dharma, artha and kama and may astute brahmins bless you with prosperity.

“Keep away from the transgressions of atheism, falsehood, anger and procrastination. Never neglect the wise nor indulge in indiscreet gratification of the senses. Do not disregard counsel in matters of state nor overlook execution of stipulated tasks. Avoid consulting men of little or no knowledge and battling on many war-fronts at the same time. Never respond to flattery.

“O Bharata, acquisition of fame without harm to righteousness, and prosperity without harm to integrity have no alternative. Do you tread the noble path that our ancestors walked? A monarch who rules the kingdom, abiding by the laws of dharma and who wields his sceptre with prudence leaves this world in glory to reach the land of the gods.”

## Sarga 101

**Перевод:**

*niskrantamatre bhavati sasite sahalaksmane.*  
*duhkhas okabhibhrtas tu raja tridivamabhyagat 2.101.6*

**Перевод:**

**"As soon as you set out for the forest along with Sita and Lakshmana, the king, overwhelmed with grief, attained heaven.**

*uttistha purusavyaghra kriyatamudakam pituh.*  
*aham cayam ca satrughnah prrvameva krtodakau 2.101.7*

**Перевод:**

**"Arise, O best of men! and offer libations to our father. I and Satrughna have already done so.**

*priyena kila dattam hi pitrlokesu raghava.*  
*aksayyam bhavatityahurbhavamscaiva pituh priyah 2.101.8*

**Перевод:**

**"O son of Raghu's race, it is said that whatever is offered by a dear son becomes eternal in the world of manes. You alone are the beloved son of our father.**

*tvameva socamstava darsanepsu-*

*tvaya vihina stava sokamagna-*  
*stvam samsmarannastamitah pita te 2.101.9*

**Перевод:**

**"Your father, deprived of you, brooding over you, wishing to behold you, unable to divert his mind fixed on you, remembering you alone and immersed in sorrow departed (from this world)".**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande ekottara satatama ssargah..*

Thus ends the hundred-one sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 101

Bharata, having listened to Rama, pleaded, “When I am already lost to righteousness, deprived of the dharma of serving you and now, when I have renounced the throne, how can I dispense royal duties? There exists an ancient custom in the Ikshvaku dynasty that decrees the ascendancy of the first-born to the throne. Come, return with me to the abundance of Ayodhya and crown yourself king for the greater glory of Kosala.

“Kings are mortal they say, but I deem them to be gods for being implicitly righteous in their pursuit of dharma. Their matchless virtues render them god-like. Bewailing you, yearning to behold you and unable to divert his mind from you, our father succumbing to his grief has departed to the land of the gods.”

**Summary**

Sarga 102

Bharata’s words hit Rama like a thunderbolt and he fell into a swoon. Weeping bitterly for not being able to even perform the last rites for that magnanimous king who had died grieving for him, he said, “I have no desire to go back to Ayodhya bereft of its king, even after the period of exile expires. I will miss his guidance and love.”

Trying to comfort Sita who sobbed inconsolably, he asked Lakshmana to get ready the ingudi cakes so that they could go to the river and offer their libations. Sumantra accompanied the princes to help them perform the ritual and Rama standing in the waters, turned south to say, “Father, you are now in the land of our ancestors, may the libations of this water reach you”. He then offered ‘pinda’ along with his brothers.

Meanwhile the waiting army hearing the mourning royals left their camp to race towards the direction of the sound terrifying the denizens of the forest.

The elephants trundled away into the neighboring jungles as panic-stricken herds of wolves, bears, buffaloes, apes and antelopes joined the flight. Petrified snakes slithered away in fright as ducks, cranes, geese, karandavas, cuckoos and kraunchas flew raucously in all directions. Into this din came the armies of Ayodhya. When they beheld Rama seated on the bare earth, their eyes brimmed with uncontrollable tears. They censured Kaikeyi and Manthara for the fate of their beloved lord even as Rama rushed to greet them.

**Summary**

Sarga 103

In the mean time Vasistha escorted the queens to Rama’s hermitage. Kausalya sighting the Mandakini said, “Look at this river, Sumitra! This is from where your dutiful son fetches water for Rama. May all those duties soon come to an end!” Noticing the ingudi cakes offered as pinda\\ her sorrow doubled. “A king, an emperor without equal and lord of the earth whose glory rivals that of Indra is offered lowly ingudi cake. I cannot deem anything more tragic and I grieve for Rama who could afford no more than this”. Tearfully reaching Rama’s humble house they beheld the light of the Ikshvakus glowing with the brilliance of an immortal cast out of the heavens. The sight shattered the queens.

Rama paid them his obeisance as did Sita and Lakshmana. Kausalya embraced Sita as a mother would her daughter, saying, “Sita my dear, your countenance bears witness to your distress and reminds me of faded lotuses and crushed lilies. Like the sheen of gold is lost in the dust that covers it, your glow is lost in the shadows of your exile”. As Kausalya anguished over Sita, Rama approached Vasistha to touch his feet in reverence,

Rama resolute in truth, Bharata in virtue and Lakshmana in strength blazed with the brilliance of sacrificial fires surrounded by the priests.

**Summary**

Sarga 104

To Rama’s query as to why he had come to Chitrakuta, renouncing a kingdom bestowed upon him, Bharata replied “Rama, while I was away at Kekaya, the king impelled by Êaikeyi, my evil-minded mother, bade you into the jungle. This shadowed father’s unblemished life and unable to endure your separation, he soon succumbed to his great grief. May that Kaikeyi, the reproach behind it all, be condemned to hell! Accept the throne which belongs to you. The people of Ayodhya, our mothers desire it and the earth wants to be united with her rightful lord.

Beholding Bharata’s anguish, Rama gently embraced him and said, “Bom of the peerless dynasty of the Ikshvakus, how can you, so disciplined, refuse to rule. I do not see any fault on your part and in your ignorance do not pile accusations on your mother. A mother deserves as much reverence as a father who is worshipped. The king alone has the authority to decide my place of domicile. You have to accept Ayodhya and I, Dandakaranya, as decreed by Dasaratha whose word is law. I do not want what he did not wish for me, even if it were the supremacy of the universe ”

Thus ends the one hundredfifth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 105

On the morrow, as every one sat around Rama but none spoke, Bharata finally said, “My mother is pacified, for heeding her wishes you gave me the kingdom. I now give it back to you. You alone can command Kosala. Just as a donkey cannot keep pace with a horse, or a small bird with that great Tarkshya, I too have not the power to emulate you. Blessed is the life of him whom others depend upon for their sustenance, but cursed is he who depends on others! Let the subjects behold you king of Ayodhya, like the resplendent sun.”

All those assembled applauded Bharata’s decision .But Rama disagreed.

Trying to reason with him Rama said, “Bharata! man is not independent of divine will nor is he master of his fate, for destiny is inexorable. Wealth amassed can vanish and lofty positions acquired can crumble. Every union ends in separation and life ends in death, just as every fruit that ripens has no other fear except that of falling from the tree. For every man bom, there is no fear other than death. The strongest homes built on mighty pillars fall to ruin as time passes and so do those who grow old perish with age.

“To grieve is unwise for whether one stands still or keeps walking, life will continue to ebb. Death walks with man and will sit, if he sits. It will travel to the end of the world with him if he wishes to travel long miles, and will come back with him when he does. The body wrinkles with age, and into the raven-black of the hair creeps the white of the snows. Youth fades and vitality diminishes but by what means can man escape these ravages of time? How can he rejuvenate himself and by what mortal power? Men rejoice over every sunrise and sunset, unaware that every passing morning and evening robs them of a day’s life. Oblivious that every season shortens his life span, man looks forward to every new season, enjoying every new experience and the mood they usher in.

“Inescapable is separation, for just as drifting pieces of wood which come together in the boundless main, toss around for a while and then drift apart, so do wives, children, relatives and riches. They remain together for some time to be separated again by the irresistible laws of destiny to which all life must bend and bow. Why lament for the dead who tears can never bring back. Like a flowing river life can never roll back to its source. It marches onward, relentlessly. Those who aspire to conquer the higher worlds must lead a life of compassion and obedience to the gurus, seeking only the pleasures that do not contradict the rules of dharma. There is no reason to grieve over our father who is now in heaven, with all his righteous duties on earth fulfilled. Lauded by men of great eminence, having enjoyed all the royal pleasures of life, Dasaratha, the lord, emperor of the earth, attained the heavens by merit of his abundant charities and sacrifices.

“After a long and glorious life, our father has reached where all men bom go. Casting away his mortal body, he now inhabits the world of Brahma. Dasaratha needs neither pity nor grief, for his life and deeds have earned him great glory and absolute supremacy over the entire earth. Higher than the glory of the kingdom is the spoken word of a king. A dutiful son should never disown his father’s righteous mandate. His wish that I live in exile while you rule Ayodhya is irrevocable. Death does not render a promise void, Bharata! return to Ayodhya and following the exemplary qualities of our father, be the king “. Thus Rama tried to convince Bharata to act according to Dasaratha’s mandate.

*vijitya tarasa lokanmarudbhiriva vasavah..2.106.27..*

**"After consecration, you too return to rule Ayodhya along with all of us like Indra who went back (to heaven), accompanied by Maruts after conquering all the worlds with his prowess.**

*rnani trinyapakurvandurhrdassadhu nirdahan.*  
*suhrdastarpayankamaistvamevatranusadhi mam..2.106.28..*

**"Discharging completely the three debts, to gods, to ancestors and to sages, subduing your enemies and gratifying your friends, you alone (have the right) to dictate me.**

*adya'rya mudita ssantu suhrdaste'bhisecane.*  
*adya bhitah palayantam durhrdaste diso dasa..2.106.29..*

*tathahi ramO bharatena tamyata*

*nacaiva cakre gamanaya sattvava-*  
*nmatim pitustadvacane pratisthitah..2.106.33..*

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande saduttarasatatamassargah..*

Thus ends the one hundredsixth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 106

Bharata, with love and admiration for Rama, said, “O Rama, misfortunes do not move you nor do joys elate you. Though most knowledgeable, you still seek counsel of your elders in all humility. What can disturb him who treats life and death, fortune and misfortune with such equanimity? How can adversities overcome him who is aware of the cause and effect of every happening in this world? You are the omniscient and omnipotent divinity. What can upset a man who condemns neither the dead nor the living, who craves neither for the unmanifest nor for the manifest. You are an embodiment of uprightness. If only the chains of dharma did not bind me, I would have punished my mother with death for her sins. Bom into the impeccable dynasty of the Ikshvakus as the son of Dasaratha, how can I take the blame for your heinous banishment? I shall not berate a god-like father in the presence of an august assembly, but tell me Rama, which man of dharma for the pleasure of a woman would commit such a sin? The saying that the minds of men are deluded at the time of their death has been proved true of Dasaratha. Set right the injury to dharma that has been caused so recklessly by the doting king.

“A true and worthy son commends his father’s righteousness but denounces his corruption. Be a worthy son and redeem the sins of your father. Protect the universe, the kingdom, our friends, our kin and the inhabitants of Kosala. Where is forest life and where is kshatriya dharma? Where are matted locks and where the governance of a kingdom? The primary duty of a kshatriya is to be crowned so that he may protect his subjects. Which man of the warrior class would set aside his duties, opting for an ascetic way of life that is dubious, purposeless and inauspicious? A kshatriya should rule the world of reality with its share of pleasures and sacrifices for his ultimate liberation.

“In knowledge, heredity and in age, I am younger than you, how can I be crowned? Let the counselors, subjects and priests headed by Vasistha consecrate you here and now. Return to Ayodhya. Redeem your debts to the devas, rishis and ancestors. Gratify the desires of your friends and subdue enemies. You alone are fit to rule. Free my mother of her blame and my father of his sin. If yet you persist, I too shall follow you.

The people of Ayodhya were proud of Bharata. They admired his reslove but watched helplessly as Rama turned down his every plea.

## Sarga 107

\[Rama advises Bharata to return back and rule the kingdom.\]

*punarevam bruvanam tam bharatam laksmanagrajah.*  
*pratyuvaca tata ssriman jnatimadhye'bhisatkrtah..2.107.1..\[183\]*

*tasmatputra iti proktah pitrmyatpati va sutah..2.107.12..*

**Перевод:**

*satrughnasahito vira saha sarvairdvijatibhih..2.107.15..*

Thus ends the one hundredseventh sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 107

Trying to convince Bharata and condone Kaikeyi, Rama said, “Bharata, your words are worthy of a noble son. But when Dasaratha married your mother he had promised the king of Kekaya that her son would be crowned king of Ayodhya. Later, in the war between devas and danavas, Kaikeyi received two boons from Dasaratha in gratitude for the services rendered by her. She has now redeemed those two boons in the form of my banishment and your coronation. Hence it is imperative that I live in the forest and you live in Ayodhya. Liberate Dasaratha from the bonds of his vows and make him happy. Return to Ayodhya now and rule the world of men and I will enter the Dandakaranya with Sita and Lakshmana to rule the world of beasts. You will be protected by the white royal umbrella from the rays of the sun and I by the leafy green trees of the forest. Satrughna will keep you company and Lakshmana, known as my best friend, will follow me.”

## Sarga 108

**Перевод:**

**"For a living being, the father is only a drop of white blood (semen). During her menstrual period this is blended in the mother's womb due to which a man is born in this world.**

*pravrtatiresa martyanam tvam tu mithya vihanyase..2.108.12..*

**Перевод:**

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye ayodhyakande astottarasatatamassargah..*

Thus ends the one hundredeighth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 108

While Rama was trying to convince Bharata to return to Ayodhya, Jabali the eminent brahmin pronounced words that were contradictory to the very concept of dharma, “Rama,” he said, “alone we come and go alone. We do not belong. Nor does this world belong to us. We are travellers and this life is just a break in our long journey. We cultivate attachment for the wrong reasons. Dasaratha was a stranger to you. He has gone where he ought to go. All that is mortal is transient and you grieve in vain. In the name of the astaka sacrifices food is offered to the spirit of the dead. Do the dead really partake of it? If what a person eats can enter the body of another, then ‘shraddha’ can be offered to one who travels long distances. Will that then become food for him on his way?

## Sarga 109

\[Rama's justification for adhering to the supreme values of dharma and truth.\]

**Summary**

Sarga 109

Unmoved by Jabali’s words, Rama said in defence of the Vedic injunctions “I respect your zeal for my coronation which prompts you to contradict the accepted norms. Your intent may sound honourable, but it is not. A man transgresses when he ignores the code of conduct. From the way one lives you know whether he is bom noble or base, courageous or cowardly, honest or deceitful, ethical or unethical. He who shirks his duties commands no respect from the upright.

“Vile or virtuous, as the king, so are his people. The lords of the earth must be righteous. Morality is the soul of governance, truth sustains and enriches it. On the foundation of truth rests the world and so do all offerings, sacrifices, libations, asceticism and the Vedas. Loyalty to one’s word is the core of virtue. Never will I abandon my duty and my dharma. The ancestors and devas will not accept the offerings of those who are false to their promises. The mind conceives sin, the tongue utters the falsehood and the body executes it. Threefold are the paths of sin.

“Sire, disregarding the commands of my father should I yield to Bharata’s wishes? Death does not change the nature of a promise made. We are bom in this world of 'karma' and must perform righteous action. Even gods reap the fruit of their action. Ahundred sacrifices earned Indra the kingdom of heaven. Rigorous penance has paved the way of the ascetics into the land of the immortals. Jabali! I condemn your failure to protect the Vedic inj unctions and I look down upon this act of my father that ordained you into his services. You are an atheist. You misguide the minds of men.”

To this-incensed reaction Jabali replied gently, “Rama, I am no atheist, nor do I believe there is nothing beyond this manifest world of reality. I instigated this controversy only to establish you in this world as one who would never deviate from the path of truth.”

**Summary**

Sarga 110

Vasistha intervened, “Rama!” he said, “it is only to prevent you from going into exile that Jabali spoke as he did. Listen to the story of the creation of this world: “In the beginning all was water from which emerged the earth. Then came Brahma and the devatas. Assuming the form of a boar, Lord Visnu caused the earth to rise out of water. The changeless and imperishable Brahma with his son Marichi brought forth this manifest world. Marichi begot Kasyapa whose son was the Sun. It was Ikshvaku, son of Manu and grandron of the Sun who was Lord of men. Manu gave this earth to Ikshvaku and thus Ikshvaku became the first king of Ayodhya.

Kukshi was bom of Ikshvaku. Vikukshi, his son, begot Bana. The renowned, Anaranya was Barn’s son during whose reign neither famine nor drought was heard of. Anaranya begot Trishanku who bodily ascended the heavens. His son Dhundhumara begot Ruvanasva. The next in the line of the Ikshvaku dynasty were Mandhata and Susandhi. Dhruvasandhi and Prasenajit were the sons of Susandhi. Dhurvasandhi’s son Bharata was followed by Asita. One of Asita’s two consorts gave birth to Sagara who dug the oceans. Asamanjasa, Sagara’s son was exiled for his wickedness. He was succeded one after the other by Anshuman, Dilipa, Bhagiratha, Kakustha, and Raghu.

After many generations down the line of the Ikshavakus was born Aja, son of Nabhaga who begot your father, the virtuous Dasaratha, You are his first-born. This is the tradition of the house of Ikshavakus. Do not violate the rule of your dynasty.”

Thus ends the hundredeleventh sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 111

Vasistha went on to tell Rama that every man born has his mother, father and teacher as his three gums. “The parents give birth to the body of man but it is the gum who instructs him in knowledge and wisdom and so is considered superior. I was your father’s gum and so am yours. By obeying me, you will not be straying from the path of dharma in ruling the kingdom of Ayodhya. Fulfil your mother’s wish, she deserves a hundred times more reverence than your father. You will neither be false to yourself, nor will you violate the truth, nor abuse your power by conceding to Bharata’s wishes”.

But Rama who thought otherwise said, “It is hard to repay the debt of parents who love and cherish their children. Dasaratha is my father and the promise I made him shall never be rendered false.” So deep was Bharata’s disappointment that he requested Sumantra to get some kusa grass on which he would lay himself, barring Rama’s passage. When Sumantra hesitated, Bharata got it himself and sitting on it asked the people of Ayodhya who had assembled there, “Can any one of you persuade Rama to return?” But the loyal subjects quietly said, “Rama who treads no other path than that of Dharma is living as commanded by Dasaratha and that makes his decision final and not open to any further debate”. Rama asked Bharata, “Did you hear what the people had to say?” Bharata then said “Ministers and men of Ayodhya! listen to me, I never asked my father to enthrone me, nor did I ever counsel my mother in this matter and most importantly, I never consented to Rama’s exile. Since one of us should remain here, it is I who will do so.”

Rama admired Bharata’s words, but, bound by his impeccable standards, said, “Death does not change the nature of an oath, Bharata. My commitment to my father is still sacred and can never be changed or broken. I wish to honour his words and liberate him from his vows. My return to Ayodhya with you will make me unworthy.”

Thus ends the hundredtwelfth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 112

The great maharshis who had heard the conversation between Rama and Bharata were amazed at this display of loyalty and love between the brothers. “Blessed is Dasaratha who has such commendable sons,” said they.

Bharata continued battling with Rama’s will by falling at his feet and imploring him to go back to Ayodhya. But Rama gently seated Bharata by his side and said, “Groomed by the gurus and armed with wisdom, you are capable of ruling the entire earth. Ministers, friends and the learned of the land will counsel you in every way. The Moon may be deprived of its glow, the snows may desert the Himalayan peaks, and the oceans may trespass onto alien shores but never shall I taint the memory of my father, nor render his promise void. Kaikeyi vested this kingdom on you, obey her, Bharata!”

Beholding Rama effulgent as the Sun, caressing as the Moon, and steadfast as the mountain, Bharata finally came to terms with the irreversible. “Rama,” he entreated, “give me your sandals, for they alone will ensure prosperity and safety to Ayodhya”. Rama protested no more. He wore his sandals once, and then gave them to Bharata who said “For fourteen years I too shall live with matted hair, clothed in bark, subsisting on fruits and roots. Awaiting your arrival, I will live outside Ayodhya. The sandals will rest on the throne and I will rule on your behalf. If at the end of the fourteen years I do not see you, I shall cast myself into the fire”. Rama agreed, and embracing Bharata and Satrughna, bade them a tearful farewell. His parting advice to Bharata was, “Protect your mother. You are under oath and answerable to Sita and me”.

Sorrowful and painful was the parting to all.

**Summary**

Sarga 113

Holding Rama’s sandals on his head, Bharata mounted the chariot along with Satrughna, Vasistha, Vamadeva and Jabali. When the royal entourage came to the hermitage of

Bharadwaja, he got off to pay homage to the sage, who asked him of Rama’s decision. Vasistha said that neither Bharata nor he could cause the smallest ripple in Rama’s resolve. Bharata would install Rama’s sandals on the throne of Kosala where they would be symbolic of Rama’s authority, while Bharata would only rule on behalf of his brother.

Impressed with Bharata’s magnanimity, Bharadwaja said, “Though Dasaratha is dead, he is immortalized by your nobility and generosity”. Bharata took worshipful leave of the holy ascetic. After crossing the cool waters of the rivers Yamuna and Ganga the royal retinue passed through Srngiberapura on the way to Ayodhya. The people and the armies that had streamed out of that city in search of Rama now flowed back. Beholding an Ayodhya bereft of his father and brother, a great melancholy descended upon Bharata who said to Sumantra, “Charioteer, behold Ayodhya, a city of unparalleled beauty, which is now devoid of all charm. Its streets are no longer vibrant with its happy throngs. Pallid and lusterless, the desolation that pervades seems to have also rendered it mute.

**Summary**

Sarga 114

In the city of Ayodhya which had grown dark and gloomy only bats seemed to fly in freedom. No elephants roamed, no chariots thundered down its streets. The sharp rays of the Sun had deprived the rivers and lakes of much of their waters. The city of the Ikshvakus which once rivalled the Amaravati of Indra is now desolate where even the golden flames of the sacrificial fire has dwindled.

Silent as a waveless sea, Ayodhya lay drab and dim like a meteor spent. The scent of flowers, sandalwood and the burning of incense no longer pervaded the air. Passing through this sombre silence, Bharata asked, “Where is the fragrance of unguents and flowers that had filled the very air of the city, Sumantra? Where is the cacophony of racing chariots, drumming hooves and trumpeting elephants? The absence of Rama has robbed Ayodhya of all its splendor and cheer. Coming back from his exile, he will be welcomed like the rain-bearing clouds on a hot, summer day!”

When Bharata finally entered the palace, it reminded him of the empty den of a lion.

**Summary**

Sarga 115

Bharata installed the queens in the palace and informed his gurus that he would live in Nandigrama. “There shall I deal with the grief of Rama’s exile that ever haunts me and await his return.” Vasistha blessed Bharata for his veneration of Rama, his love for his kinsmen and his adherence to dharma. Bharata then took leave of the queens, his gurus and ministers and rode away, accompanied by Satrughna, preceded by Vasistha and the brahmins. As they travelled towards the east, even the inhabitants and armies of Ayodhya followed him to Nandigrama without invitation.

Bharata installed Rama’s sandals ceremoniously on the throne of Kosala and coronated them as he would the person of Rama, declaring, “As custodian of the kingdom, I shall protect them and when Rama returns from his exile, I shall serve him with the same veneration as I would Dasaratha”. True to his word, Bharata lived the life of an ascetic. Robed in bark, with his hair matted, he lived humbly and ate frugally. Bharata ruled Kosala from Nandigrama with his ministers and counselors. All authority and power rested with the sandals, symbols of Rama’s rule. Any event, small or big, had to be graced by them and any article of value, gifted or brought, was to be first presented to the throne.

Rama’s royal presence was felt at all times.

Thus ends the hundredsixteenth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 116

Meanwhile, at Chirtrakuta, as Rama prepared for his departure to Dandakaranya, he noticed that the sages too were preparing to leave. They kept looking at Rama, their faces full of animation as they talked in low tones among themselves. Beholding their restlessness, Rama reverentially asked their leader “Have I transgressed any way? Why do these holy men want to leave? Has Lakshmana harmed them any time? Has Sita, engrossed in my service, ever overlooked anything to cause you displeasure?”

The chief of the ascetics said, “How can Sita, the most virtuous among the women of this world, ever steeped in dharma, commit a sacrilege especially against the sages? In this forest lives Khara, the rakshasa brother of Ravana who destroys all that comes his way feasting on the flesh of men whom he ruthlessly massacres. Many are the marauders who descend upon the hermitages repeatedly with their abominable forms, which are unseen and unheard-of on this earth. When these wretches with twisted limbs and blood-shot eyes go on rampage they leave behind the dead, the mutilated, and the tortured. They disrupt sacrifices and create fear in this region; their carnage is beyond human endurance. We are moving back to our peaceful hermitage, which we had inhabited earlier. Though you are mighty and invincible, life here will always be imperilled. Come, travel with us.”

Rama tried to dissuade the sages but in vain. Walking with them for a while before bidding them farewell, he remained for some more time at Chutrakuta.

Thus ends the hundredseventeenth sarga in Ayodhyakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 117

Sometime after the exodus of the sages, Rama too moved away from Chitrakuta as memories of Bharata’s visit of the places where he had seen his mother and met with his people kept coming back to him. Their journey soon brought them to the hermitage of sage Atri who along with his wife Anasuya gave them a warm welcome. He told them that for a period of ten years, while the world went through a great famine, Anasuya had not only kept producing roots and fruits but had also kept the Ganga flowing. A lady of relentless discipline, she had spent ten thousand years in penance. “Anasuya who is steeped in dharma is like a mother to you, pay her obeisance,” said Atri. Sita did so to that sagacious lady, true to her name, and worshipped the world over.

Anasuya, old, wrinkled and fragile, looked at Sita with great affection and said, “Sita, you are so fortunate and your adherence to dharma so commendable. Leaving behind your parents, relatives and position, you followed Rama during his years of exile. Noble women, who love and serve their husbands regardless of their being rich or poor, sinful or righteous, will ascend to the land of the gods. There is no kinsman closer than a husband. Walk the path of dharma with your Lord.”

**Summary**

Sarga 119

At the end of the narration, Sita found herself in Anasuya’s warm embrace. Anasuya kissed her tenderly and said “Sita, your story told so gracefully and sweetly gladdens my heart. The mantle of darkness has descended upon the earth, birds have reached their nests and sages, their clothes dripping wet with their evening ablutions, return home. The marauders of the night prowl and the deer sleep. Go to Rama, adorn yourself with the silks and jewels so that I can feast my eyes on you”.

Sita, robed in all finery and bejewelled, looked like a goddess, a radiance that had taken the form of Sita.

Happy at all the attention and affection showered on Sita, Rama spent that night in the sacred hermitage of sage Atri. On the morrow, their ritual worship done, they bade farewell to the holy men, who warned them of rakshasas that infested the forests: “Beware of man-eating demons and blood-drinking beasts who, with their hideous forms, terrorize all and any that cross their path. Travel the way frequented by the rishis”.

Blessed and honored by them, Rama entered Dandakaranya

Amrutakataka - Rama, Lakshmana and Sita visit the hermitage of Sage Bharadwaja 2.54.1-27

Bharadwaja offered them ‘Madhuparka’ (bananas dipped in milk and honey).

Dharmakutam - Greeting a brahmin 2.54.10-12

On entering the hermitage of Bharadwaja, Rama followed by Sita and Lakshmana, stayed away at some distance.

Makhi explains why: 1) to inform the sage about their arrival through one of his disciples, 2) to avoid greeting the sage in case he is preoccupied with the daily ritual of fire-worship and 3) to avoid causing delay to the ritual as the sage would need to attend to the atithis.

Apastamba- ??? One must not greet a brahmin preoccupied with japa and homa.

Worshiping a king 2.54.17, 18

Even a brahmin should offer madhuparka (ceremonial welcome-worship) to a king.

Apastamba, Grihya of Chandogas, Bodhayana, Manu, Gautama are quoted as authorities and for details of worship like the persons who deserve such worship, the occasions and the objects to be offered.

Makhi further explains: These special guests must be offered this honour when they come home for the first time. Later it should be offered when they come after a gap of one year. On the occasions like wedding, sacrifice and so on it must be offered even within a year. If a king is also a Vedic scholar this honour must be given to him every time he comes and if he is just a king only a seat and water should be offered every time.

Tattvadipika -Bharadwaja’s perception of Rama's true form 2.54.19-26

Bharadwaja along with birds and beasts of the forest worshipped Rama. The idea is, even birds and beasts served Rama like sages on account of Bharadwaja’s influence. He tells Rama that he has seen him after a longtime, meaning that he has always contemplated upon him as God who cannot be comprehended by sense organs. “It is a wonder that I see you in front of me after a long time. How can I describe my luck!” he exclaims.

Rama tells Bharadwaja “Omniscient seer! if you disclose that I have descended into this world for slaying Ravana, the the people will know I am Visnu and Sita is Lakshmi and will come here to see us. I do not like that kind of revealed living. Youbeing very dear to me you may see my real form, which is a secret of secrets. But do not disclose the same. \|n my form which is full of bliss Vaidehi alone revels and is one who is sought by Lakshmi who carries a lotus in her hand and who is herself sought and served by all other beings. Lakshmi is always yearning to experience me. Even though she has that experience of bliss continuously she loves to have it as if she started it just now. That abode of mine is the support of the whole universe. By virtue of its state, qualities and glory it is higher than Brahma and Rudra. So do not reveal this form of mine.”

\[The commentator attributes many meanings to the words of Rama and tries to show that Rama is an incarnation of Visnu and that Rama does not want thatfact to be revealed to ordinary folks.\]

Holiness of Prayaga 2.54.22

This refers to the holiness of Prayaga.

Maha. (Vana.) Sage Dhaumya explains the derivation. Prayaga is so called because in the past (pra=prak=prachinakale) Brahma performed a sacrifice (yaga) here.

Pulastya’s pilgrimage, Upashtambhika Shriti, ancient traditional citations also describe the holiness of the place and the mythological stories associated with it.

Kalidasa - ???

(This place is so holy that those who end their life here are released from rebirth even without being enlightened regarding the final truth).

Moha 2.54.28-31

Maha. (Vana.) describes the exalted status of mount Chitrakuta as a holy place.

Tilaka - Kapalasirasasah 2.54.31

To some, Kapalasirasasaha means ‘entering the heaven with the physical body.’ But to Kataka, ‘It is true that Yudhishtira went to heaven with his physical body but only to watch the pleasures and comforts of heaven. But when his time came to go to heaven, he left his body and entered heaven.’

Crossing a river 2.55.14-18

One should never swim across a river, say Apastamba and Manu.

Praying to trees 2.55.24, 25

This suggests that one must pray with folded hands to big trees standing on the way during one’s journey. See Apastamba.

“O tree, may fire, wind and axe stay away from you. (May you be always protected from dangers which can destroy you). May rain pour on you. May fortune favour you.

Ideal place to reside in a forest 2.56.12, 15

Rama likes Chitrakuta where there were many trees that yielded fruits and where many sages were already residing and finds it a very comfortable place to stay in. Gautama- “A place where sacrificial fuel, water, fodder, kusha grass, flowers are available in plenty, where there is a way nearby for going out, where saintly people already reside in majority and which is well-equipped with similar facilities is an ideal place for residence in forest”.

Meeting with Valmiki 2.56.15-18

In the beginning of the Ramayana, it is said that sage Valmiki lived on the bank of river Tamasa. How is it that the three met him in Chitrakoota? The answer is, he was originally living here, and when the coronation of Rama was to take place after a long time, he had shifted to the bank of the river Tamasa.

On Valimiki 2.56.16

Perhaps the same Valmiki whom Rama, Sita and Lakshmana met in the hermitage of Chitrakuta later went to the bank of Tamasa during the reign of Rama.

Rama undertakes the time-honored house-warming ceremony 2.56.22-35

Rama and Lakshmana killed a she-deer for sacrifice to the gods presiding over the newly built hut. It is no sin, no cruelty as it is a part of the prescribed rite according to the sacred texts. Even the prey sacrificed attains final beatitude.

Vastusamanam 2.56.22

The word vastuis a synonym of grha, which means ‘a house’. Howeverhere it signifies the fortyfive presiding deities of a house like Agni Parjanya etc. Samana means propitiation with homa, naivedya (offering food) and bali(items of worship).

Animal sacrifice as an offer to (God 2.56.23—26

Rama clears the doubt about the blemish or sin that could arise from animal sacrifice as described by Bodhayana. \|t is a dharma and there is no possibility of any sin caused by violence. Since the animals that are killed forsacrifice reach higherand betterworlds, slaying is a boon for them. The Vedas state that they do not die, but take a sacred path to the place of the gods. They go to a place where only the meritoriousgo and not the sinners. Lord Savitr(Sun-god) helps them in theirjoumey.

\[The commentator quotes the sruti and smrti to show that Ra ma did not commit any sin when he got a deerkilled forthe rituals of house-warming.\]

Vasthusamana 2.56.29, 35

Describes the details of Vastushamana i.e. purifying rites performed to propitiate the deity of the residence before entering it. This suggests that worship of the Vastu (site of residence) deity, offerings to beings and such other rites must be performed before entering a new house after ascertaining an auspicious time, Ashvalavana, Apastamba, Cchandoga Brahinana, Khadira Grihya:

The site for the house should have a natural growth of harmless trees and plantr in abundance. The land should not be saline. Trees containing milky saps or thorny plants if any must be uprooted. Natural growth of kusha (Poa cynosuroides: sacred grass used at certain religious ceremonies, a grass with long pointed stalks) and virana (Andropogon Muricatus: a type of fragrant grass) type of grass is desirable, apamarga (Ackyranthes Aspera: the plant commonly called prickly chaff flower employed very often in incantations, in medicine, in washing linen, and in sacrifices), shaka (Tectona Grandis or Acacia Sirissa or Terminalia Chebula: the teak tree), tilvaka (Symplocos racemosa or Terminalia Catappa) and parivyadha (Calamus Fasciculatus or Pterospermum Acerifolium) should also be removed. There should be plenty of water easily accessible. The shape of the plot should be square or a rectangle. Specific colour of the soil is recommended for different castes, etc.

The period from Rama’s departure to Dasaratha’s death 2.57.2

Informed by the spies of Guha, Sumantra left for Ayodhya. Rama along with Sita and Lakshmana took two days to reach Sringaverapura. On the second day, they crossed the river Ganges. Sumantra stayed at the place of Guha for three days. In the afternoon of the third day, having got the information about Sri Rama from the spies of Guha, he returned to Ayodhya. In the morning of the sixth day he reached Ayodhya and in the midnight of the same day, the king expired.

According to Tilaka, the schedule of Sumantra and Dasaratha’s death mentioned in the Valmiki Ramayana synchronizes with that of Padmapurana. Thich says, ‘On the midnight of the sixth day of Rama’s exit from Ayodhya the king died, muttering ‘O Lakshmana! O Sita! O Rama!’

Sumantra delivers the message of Rama 2.58.5-12

I shall survive on the strength of the fullest account of my sons and daughter-in-law, even as King Yayati, when hurled down from heaven with the stock of his merits exhausted through self-praise, lived happily in the midst of pious souls’ says Dasaratha to Sumantra.

The account of Yayati, as told in the Mahabharata is as follows: (vide - Adiparva - ch 82): Rajarsi, Yayati attained heaven by his enormous merit. Once Indra, in order to test him, asked, “Yayati, who indeed is equal to you in austerities?” Yayati, in utter arrogance, replied, “None among the celestials, humans, gandharvas or renowned sages.” As he insulted all the species by his reply, Indra cursed him: “Drop down, O Yayati, from heaven.” Yayati requested Indra, “O King of the gods, having lost my abode in celestial region, pray, permit me to live in the midst of virtuous souls.” Indra granted him his wish.

Similarly, Dasaratha says, “I must live in the midst of hearing the account of my virtuous son, Rama, his younger brother, Lakshmana and my noble daughter-in-law, Sita.” Or, “give me the account of Rama who was thrown out of my kingdom, resembling heaven and went into the midst of virtuous ascetics in the forest.”

(Note: Actually, it was only Rama who sent the message as per earlier references. But it is now understood that Lakshmana also had his message sent.)

Legend of Yayati 2.58.12

When Dasaratha asked Sumantra about where Rama lives and what he eats, Sumatra tells him that Rama is like Yayati who volunteered to go down to the earth and live in hermitages. Like Yayati who prayed to Indra that he should be allowed to fall down on earth where sages lived, Rama left Ayodhya for the hermitages of good souls in the forest.

Dasaratha asks Sumantra to describe Rama’s living in the forest so that he could live by hearing of Rama.

Lakshmana’s remarks on Dasaratna’s decision2.58.26—33

“Even an elderly person should be abandoned if be is devoid of the ability to know what is right and wrong, How can the world love Dasaratha? How could he be a king?”

Lakshmana’s attitude is natural but contrasts with that of Rama, whose nature is exemplary. Rama shows full respect to Kaikeyi who was the cause of his banishment.

Lakshmana’s message to the king 2.58.28-31

‘Your Majesty, for what offense is Prince Rama banished? You have carried out the command of Kaikeyi forthwith. You did not think whether it was right or wrong as a result of which we are put to unnecessary suffering. Whether Rama has been exiled out of Kaikeyi’s greed for power or because of the so-called boons, you have perpetrated a wholly unwelcome act. As a husband, your Majesty had a right to properly educate her and persuade her to righteousness. If she did not mend, she ought to be put out. Your Majesty ought to have told her that the question of kingship should be resolved ‘not by me only, but by the ministers, leaders etc.’ On all these counts, I do not regard the emperor as my father at all. Rama is my elder brother, master, and a father too. You, as king, may be good for your subjects. But the populace will not condone this act of yours. Having committed this offense, you have gone against all righteousness.”

Who can’t become a king 2.58.33

A person causing anxiety to people can never become a king and even though he does, he is very soon deprived of that position: Maha. (Udyoga.)

Feelings of the horses 2.59.1-2

The horses were unwilling to tread the path Sumantra showed. The idea is, the horses thought that the opportunity to serve Rama, but luckily and accidentally obtained by them as now lost which is not easily available even to gods like Brahma, Rudra and \|ndra because of unkind kaikeyi, they think their life is futile. They shed tears.

Grief of the citizens of Ayodhya 2.59.14

Though Rama went into exile on the command of Kaikeyi or by the dictates of destiny, the grief of the people makes one unable to identify whether they are Rama’s friends, his enemies or his neutrals. The purport is, all the people of Ayodhya, including Rama’s friends, enemies, if there were any, and the neutrals lamented equally without any difference.

Kausalya’s fear 2.59.18-33

Kausalya was caught in a two-fold fear: What will happen to Rama in the forest and to Dasaratha in Ayodhya?

2.59.18-20

The repentance of Dasaratha suggests that a king must never take important decisions without consulting his ministers, advisers in matters of religion, and close friends, otherwise big calamities await him Maha. (Sabha.) Narada tells Yudhishthira about the fourteen blemishes of a king among which is listed ekachintana (self-counselling). Even well-established kings are ruined due to these flaws.

Dasaratha’s lamentation 2.59.27; 61.20

Dasaratha’s grief which was immense like the sea was due to his feeling that he may not live till the time he meets Rama again. He suspected Rama, being an elder brother, may not accept the sovereignty which was already enjoyed by his younger brother as it becomes like a left-over food. Compelled by the desire to see his father he may remain with him as long as he lives, but certainly he would not accept to rule the kingdom.

Sumantra consoles Kausalya 2.60.1-23

Sumantra was a man of worldly wisdom. Never tell a truth that is not pleasant. It is a keynote instruction. As such, though Sita had uttered the words in her sorrow, he did not repeat them before Kausalya, as it would increase her sorrow. Therefore Valmiki says: Avoiding the reference that had slipped off his lips through inadvertance, Sumantra began to speak agreeable words that brought delight to the queen.

Sumantra reports about Sita 2.60. 11-20

Sita plays with Rama like a young girl. Since Sita’s mind is fixed on Rama, even the forest appears to her like Ayodhya in bis presence. Sita does not wear ornaments because they impede walking. Even so while she walks, she appears to be having all the charm of the ornaments, or Sita likes the ornaments and wears them even when she has to walk.

This suggests that Sita always wore ornaments. Bharata’s word (manye sabharana sputa), that is, "I think she slept with her ornaments on”, supports this idea.

Queen Kausalya blames the King 2.61.2-26

“Illustrious monarch! great, indeed is your glory, which is extended to the three worlds. You are hailed as compassionate, generous and soft in speech. But, in the case of Rama and Sita, your action belies your glory. They are banished without any compassion. How can your sons along with Sita brought up in the comfort of the royal palace endure the misery of living in a forest? How will that young and lovely Sita, delicate in frame, bear heat and cold? How can she who enjoyed refined music withstand the harsh roar of lions that feed on flesh? How can Rama repose, pillowed upon his arm? When shall I see his lovely countenance decked with lovely locks, looking like a fully blossomed lotus? Alas! My heart does not break.

“Granted that Rama returns to Ayodhya in the fifteenth year from now on, it s not expected that Bharata will give up his kingship or exchequer. There is no guarantee that Bharata, on his own volition, will hand over the sovereignty to Rama as a mark of his brotherliness. Even granting that Bharata agrees to pass on the reins of sovereignty, how can Rama accept it, once it is enjoyed and left over by a younger brother?

“Illustrious brahmins, virtuous and learned will not like to enjoy the food left over in a shraddha. They deem it an offense and disrespect just like the mighty bulls feel when their graceful horns are cut. Cutting off the tip of the horn may also mean: just as the mighty bulls refuse to enjoy eating the tender grass already cut at the top and eaten by younger ones, so the virtuous seniors reject what has already been enjoyed and left out by the juniors. Likewise, O Monarch, how can Rama, the seniormost, both in terms of age and virtue accept the kingdom already enjoyed by Bharata, junior both in terms of age and virtue? He may take it as an insult. It is well-known that a mighty tiger will not like to eat the flesh brought and eaten by other low animals like fox. In the same way, Rama, a tiger among men, will not enjoy the kingdom, which is ruled and tasted already by his younger brother like ghee, purodasha (rice-cake left over after it is offered in fire), kusha grass, khadira wood, etc. Sacred texts enjoin that no sacrificial object left over is used in another sacrifice. Rama will not suffer such indignity any more than a mighty tiger would brook the twisting of its tail (Rama’s prowess is suggested)”.

The king brought to naught a son whose devotion to righteousness remains matchless.

Kausalya censures the king again: “When your Highness has exiled a son so much devoted to righteousness, the question arises, whether the path of virtue exhorted by the sages and followed by the twice-born (brahmins, kshatriyas and vaisyas), has any meaning at all to you. If you had any respect for it, you would not have exiled your son, Rama.”

(Anu.), Markandeya Purana.

The curse of the sage on Dasaratha 2.64.54

The old man curses Dasaratha.

What kind of offense Dasaratha had committed, how serious it was and whether it could be called ‘brahmahatya’ (killing a brahmin-one of the five unpardonable heinous crimes) are the questions which Makhi discusses as per the legal implications in the context of that time. The boy was a son of a vaisya father and a sudra mother. His caste was therefore, karana (born of a mixed caste). Even in the event of killing him deliberately the sin of Brahmahatya would not accrue to Dasaratha. But as per Brihadvishnuvachana when a kshatriya kills a sudra the sin equivalent to one fourth of brahmahatya does accrue.

The boy’s caste (karana) is slightly higher than that of a sudra. Besides, he was endowed with merit due to service to parents. Hence had he been killed deliberately it would not be wrong to call it ‘brahmahatya’.

It appears that all this deliberation is intended to justify the curse that Dasaratha received from the boy’s father and not to pass judgment on Dasaratha’s act.

Dangers to a state without a king 2.67.9-end

The various types of danger that might attack a kingdom without a ruler:

- 1\. The thundering cloud wreathed with lightning brings no timely rains.
- 2\. Seeds will not be sown for uncertainty of rain.
- 3\. Sons will not be amenable to the control of the father as there is no fear of punishment.
- 4\. A wife will not be amenable to the control of her husband as there is no authority to enforce correct conduct.
- 5\. There can be no safety to personal property in the absence of enforcer of law.
- 6\. Women will not be faithful to their husbands, as there is no authority to check adultery.
- 7\. When the bond between husband and wife is broken, how can any other form of truthfulness prevail?
- 8\. Philanthropic people will not come forward to build public utility buildings, temples, dharmashalas or parks as lawless people might destroy them.
- 9\. Rites like sacrifices, public worship will not take place for fear of eruption of trouble.
- 10\. Even rich people will look niggardly, afraid of robbers and brigands.
- 11\. Dance, drama, music and such festivals of fine arts that delight people will not take place.
- 12\. Lawsuits are not settled as there is none to pronounce judgment.
- 13\. Study of religious texts comes to a stop.
- 14\. Unmarried girls dare not visit gardens and parks for fear of being outraged by trouble-makers.
- 15\. Merchants and farmers including cow-herds will not be able to sleep with open doors for fear of dacoits, thieves etc.,
- 16\. Lustful men and women rejoice at gardens and pleasure groves openly.
- 17\. Even aged elephants will not walk boldly on roads.
- 18\. Kshatriya youth will cease to practise bowmanship.
- 19\. Merchants, travelling to distant places do not safely move with their wares.
- 20\. Ascetics, contemplating on self will not move freely for want of hospitable householders.
- 21\. There is no acquisition of property as there can be no security of possession.
- 22\. Even the army cannot fight the enemies, as there will be no guidance.
- 23\. Well-to-do citizens cannot move freely as there will be no proper security.
- 24\. Discussion on Sastras or vedas cannot take place.
- 25\. The finest flowers, sandal paste, sweetmeats etc., will not go to the deities for worship.

Chaos in the kingdom in the absence of the king 2.67.11-38

When a country has no king there will be no fear in the anti-socials, Brahmins do not perform yajnas of long duration at places of worship where merit (punya) is earned. Festivities related gods and processions would not be found. Litigants do not settle disputes or those that live on commerce do not earn profit. Those who narrate stories of Ithihasas and Puranas do not entertain people because both tellers and listeners are not in a calm state.

The king is the cause of dharma and satya as well as the maintenance of tradition in families. Since the king gives all types of protection to the people, he surpasses Yama, Kubera, Indra and Varuna. Yama gives only punishment, Kubera gives only wealth, Indra gives only protection and Varuna maintains universal order. Since the king has all the four qualities he excels them.

An able king, by the virtue of his conduct, outstrips Lord Yama in punishment Lord Kubera in generosity Lord Indra in administration Lord Varuna in hospitality.

Cities, mountains, woods and rivers on the way to Kekaya 2.68.11-22

The messengers galloped on reaching the Malini river flowing between the extreme southern end of Aparatala Mountain and the northern end of Pralamba Mountain. (Malini is a small river that joins Ganga. On its bank the hermitage of sage Kanva existed.) Crossing the Ganga near Hastinapur, they proceeded westward and reaching the territory of Panchala through Kurujangala and observing lakes with full-blown flowers and rivers containing crystal-clear waters (Kurujangala lies on the western direction of the Kuru territory. It is a woodland.) Thereafter they crossed quickly the river Sharadanda, by name, which had pellucid, limpid water crowded with a variety of birds and people all round. Then they approached the divine Nikula tree on the west of Sharadanda, an abode of numerous boon-granting gods (hence, also called Satya-upyachana), which they circumambulated before touching a city called Kulinga, which is in the south of Kekaya territory and north of Kurukshetra, on the bank of river Sarasvati.

Thereafter they reached Ahikala and descended from the mountain called Bodhi-bhavana. They crossed the holy river, Ikshumali associated with the father, grandfather, greatgrandfather, etc. of the late King Dasaratha. From there, they beheld the illustrious brahmins who were masters in the study of the Vedas and lived on as much water as the hollow of their palms would contain. (It is just a measure. Drinking water in the palm of the hand is forbidden.)

Even though their horses were fatigued, the messengers quickly reached the beautiful city of Girivraja (also called Rajagriha).

Propriety in Bharata performing funeral rites 2.75.9-14

It may appear that Kausalya’s words, “I will go to Rama along with Agnihotra’ (the sacred fires) are unreasonable on the ground that the last rites of the dead husband deserved prior attention. When the dead body of the king that urgently needed the last rites as also the son Bharata who had to perform the rites were both present, the thought of carrying away the sacred fires along with the body was most improper. Nor could the words be justified on the ground that Dasaratha had prohibited Bharata from performing his obsequies and hence it became necessary to take the body to Rama. Dasaratha’s words were based on the presumption that Bharata too would be willing to benefit by his mother’s plan but such was not the case. Besides, in that case Bharata would not have performed the rites at all but ultimately he did. Besides, going away without Kaikeyi would also be wrong as she too, was a lawfully wedded wife of Dasaratha and had equal right to be present for the last rites.

Makhi rules out this objection stating that Dasaratha did not want Bharata to perform the rites if he approved of Rama’s exile. That Bharata censured those who were responsible for Rama’s exile was not known to Kausalya then and hence she presumed that Kaikeyi’s wicked plan must have had Bharata’s approval. In that case her desire to carry the sacred fires and the mortal remains of her husband to Rama is justifiable.

The argument that Kausalya could not proceed with her plan without Kaikeyi, also is untenable as authorities sanction the right to the eldest queen irrespective of the presence of other queens. Dharma recognizes marriage only with the first queen with fire-god as the witness. Besides, Dasaratha’s words to Kaikeyi, “I disown you as my wife who has swerved from the righteous path and who is intent only on obtaining material gains” clearly show that Kaikeyi is deprived of all such rights and privileges to which she would be entitled by virtue of her being Dasaratha’s wife. Hence the objection is ruled out. Convinced of his innocence, Kausalya approves of Bharata performing the funeral rites of Dasaratha and gave up her plan to go to the forest.

Kausalya blames Bharata 2.75.11-16

Visnu is known as a god with ‘a golden navel’ from which Brahma sprang up. Rama is a human incarnation of Visnu, come down to achieve the job of gods. Kausalya being the seniormost of the wives, is expected to keep and worship the sacred fire on the death of her husband as Dasaratha forbade Bharata from doing the obsequies if Bharata also follows the path of Kaikeyi. Kausalya decides to take the sacred fire (agnihotra) to Rama and Lakshmana on her head followed by Sumitra. “I shall myself proceed happily along the route by which Rama went to the forest. Or, I seek your cooperation in leading me personally to the forest where my son is practising asceticism. Your mother, Kaikeyi, has secured the sovereignty of this vast and rich kingdom for you. Enjoy it.”

Kausalya says to Bharata ‘I have nothing against you for becoming king, as you are also a son to me. 2.75.21

This suggests that disbelief in the sastras is a sin.

Maha. (Anu.) ???

What is a sin 2.75.22-37

Serving the debased is a sin.

Maha. ( Udyoga). Passing urine or stool facing the Sun is also a sin. ???

Parashara- Those who pass urine facing the Sun, fire, cow, brahmin and who pass urine on the road are deprived of life.

Kicking a cow is a sin: Apastamba forbids even touching a cow, deity, king and brahmin with foot.

Maha. (Sahha.): Not paying workers the wages of their work is a great sin.

Maha. (Anu.) and Garuda Purana: Treason against a good king taking proper care of the subjects is a sin.

It is a sin on the part of a king who collects the sixth part of the income from the subjects without providing them security and protection.

Manu: A king who cannot protect his kingdom after collecting taxes from the people collects not the taxes but the stools of all.

Madhaviya, Apastamba: It is a sin not to give the promised amount to the ascetics invited to the sacrifice:

Manu: It is a sin to reject shastras and the Vedas learnt from a competent preceptor.

Manu: It is sinful to eat good food without any occasion and without offering it first to God and brahmins.

Manu: Guru must never be disobeyed:

Touching a cow with foot is a sin: Apastamba prescribes severe punishment. One must never detest his Guru: Parashara.

Betraying a friend is a sin. GarudaPurana. says, such people are born as insects or as cruel animals like tiger.

Revealing to others any confidential communication like accusation against someone etc. is a sin.

Samavidhana Brahmana says that̮one who does so is a disbeliever.

Maha. (Anu.): Violation of trust is a sin leading to rebirth in subhuman species.

It is wrong to eat rich food amidst other members of the family without sharing it with them.

Vamana Purana. One who enjoys food alone while servants are hungry is reborn as a dog.

Madhaviya, Markandeya Pur ana: Not getting a suitable wife, childlessness are results of sin.

Murder of a king, woman, child, old people and abandoning good servants etc. are heinous sins severely punishable.

VishnuPurana: Severe punishment is stated for the murderer equivalent to that awarded to one who keeps sexual relations with his sister. Killing a woman, a virgin daughter or a foetus are crimes punishable by severing both hands and expulsion from the home region.

Maha. (Anu.): Forsaking good servants, teachers, devoted friends, relatives and so on and an ugly-looking wife are severe crimes.

A warrior must die while fighting on the battlefield. Running away from the field with fear is a crime. Manu: The employer of the warrior is credited with all the merit of a warrior running away from the field.

Manu, Markandeya suggest a severe punishment for the killer that consists of expulsion, exile, and begging for twelve years.

Manu and Gita: Addiction to liquor, unrestrained lust and wrath and womanizing are offenses severely punishable:

2.75.42

Maha. (Anu.), Gautama and Manu: Hatred for dharma, fondness for adharma and charity to undeserving cause are sinful acts:

2.75.44

Manu: Sleeping (or lying down) during twilight is sinful.

Burning somebody’s house, sexual relation with guru’s wife, and betrayal of a friend are heinous sins.

Maha. (Anu.): Not taking precautionary measures against bursting of fire is a sin equivalent to that resulting from killing a brahmin.

Madhaviya suggests punishment for one having sex or even its thoughts about guru’s wife.

Hating service to gods and parents is sinful.

Manu: Service to gods, forefathers and parents is the highest kind of penance. He who neglects them is not entitled to fruit of any religious or meritorious deed.

Madhaviya: Falsifying hopes of the poor is a sin.

Not approaching sexually one’s wife after her menstruation period is an offense.
