Sinful acts 2.75.56, 57

Taittiriya Shriti and Vishnu Purana: Contaminating water or giving poison to someone is a heinous crime:

Maha. (Anu.): Obstructing worship offered to a brahmin or milking a cow having a new-born calf is a sin punishable with severe penalty:

Maha. (Anu.J: It is a sin not to give water to the thirsty in time.

In the thirty seven verses (21-57) commented above, Bharata curses him whosoever was responsible for sending Rama to forest suggesting thereby that if he had a hand in the plan of Rama’s banishment as suspected by Kausalya in the fit of her anguish, he would be cursed. The curses are for the sinners and the sins are listed in the verses which have a burden ??? (whosoever is responsible for my brother’s exile). As the sins listed here are of a varied nature covering several areas like morality, devoutness, truthfulness, trustworthiness, human relations, habits, customs and manners, politics, jurisprudence, individual behavior with reference to family and society and so on the matter is of vital importance for Dharmakuta.

The sin obtained by witnessing a dispute 2.75.58

Those who quarrel among themselves on the strength of the sastras to prove the greatness of Saivism onVaisnavism are guilty of sin. The Sivapurana says, ‘one who discriminates Lord Siva and Lord Visnu will certainly enter into the womb of a ghost.’ Karmavipaka Sastra: ‘one who discriminates between Brahma, Visnu and Rudra will be reborn with a stomach disease.’

To Tirtha, the sin is attached to him as he did not reveal the secret of victory. To Kataka, the sin is attached to him for not compromising the quarrel and enjoying the same, being a mediator.

2.75.59-62

Maha. (Anu.): The sages offer challenges of self-punishment when suspected of the theft of lotus fibres.

Bhrigu offers oaths when suspected of theft, of Pushkara.

Bharata performs the funeral rites of his father 2.76.10-23

'Ashaucha' lasts only for ten days in the case of a righteous king, a rajarsi dedicated to his duties. (Parashara - Smrti texts)

2.76.13

Sacred fire from Dasaratha’s fire-place is removed and carried along with the body. Apastamba and Gautama are cited for the details of the injunction.

2.76.18

Gautama is quoted for the *Samans* to be recited on the occasion.

2.76.23

After offering oblation to a deceased relative, one must eat only such food as is cooked without salt and spices; sleep on the ground and so on.

*Manu,* Bodhayana, Apastamba are quoted for the details of the austerities to be observed by the relatives over a period as a mark of respect for the departed soul. While others prescribe it for ten days Apastamba enjoins it lifelong for the wife of the deceased.

Sangraha and Harivamsha are cited for a long list of do’s and don’ts for the widow.

Defilement to be followed by kshatriya 2.76.23

Parasara: ‘A kshatriya gets purified after observing ten days atonement.’

Rituals after death 2.77.1-3

Rituals after death:

The verse refers to termination of impurities after ten days and performing of the *shraddha* ceremony (a ritual, strictly observed by the relatives of the dead with great solemnity with the priest reciting mantras, to provide him with water and food in a specific form) on the twelfth day. The days are counted from the day of funeral (and not the day of demise) for *agnihotris* (those who observe the vow of fire-worship, lifelong.

Views of Paithinasi and Ushanas are cited in support.

The number of days of impurities differs from caste to caste according to Manu, Gautama and others. The subject is discussed and Shatatapa’s opinion that impurity is over for all the castes after ten days is cited to validate Valmiki’s stand.

One must give charities to ensure good path of progress hereafter for the dead.

*Maha. Ashrama.* Dhritarashtra gave bountiful gifts to Brahmins in the name of Bhisma and others.

Collection of mortal remains 2.77.22

Collection of mortal remains after the funeral is to be done on the thirteenth day. Objection is raised to this on the basis of Apastamba’s injunction. Makhi overrules the same by stating that the reference here is to the collection of what remains at the funeral ground after the collecting of bones *(loshtha sanchayana)* and that Apastamba has enjoined thirteenth day for the same. Thus Valmiki’s statement is vindicated.

Collection of the bones of the dead 2.77.22

The bones of the king were collected before the tenth day of death and on the thirteenth day the place of cremation was cleaned, It should be understood that this does not contradict *Smrti,* which prescribes that the collection of bones should be done on the thirteenth day.

Consolation of the bereaved 2.77.23

Elders and knowledgeable persons should console the bereaved by narrating the Shastras emphasizing the transitory nature of everything in the world.

Yajnavalkya and Katyayana are cited for support.

Three pair of opposites 2.77.23

To Tirtha, grief and delusion in the hungry and thirsty, old age and death in (cycle of) birth and death, profit and loss in joy and sorrow are the three pair of opposites. To Kataka they are: to exist and to be born, to grow and to decay, to charge and to destroy.

Justification of Bharata’s succession 2.79.3

According to some, since the elder brother has been exiled under the command of his father and Bharata has also been nominated by his father as his successor, he should not be blamed. He does not violate *dharma.* He commits no sin against his elder brother or the world since both Rama and Bharata are bound by their father’s orders. Tirtha opines that since the kingdom is without the ruler, Bharata should rule it, having been instructed by the counselors.

Benedictions showered on Bharata 2.79.14-18

Some are of opinion that this *Sloka* is superfluous. Such a charge does not have any sense as the vast *Ramayana* could as well have been told briefly.

Preparation for Bharata’s journey 2.80.1

This describes how various artisans, workers and others worked hard to construct, level and decorate the road for Bharata’s comfortable journey from the city of Ayodhya to the forest. The prose passage is in a classical Gaudi style (literally meaning typical of Gauda-Bengal, but in literary criticism it signifies a grandiloquent style of expression often used by Sanskrit prose writers, Vaidarbhi and Panchali being the other options) and displays the commentator’s command on language. The work of laying the road involves digging by axe, spade, a digging machine, cutting with chisel, sickle etc., clearing thickets of bushes, trees and rocks, transplanting of trees, filling of hollows and chasms on the way with mud. constructing ponds and lakes, decorating floor with various stones, covering with shades of thickly growing trees with blooming fragrant flowers, sprinkling of water sainted with sandal, constructing of spacious tents on the way at regular intervals for halts, and raising of flags on the terraces of high-rising buildings on the sides.

Vasistha’s order for the council 2.81.11-13

*Nandi* was performed to help Bharata to bring back Rama or Sage Vasistha performed it as a preliminary rite to Bharata’s coronation? *Nandi* is a rite to propitiate gods and especially manes and invoke their benediction. Generally, before every major auspicious function like *upanayana*, marriage, *griha-pravesha* etc. *Nandi* is performed.

Bharata’s assembly 2.81.16

The word *hruda* means ‘an ocean’, which is referred to as ‘the assembly’. *Nagaha* refers to both the ‘sea-elephants’ and ‘serpents’ *sarkara* to ‘the dust of gold taken from gold mines, *sthimithajala* to ‘the brilliance of the assembly’, which shone like water. One can see in this simile the figures of *timis* and sea- elephants painted on the floor of the council-chamber. The sheen of the glittering pavement of the chamber is compared to the still waters of the sea, the gem with which the floor is inlaid to those embedded in the depths of the sea, the figures of conches in the pavement to conch-shells found in sea-beds and the gold casting on the floor to the dust of gold found in gold mines in the bowels of the sea.

Kataka, however, compares Vasistha with the water, the fish and the sea-elephants with Bharata and Satrughna, and the gems with the counselors and the subjects.

Bharata’s instructions to the members of the council 2.82.17-20

Kaikeyi, Sumitra and Kausalya journeyed in the same chariot. Kaikeyi’s name is put first to suggest her deep repentance for her evil deed. To show that all the three had become one in their mind at that time, the poet says they journeyed in the same chariot. There was forgiveness all round!

2.84.1

Guha goes forward to greet Bharata with customary gifts of eatables etc.

This suggests that one must not go to meet the worthy and respectable with empty hands.

A verse from *Mahabharata* is cited in support.

Guha guesses 2.84.6

The words, *mahakayaha*, *kovidaradhwajah* etc., suggest that it was none other than Bharata. It was Bharata accompanied by his army who had come to kill Guha for being the disciple of Sri Rama.

Guha was the supporter of Sri Rama. So he was possibly the target of Bharata.

*Manisaphalamutasanaha* refers to ‘those who survive on meat, roots and fruits’. This implies that since they cannot cross the river let them remain there by eating meat etc. stored in the boats and sustain themselves on their strength.

According to Tilaka, the repetition of Bharata’s words show his respect. To Guha, bringing the large army is merely a waste, if the purpose is only to see Sri Rama.

Bharata proceeds to Bharadvaja’s hermitage on foot. This suggests that one must enter penance groves with humility.

*Maha. (Adi.)* Example of Dushyanta entering Kashyapa’s hermitage in humility is cited.

Rama accepts the offerings of Bharadwaja and rejects the offerings of Guha 2.87.17

Rama accepted *madhuparka* i.e. a mixture of honey and other traditional ingredients offered by the sage Bharadwaja as a mark of honour, because the sage was a brahmin. Anything offered by a brahmin brings prosperity to the receiver.

Rama rejects the food offered by Guha. Since Guha was a tribal, he had no right to honour a king. Further, since he does not belong to Rama’s country, he was not entitled to touch even the hands of Sri Rama. Moreover, Guha was aware of the truth that he should not honour Sri Rama and that Rama was under a vow not to accept his offerings.

Boats offered by Guha to Bharata 2.89.11

Guha offered excellent boats, known as Swastika to Prince Bharata. Swastika is a popular kind of boat marked with the symbol of swastika: It was used by kings. Guha further gave boats distinguished by flags and equipped with rowers, were strong-built and had large bells tied to their sails.

*Siromani - ta iti* 2.89.18-23

Landing on the other bank of the river, the army, purified in Vasistha’s company, marched on to the forest of Prayaga on an auspicious hour called maitra, which commenced on the third period of time (that is, after 96 minutes of sunrise). On reaching the forest, Bharata halted the army, and set out to the penance grove of Bharadwaja.

The seer, the knower of Parambrahman, was the foremost among those who thoroughly studied the Vedas with auxiliary texts, and hence, attained the name Vipra. Born of Brhaspati and wife of the seer Utathya (the son of Angiras and the elder brother of Brhaspati), he obtained the status of the gods’ priest. On reaching near the ascetic grove, Bharata beheld a lovely thick forest interspersed with leaf-huts.

Muhurtas 2.89.20

The auspicious time called Maitra Muhurta is the third in the list of the fifteen muhurtas enumerated as Raudra, Sarpa, Maitra, Paitra, Vasava, Apya, Vaisva, Brahma, Prajesa, Aindragna, Aindra, Nirti, Varuna, Aryama and Devata.

Muhurta 2.89.21

Muhurta is measured as naadidvayam i.e. ‘the measure of time which consists of 48 minutes’.

Bharata goes to meet Bharadwaja 2.89.22-23

Muhurta: 48 minutes of the day and so there are fifteen muhurtas in a day.

The story of Bharadwaja 2.89.22

Bharadwaja is called ‘Devapurohita' (priest of the gods) because he is the son Of Brhaspati, guru of the gods. Brhaspati produced a son in Mamata, wife of Ucathya. She wanted to desert the child being afraid of her husband. Then the gods told her “The child is legally a son of Ucathya and biologically of Brhaspati. Retain this child who is the son of both”. So the child came to be called Bharadwaja.

The birth of Bharadwaja 2.89.23

Sage Bharadwaja sprang from the loins of Bruhaspati through Mamata who was the wife of Utathya. When afraid of her husband she was going to abort the child, the gods said, ‘Bear this Bharadwaja.’

Hospitality to the king 2.91.1-4

Bharata politely requests sage Bharadwaja not to take the trouble of elaborate hospitality he offered to him and his retinue.

This suggests that hospitality offered to the king must also include his retinue.

Passages from Taittiriya Shriti and Aitareya Brahmana are cited in support.

Literary style of Valmiki 2.91.6, 7

Long and involved compounds, figures of speech both of words and sense, lengthy and complex construction of sentences appear to have been used deliberately to display the command on language.

The commentary elaborates this simple import of the epic inserting in a typical classical style, several epithets to describe the fire-place, the radiant face of the sage offering oblations to the fire-god for invoking the deities and adding details of which one of the divine and semi-divine beings was prayed by the sage to provide which particular facility, food item or luxury. Makhi uses the same embellished literary style to elaborate this portion of the text.

Tirtha on the three gods 2.91.13

To Tirtha, the three gods were Yama, Varuna and Kubera.

2.91.22, 23

Except the literary aspect of the style the commentary does not contain any matter that would be pertinent to Dharma, the central theme of Dharmakuta. These passages are of course important for studying the literary skill of the commentator.

Proper pronunciation of a word 2.91.22

A word well-understood and correctly used grants the desired object in the heaven.

Bharadwaja’s hospitality and Bharata’s humility 2.91.39

Tilaka construes the reason for Bharata occupying the seat meant for the Chief Minister. Having thought that the throne was meant for Sri Rama, Bharata bowing himself down low to Sri Rama (as though the latter was seated on it) paid homage to the throne and sat down by its side.

Though Bharata expressed his unwillingness to accept the throne, the people might not have believed him. So he did this. Sage Bharadwaja, too, to make the world believe, might have given an opportunity to Bharata, at the cost of his penance, by extending hospitality.

Having considered Bharata a part of the incarnation of Lord himself, he offered prayers to Bharata with flowers etc. This shows he was very much sure that Bharata had no evil intention in coming to the forest. He might have wanted to show the heavenly joy on the earth to those who have concentrated their minds on the Lord. Or, he might have done this to show the importance of being devoted to Rama and also to impart more love to those who meditate Rama.

The dishes offered by Bharadwaja 2.91.72-75

According to Kataka, the word sthali refers to ‘the vessels containing curry’, and pathrani to ‘the plates used for eating food’.

To Tirtha, pathrani refers to ‘the bowls used to wash hands’ and sthali to ‘the drinking vessels that used by sudras. Kumbhyah is ‘a kind of vessel used for drinking,’ karambhyah is vessels used for churning curds, yavanasthasya is ‘tanks full of fragrant butter milk, tinged yellow with saffron prepared only a few hours back,’ kapitha is ‘butter milk’.

The word rasala refers to ‘a kind of butter milk’, vyosha is ‘a mixture of ginger, pepper and fig.’ churnakasaya is ‘a decoction of the mixture of powdered fragrant roots,’ anamshumataha is ‘a kind of tooth -brush made up of collection of the sticks of a tree called apamarga and chandanakalka is ‘the paste of white sandalwood for being used as shampoo’.

Rama in exilement brings good to the gods 2.92.31

Bharadwaja tells Bharata that the delusion in the mind of Kaikeyi aroused by Manthara was indeed a plot designed by the gods. Hence there is no fault on the part of Kaikeyi and that it also leads to the welfare of the gods.

Some interpret Bhavartaya as an idea for achieving the purpose of obtaining the world of Hiranyagarbha.

To Kataka, it is ‘liberation from miseries of the world.’

2.96.17-24

Apastamba: is cited in support. There is no sin in meting out capital punishment to one who having gone astray from the righteous path takes an offensive stance.

Consequences of public calumny 2. 97.2, 3

Any act that would invite public calumny leads to Hell.

Maha. (Vana.) ‘One who is censured by people in this world is destined to reside in the vilest of the regions hereafter until the censure lasts’. Also,

‘I shall never own assets which are utilized for destruction of relatives and friends’.

The season 2.99.7-11

Rama set out on the tenth day of the bright half of Chaitra. The word, sitakarmat refers to ‘the cold climate that had set in the later part of the night during the end of Vaisakh. The strips of cloth fastened to the trees high up indicate Lakshmana’s going out to draw water from the river at an odd time. ‘Odd time’ suggests the time when one cannot have the vision of the way clearly.

Duties of ideal king 2.100.1

In the chapter Rama asks several questions to Bharata each starting with the word, kacchit (are you sure, do you truly) and referring to the duties of an ideal king which Rama knows Bharata would be but which he wants to ascertain from Bharata. It appears that Rama has presumed that Bharata has already taken charge of his duty as the king of Ayodhya and wants to know that he was following the ideals set by the house of Ikshvakus unfailingly. This meeting of Rama and Bharata is an event charged with intense emotions due to the long period of their separation preceding it and more so due to the latest developments in the royal family in which the values of family relationship were passing through the hardest tests. This long discourse on polity and kingly duty by Rama may appear out of place at this juncture but it emphasizes devotion to duty at any cost subjugating emotions. The principles of polity recounted here are the same as have been enjoined by the Smritis and other works on Dharmashastra. The chapter is known as ‘kacchit sarga’ as every verse begins with ‘kacchit (I hope)’. Makhi quotes practically all from the seventy six verses of the chapter adding his comments spread over 39 pages of the text as the topic of ‘Rajadharma’ are very important for ‘Dharmakuta’.

Bharata’s robes before and after meeting Bharadwaja 2.100.1-3

It is stated in the eightyeighth sarga that Bharata wore matted locks and bark robes. But in the ninetieth sarga, Bharata is said to have worn silken clothes when he met sage Bharadwaja. Now again the poet says that Bharata wore bark and had matted locks. How could this be?

Bharata took, the oath of wearing bark and matted locks in the town of (Guha at night. In the morning of the next day he was invited by Bharadwaja. There was no time to put on the bark and get the hair matted. So he wore them after leaving Bharadwaja’s hermitage.

Bharata’s bark garments 2.100.1

The bark garments of Bharata make him recollect the vow taken by him, which is mentioned in the 88th canto of this Kanda. There could be a contradiction, as he wore silk garments at the time of visiting sage Bharadwaja with reference to the 90th canto. But it should be understood that the vow taken by him in Guha’s city is applicable only from the time of coming out of the sage’s hermitage.

Kingdoms that perish 2.100.1-5

Maha. (Yiduraniti): Kingdom headed by a child is sure to be destroyed, ???

Kingdoms ruled over by a woman, a fraudulent person or a minor perish as certainly as boats manufactured with stone are sure to drown in the river.

Rama’s inquiry 2.100.3-86

A question now arises whether brahmins can adopt the profession of a medicineman as in some sruti texts it is prohibited. But it is prohibited for quacks, not for good doctors.

Do you keep track of the eighteen functionaries of the enemies and the fifteen functionaries of your own through your spies? They are ministers, royal priests, crown prince, commander-in-chief, chief warden chamberlain, superintendent of prisons, chancellor of exchequer, the herald, government advocate, judge, assessor, officer in charge of disbursing salary to army-men, one in charge of disbursing salary to officers, the city guardian, the person in charge of the border of the kingdom, the magistrate and the officer in charge of conservation of water, hills, forests.

It may also mean a revenue collector and an officer who kept the council chamber trim, allotted seats to the counselors according to their ranks and looked to the safety of the counselors. Last fifteen in the list above form the functionaries of one’s own side (minus the first three).

This is quite a long sarga of eightysix slokas. In it, Rama inquires Bharata about his administration. Bharata has not yet assumed sovereignty. Instead, after performing the obsequies of his father, he set out to the forest where Rama sojourned. It took some forty to sixty days. When such was the short duration, there seems no relevance for Rama’s inquiry on administration at length. Some people well-versed in judicature might have added this. But, Madhavayogin’s ‘Amruta Kataka’ does not go into that question of relevancy. This sarga is called ‘Kacchit Sarga’, as Rama’s inquiry starts with the word ‘Kacchit’, which means ‘have you’ at the beginning of every verse.

2.100.7

This suggests that one must always serve one’s father and elders.

Rajadharma: Service to mother, brother, spiritual guru and preceptor are also treated on par. Manu considers such service to elders as equivalent to penances.

Qualities of ideal minister 2.100.22-27

This suggests that even a single ‘wise’ minister is preferable to a thousand fools.

Rajadharma is cited extensively to enumerate the qualities of an ideal minister like boldness, fame, sense of time, presence of mind, respect for the worthy, competence, commitment to dharma in the face of challenges, truthfulness, self- restraint, self-respect, and lack of self-conceit.

Kings should entrust good, mediocre and inferior type of work to the good, mediocre, and inferior type of ministers, respectively.

Maha. (Udyoga) and Rajadharma are quoted for concurrence.

Kings should appoint such ministers who are honest and hail from families devoted to them for generations.

Rajadharma is cited for support.

Ministers appointed on important missions should have an orderly mind, be intelligent, fully dedicated, honest, capable and deeply attached to the king.

Ministers must not tolerate harassment of people by impudent royal officers. Rajadharma:

A dutiful and vigilant minister must protect the subjects virtually placed at the mercy of the demonical and fraudulent royal officers who desire to destroy them, have evil intentions, and are bent on looting them.

2.100.28, 29

People disrespect negligent kings as priests do sinner patrons or women do men desiring intercourse from them by threats.

Rajadharma is cited for concurrence.

The king who does not eliminate the employee as described in the verse is himself killed by him.

Kamandaka:

???

(A king who does not exterminate a minister who is equally rich, powerful, knows the vulnerable points of the king, who acts with determination, who has half of the territory under his command is himself finished).

Ideal commander in chief 2.100.30, 31

This describes an ideal commander in chief of the royal army. Rajadharma:

An ideal minister as also the army chief of the king must be proficient in politics and economics, know the propriety of war and peace, have sharp memory, intelligence, and humility, must keep the secrets, have good family background and be of spotless character. The army chief must in addition, be well-versed in military arrays, war missiles and weapons, be adventurous, healthy and strong enough to bear atmospheric changes and know the vulnerable points of the enemy.

Rajadharma: Kings should appoint army chiefs only after thorough verification of their past records and background and should bestow gifts and honors on them.

The soldiers of the king 2.100.32, 33

It is most important to see that the soldiers eat on time and are paid salaries promptly.

Manu: ???

Kings must pay daily wages suitable to the place and nature of work to menial workers, women and messengers.

Employees of the king 2.100.34

Only such persons must be employed in army who are willing to sacrifice their life for the king.

Maha. (Udyoga): Experts advise that kings must get hold of gallant heroes who courageously lead soldiers who are running away from the battlefield, are defeated and are about to surrender (to the enemy) and employ them even for thousands.

Kamandaka and Rajadharma are also cited for similar opinions.

Emissaries 2.100.35

Kings must employ ideal emissaries. They should be ready-witted, shrewd, and honest.

Manu adds some more qualities like proficiency in all Shastras, cleverness in inferring truth from signs and appearance, spotlessness, vigilance and good family background.

Important persons to be kept to watch 2.100.36

There are eighteen important persons on the enemy’s side and fifteen on one’s own in whom the king must keep a constant watch through several spies who are unknown to each other to obtain secret information about their movements and motives. Here the word tirtha is used in the sense of ‘certain counselors and trusted persons in the service of a king’ as per Halayudha’s dictionary. They are: Enemy’s side-ministers, counselors in religious matters, princes, doorkeepers, family relatives, jailors, collectors, superintendents, officers in charge of legal matters, army chiefs, mayors, disbursers of salaries, judges, head priests, judicators, governors of fortresses and border forces.

The same excepting the first three on one’s own side need to be observed according to Chanakya.

2.100.37

Kings must not underestimate enemies raising war against them although defeated on earlier occasions.

Maha. ( Udyoga.) and Danadharma are authorities quoted for concurrence on this point.

Asta Dasanyesu 2.100.37

Rama asks Bharata “Have you spotted the spies, eighteen in the opposition camp and fifteen in your camp through three sleuths who do not know one another and are disguised?”

2.100.38, 39

Kings must never entertain non-believers in the Vedas (Lokayatikas) and fraudulent persons.

Manu adds some more of the category and advises kings not even to speak to then.

It has been said that the king should employ secret sleuths in order to know about the spies (tirthas) in his own camp as well as in the enemy’s. The sleuths may be in the guise of atheists (pasandas). They should not know one another. The tirthas are eighteen in the enemy’s camp and fifteen in own camp excluding the three from the list viz., the minister, the crown prince and the purohit (priest).

The tirthas are minister (mantri), royal priest (purohita), crown prince (yuvaraja), commander-in-chief (senapati), gatekeeper (dauvarika), superintendent of women’s apartment (antarvansikha), officer of the prison (karagaradhikrta), collector of taxes (sancayakrta), officer-in charge of omission and commission (krtyakrtyaniyajaka), expert in-law pradvivaka), leader of the battalion (senanayak), head of the city (nagaradhyksa) police chief (dandapala), officer of the fort (durgapala), protector of the boundary (rastranta palaka). These have been mentioned as tirthas in Nitisastra.

Pradvivaka is ‘one who poses questions and cross-examines (the witnesses) in a dispute’.

kaccid iti 2.100.39

“Trust, you have appointed eighteen officials in each neighbouring state, such as: chief minister, family priest, crown prince, General, chief warder, chamberlain, warden of prison, chief treasurer, herald, minister of justice, judge, assessor, officer discharging salaries of army, civilian paymaster, city watchman, forester, magistrate, officer of water, hills, fords. I am sure you have chosen fifteen functionaries, except the first three in your state, and you watch their functions through three undetectable spies working in each state.

“Bharata, don’t be friendly with lokayatikas, bauddhas, and carvakas, though they are bom in the family of brahmana. Frivolously arguing on the authority of perception by senses, they harm the peoples’ faith on the highest truth. With no knowledge of the other world, they oppose the vedas. ”

2.100.40-46

Kings must protect the state and the capital city.

Rajdharma enlists seven such vulnerable points to be guarded by kings with extra care. They are: One’s own self, minister, treasury, judiciary, friends, villages and cities.

Kings of protectors 2.100.47, 48

Kings must protect all people including citizens and villagers.

Manu and Rajadharma are cited for reiteration of the same.

\[In the original text farmers, cowherds and others subsisting on agriculture are specifically mentioned. ‘Villagers’ in general have already been included in the previous verse. Makhi did not add specific comments on the importance of providing special care and protection to this class of the villagers on whom depends the wellbeing of the state. The passages cited in support also refer only to villagers in general.\]

Respect of women 2.100.50

Maha. (Udyoga.): Kings must respect ladies and keep them satisfied by charities but must not confide in them secrets of any kind. Kings should be soft- spoken and gentle to women but must never be subjugated by them. They are the glory of every household and deserve special protection. They should worship the great and righteous ones of them.

The wise never trust women, kings, serpents, memorized knowledge, enemies’ employees, objects of enjoyment (wealth, power, prestige etc.), and one’s life-span.

Apastamba: One must never entertain women for confidential talk.

Bhojaniti: Women cannot think of anything except money and sex. One must never trust them nor should be too much attached to them.

Kings must protect forests where elephants breed and should never say ‘no’ to elephants and horses. (No number of these animals is too large).

Rajadharma: Forests, mines, harvests, collection of taxes, must never be entrusted to persons other than ministers, relatives or well-wishers.

Kings should never feel contented with their pursuit of the three aims of life as also with the counselling.

King’s duty to public 2.100.51

In the first part of a day, kings must make themselves available to the public and listen to their grievances and they must at that time appear in their formal royal attire.

Maha. (Ashramavasika) adds that kings must be very liberal in helping out people seeking there help.

2.100.52

Kings must not be too familiar with or too distant from servants and artisans. They should be kept at a proper distance.

2.100.53

Forts must always be well-equipped with money, grain-stocks, and other necessities.

Manu adds to the list, means of transport, brahmins, artisans and fodder.

2.100.54

Kings must always be thrifty and the expenditure must be for the worthy cause.

Rajadharma: Spending money on those who are habitual petitioners or who are fraudulent is like offering oblations into forest-fire.

Kamandaka: Spending money on the unworthy persons and matters, results only in exhausting the royal treasury.

2.100.55

State money should be spent on gods and other worthy matters listed here. Kamandaka:

???

(Depletion of royal treasury due to expenditure on religious matters embellishes kings, like that of the autumn Moon whose lustre is dimmed being the remnant of consumption of her digits by gods.)

2.100.56

Kings must not punish anybody without consulting the counselors lest some innocent gets punished.

2.100.57

When caught and proved guilty, no thief should go unpunished by the king for financial considerations.

Rajadharma: None should be forgiven for selfish desires.

On judgment 2.100.58, 59

Especially when a poor person faces charges, officers must never deal with the case guided by selfish motives. Hence Manu recommends punishment for those who act otherwise.

Manu: Judgment passed out of greed should be punished by a thousand and passed out of infatuation, with the highest fine.

Umamaheshvarasamvada: Those who treat adharma as dharma are under the spell of infatuation and are the mortals who should be dismissed from their office even before superannuation leaving no hope in life for them.

Judgment should not be passed in favor of one just to please him if he has made false accusations against someone.

Rajadharma: Indiscriminate judgment results in denigration here and ‘hell’ hereafter. Judgment should never be passed against anyone on the basis of somebody’s report.

People to be honored by kings 2.100.60

Elderly people, physicians and such others must be honored with gifts and hospitality.

Manu: Kings must always favor Vedic scholars, diseased and afflicted, children and elderly people, beggars, persons of very high lineage and those of high esteem.

Ideal king 2.100.62-64

An ideal king must never let adharma violate dharma or vice versa. Nor should he let Kama suppress either of them.

Maha. (Vana.): Both dharma and artha desert one who fails to uphold dharma in all circumstances, as certainly as happiness and sorrow depart from the dead. He who pursues beyond all limits, only artha (financial interests) at the cost of everything else perpetrates the sin of killing a brahmin and abhorred as he is, deserves to be punished with death. Such kings indulging only in kama (objects of pleasure) at the cost of dharma and artha are sure to meet their end in the pursuit of pleasures like fishes do on the evaporation of water. Dharma and artha should not be intermingled. Like everything else artha should be founded on dharma. Acquiring artha is dharma for a king. Like cloud and ocean the two are mutually interconnected. Pursuit of any one of dharma, artha or kama alone to the exclusion of the remaining two is not advisable. The wise should pursue all the three with proper discretion.

Rajadharma: Kings who foolishly pursue artha guided by their personal pleasures and anger acquire neither dharma nor artha.

Dharma, artha and kama must be pursued with propriety of time.

Maha. ( Vana.) The wise should pursue dharma, artha and kama all discretely as per the need of time. Everyday, dharma should get first preference, artha the second and kama the last. That is the injunction of the shastras.

Kings must respect brahmins proficient in various shastras with such respect as they always feel confident of happiness in future.

Rajadharma Interests of brahmins must be protected. This is the blessing for all ideal kings.

An ideal way of spending the day for a king 2.100.63-65

The earlier part of the day is fit for accomplishing dharma, the middle part for earning artha and third part for kama without doing damage to dharma and artha.

2.100.65-67

Holding on to the five meanings being under the influence of the five sense organs and rising of dissent all around are ills which the king must shun.

nastikyam iti 2.100.65-70

There are fourteen failings, viz. atheism, falsehood, anger, inattention, procrastination, shunning the wise, sloth, sensual indulgence, solitary determination of political thought, counsel with the wise, failure to execute projects undertaken, failure to keep secrets, failure to perform sacred rites, and indiscriminate courtesy.

Manu mentions ten evils, born of lust, viz. gambling, hunting, day-dream, censure, woman, passion, instrumental music, travelling for pleasure etc. There are eight evils engendered by wrath. They are: wickedness, violence, treachery, envy, indignation, prodigality, abusive words, and harsh punishment. An attentive king should avoid them.

Manu refers to five kinds of fortifications, such as audaka, parvata, varksya, airina, and dhanvana, which are impassable and difficult to access. Kamandaka states the four means of success against enemy, which are termed as saman, dana, bheda, and danda. The scriptures assert that the kingdom consists of seven parts, viz. king, minister, treasury, territory, fortresses, allies etc. The king must go ahead with them.

The king should strenuously cultivate the three highest human pursuits, such as dharma, artha, and kama, and possess the three vidyas or sciences, viz. Trayi, Varta, and Dandaniti or the knowledge of the three vedas, of agriculture and so on, and of political wisdom.

“Prince, actively adopt six strategic expedients against the enemy, viz. sandhi or treaty, vigraha or waging war against him, yana or marching against him, asana or seeking favorable opportunity, dvaidha or causing dissension in enemy’s rank, and asraya or seeking protection of a mighty friend. Are you aware of six prakrtis or basic elements of conquest, viz. minister, territory, fortress, treasury, and government?

“Brother, you are aware of divine and human adversities. The former are fire, flood, famine, disease, and plague, while the latter spring from the official, thief, enemy, king’s favourite and king activated by greed” says Rama. According to Kamandaka, an alert king may split the enemy’s men who are greedy, haughty, dishonored, deprived of salary, angry, irritated, fearful, and frightened.

Kamandaka, further, expounds twenty types of monarchs who are not worthy of friendship, viz. child-king, aged, bed-ridden, expelled from kin, fearful, cowardly, greedy, with greedy allies, with disaffected subjects, voluptuous, counselling with the fickle-minded, speaking ill of gods and brahmanas, ill-fated, fatalist, afflicted by famine, in the company of military reverses, away from territory for a long time, having numerous foes, in clutches, and disinterested in truthful dharma.

A king wishing victory in the battlefield must be surrounded by twelve-fold commanders. Enemy, ally, friend of the enemy, friend of the friend, and friend of the enemy’s friend remain in front of a king. Parsnigraha attacking in the rear of the army will stay behind a king, and akranda or the king of neighbouring state will follow the former. Both are the kings whose dominions are separated by other states, and are allies in the war.

Behind both of them, the madhyama and udasina princes stand. The madhyama or the middlemost king will remain at a distance from the enemy and the victorious king. He controls the united group, and the individual warriors of the rear guard. The udasina or the chief with a huge army stays beyond the circle of the rear guards. His territory lies between a king seeking conquest and a king of his foe. Keeping watch over two groups, he is not directly involved in the war.

The expedition of a king is six kinds. 1. On separating the rear guards of the enemy, a king makes an attack. 2. He draws his army after terms of peace with his rivals. 3. Forming alliance with his feudatory princes, he sets forth his attack. 4. He marches at different directions, and incidentally attacks his foe. 5. Disregarding the mightiest foe, he proceeds to the friend of the foe. 6. He arranges his troops in a military array.

Further, a king makes treaty of peace with the enemy, negotiating the latter’s alliances. He wages war against him in proper time or when a friend of the former is assaulted by the foe. These measures are called sandhi and vigraha, respectively. Some of them are to be avoided, while others are to be strictly adopted.

The mention of these terms occurs in connection with six strategies of expedition. Here sandhi refers to dvaidhibhava where a king behaves as though unseen in the quarrel between hostile foes, like an eye of a crow. An asraya means that he seeks refuge of a strong ally at the terrible assault of a foe.

2.100.68-70

These verses enumerate dos and don’ts for the king as enjoined by the science of polity.

Manu: Kings must turn away from ten evils arising from pursuits of carnal pleasures and eight from fury. Between these evils and death, is better as the evils push the king lower and lower while, free from them, he goes in to heaven.

Manu enumerates the group of ten etc. as under: Hunting, gambling, sleeping in the day time, slander, women, intoxicating drinks, triple symphony (song, dance and instrumental music), frivolous wandering, are the ten evils kings must turn away from.

Kamandaka: Greedy, cruel, lazy, hypocrite, fraudulent, cowardly, fickle- minded, foolish, unruly, discourteous enemies are easily overpowered. (Ideal kings must not be like them lest they too, become an easy prey to the rivals). The evils hinted here comprise ‘the group of ten’ according to Kamandaka.

Groups of ten, five, eight and four for a king 2.100.69

The group of ten are often avarice, anger, lassitude, lie, carelessness, cowardice, and lack of firmness in decisions, foolishness, lack of tactful ness and snobbery.

It could be hunting, gambling, sleep during day, gossiping, womanizing, tipsiness, indulgence in dance, song, instrumental music and purposeless wandering. The group of five, after Karmakanda, consist of enmity born from five sources: enemies, objects, women, speech or offense. Or, may be water, mountain, tree, barren land and desert.

The group of four called chaturvarga comprises four means viz. conciliatory talk (sama), producing rift (bheda), giving gifts (dana) and punishment (danda). Or, friendship due to blood relation, due to matrimonial relation, relation of two families, and protecting some one from danger.

The group of seven consists of the king, minister, country, fort, treasury, army and friend.

The group of eight (astdvarga) has agriculture, trade, fort, bridge, catching elephants, mines and collection of taxes and vacant land.

The group of three are attempt to gain impossible results, not making efforts for possible achievements and making efforts for possible results at the wrong time. Or, it includes three powers: king, mantra and enthusiasm to achieve.

The three vidyas are three vedas or agriculture, trade and the science of punishment.

Five means of conquering the five senses 2.100.70

The five means of conquering the five sense organs are the sadgunya, the divine and human dangers, the krtya, the group of twenty and the prakrti mandala.

The sadgunya or the six gunas or aspects of polity are truce (sandhi), battle (vigraha) moving away (yana), staying in a safe fort (asana), producing a split in the enemy camp (dvaidhibhava) and refuge (samasraya).

The causes of difficulty or fear are four. They are human and divine. Each of these is of five kinds as enumerated in the Kamandakiya. The divine difficulties are fire, water (flood), plague (vyadhi), drought, and death.

The human hindrances are royal officials, robbers, and enemies of the kingdom, a favourite crony of the king and the king’s avarice.

Krtya means producinga rift in the enemy camp by making gifts to those who have not got salaries, those that are derided, those that are angry and those that are threatened. The Kamandaka says, one should produce rift in the enemy camp by giving what is desired to those who are covetous but have not got their salary; to those who are proud but are humiliated, to those who are naturally angry and have been enraged and those who are timid and also have been threatened.

In the Kamandakiya it is said that there are twenty types of persons with whom no negotiation can be made but only a battle has to be fought. They are a fool, an old man, one suffering from a chronic disease, one who is banished by his own relatives, a coward, father of cowards, a covetous person, one who is disinterested, one who indulges in too much of sensuous enjoyment, one who has many minds and thoughts, one who censures gods and brahmins, one who is unlucky, a fatalist, a poor man, the vicious, one who lives not under his own roof, one who has too many toes, one who has too many woes and one who has forsaken truth and dharma.

Prakritmandalam: the Kamandakiya says that the prakritis for a king who wants to conquer other kingdoms are ministers, the kingdom, forts, treasury and the power of punishment. Mandala consists of twelve types of kings. The king who wants to conquer others (vijigisu) stands in the middle. His friend, his enemy, his enemy’s friend, his friend's enemy, the friend of his enemy's friend are the ones that stand in front of him.

Parsntgraha: An enemy in the rear, protector of the army surrounding the rear enemy and the army surrounding the protector are the four kings on the rear side. Thus (5+4) there are nine. \\/ijigisu himself is the tenth. One who is on the flank is a fence-sitter and one who is outside is a neutral king. Thus there are twelve kinds of kings.

Kamandaka says, one who is rich, enthusiastic, and industrious and desirous of conquering other kings is called vijigisu. The enemy, the friend, the friend of the enemy, the friend’s friend stand in front of the vijigisu. An enemy in the rear, the protector, army of the rear enemy and the arms of the protector stand behind the vijigisu. A king who is next in area for the vijigisu and his enemy will be the fence-sitter. One who is capable of blessing or devastating the combatants and whose territory is outside the area of combat is the neutral (vasina) - He is more powerful and may help when the combatants are together or may destroy when they are against each other.

Arrangement of the army in a combat 2.100.71

Expedition for destroying the enemy is of five kinds. When the king has overwhelming ability and starts expedition without caring about the enemy in the rear, the expedition is called vigrhyayana. When the king has reconciliation with the enemies behind and starts the expedition on another enemy, it is called sandhayayanam. When the king goes on an expedition along with his vassals, it is called sambhuyayanam.

When the king declares openly an expedition on one enemy and actually conducts it on some other enemy, it is called prasangayanam. When the king starts expedition on a particular enemy, but later ignores the enemy and conducts the expedition on the enemy's friend, it is called upeksyayanam.

Making a treaty (sandhi), battle (vigraha), expedition (yana), sitting firmly in a safe place (asana), offering oneself to two strong enemies (dvaidhibhava) and recourse to protection (samasraya) are stated separately under sadgunya. Now the commentator is speaking according to the school of dvaigunya which includes yana etc. under sandhi and vigraha. That is why it is named dviyoni.

Kamandaka says that taking sandhi and vigraha as the basic points of polity is called dvaigunyam. Yana and asana are the forms of vigraha, while the other two are the aspects of sandhi.

Yana is the expedition of a king desirous of conquering the enemy. When the king and his opponent are tied with each other (one blocking the power of the other), staying quiet, waiting for a good time to strike is called asana. When a weak king offers himself to two strong foes through speech, it is called dvaidhibhava. It is said that one should offer oneself by speech to two strong foes simultaneously and should stay inconspicuous like the eye of a crow.

Rama asks Bharata whe ther the vedas learn the had are translated into action, whether his wealth is being utilized properly, whether his education has influenced his character. The commentator quotes the Mahabharata which says that the purpose of learning vedas is maintaining Agnihotras and the purpose of money is in giving and enjoying and the purpose of having a wife is for pleasure and sons.

\[The commentator does not quote \|Kautilya’s Arthasastra but Kamandaka, a later writer.\]

Rama’s opinion on kingship 2.101.4

Rama tells Bharata that there is no use of coronation in a kingdom if one gives up penance which ensures the status of a god. He says that even though a king is a human being, his actions bring godhood. The idea is that the state of godhood is obtained with great difficulty through austerities while it can be obtained with pleasure by means of kingship.

Ritual bath following death of a close relation 2.102.21-27

Pitrmedha Sutra says that all the brothers must proceed for the ritual bath with the youngest in front and women following the youngest. After a dip in the river Ganges Rama offered holy water saying, ’Father, this water is for you’ and all the brothers came to the bank and offered pindas.

Meeting with the queens 2.104.4-16

Surrounded by their kins, Rama, Lakshmanaand Bharata shone brilliantly on the sacrificial ground like the three sacrificial fires, i.e. Garhapatya, Dakshinagni and Ahavaniya, accompanied by the Ritviks. (Satrughna’s role being not that important, only three brothers are mentioned, says Amrita Kataka.)

Rama on the death of Dasaratha 2.104.27

On Dasaratha’s death Rama did not express any grief but only rejected the proposal of his coronation. Why is it so?

Such a charge is not right. Bharata, only passingly referred to his father's death and mainly on Rama’s acceptance of the kingdom. So Rama thin ks that Bharata is calling his dead father back because he was almost dead due to the grief caused by his son’s abandonment. Mothers were also called widows because they were nearly widows. Th e main concern of Bharata was his coronation. "Therefore Rama does not express his grief but rejects the proposal of Bharata. When Rama talks about his father’s death the reference is equally incidental, comments the commentator.

There appears to be a lapse in Valmiki’s handling of the topic. Rama should have expressed his grief over Dasaratha’s death before rejecting the proposal of his coronation. He does not do so. The commentator tries to cover this up by explaining away Bharta’s statement in another way.

Duty of a son 2.105.14-18

The duty of a son is to do the right thing always. Bruhadaranyaka states: A king is one who follows his duty to protect the people of the country, to nourish the relatives, to defend the friends.

Bharata’s righteous submission to Rama 2.106.1-end

Not only does Rama cheerfully give the kingdom up in favour of Bharata but also Bharata, in his turn, shows the same self-denial and would have given back to Rama if Rama had yielded! That is extraordinary, each brother vying with the other for making over the kingdom.

The commentator says Bharata’s submission was astonishing to the world in that it was couched with agreeable and reasonable submissions. Well-said arguments were the substance of his submission: “You are a kshatriya not a kshatriya-bandhu (a so-called kshatriya which is a positive insult to your status and valour). As an apatya (a son who prevents his father from falling down) you should follow the righteous traditions of the father, which will not let him down. Life in a forest is not given to a kshatriya. Protecting the subjects is your prime duty.

Smriti writers like Gautama, Apastamba, etc. declare the life of a householder to be the noblest and best of all four stages of life in as much as all other stages depend upon it. “How then do you seek to abandon it by staying as an anchorite in a remote forest?”

“I am junior to you in every aspect of life, be it age, learning, experience. As such, how shall I be able rule over the earth when an illustrious elder brother like you is present? I cannot live without you, much less rule over the people.

Rama speaks about Bharata’s duty 2.107.1-end

One who delivers his father from hell (Put), he is called a son. Or, a son is he who saves his father.

(Commentator’s views on Dasaratha’s promise to Kaikeyi 2.107.5-6

Dasaratha thought of retracting his promise, He thought it would not be a fault to break that promise. Whatever is said at the time of marriage or co-habitation or death or robbery or for the sake of saving a brahmin will not be a sin even if it is a lie. These five lies are no sins. "This is corroborated by Lord Siva’s words addressed to Parvati in the Uma Samhita. The king who was foremost among those that protect the sacred fire had said to Kekaya: “O King, I must be reminded about this at the time of coronation either by you or by any other king”. This was the agreement between the king of Kekaya and Dasaratha during the marriage of Kaikeyi. "Therefore there is no flaw in this regard.

Importance of Sraddha at Gaya 2.107.13-14

Doing sraddha at Gaya is very auspicious. It is stated in Visnupurana - “O king, whoever performs sraddha at Gaya, will have his birth sanctified and his fore fathers pleased”. Brahmavaibartapurana says: whoever offers rice at Gaya will go to heaven and would be liberated in due course. Whoever worships the banyon tree, would attain eternity. “Vanaparva” opines: whoever performs sraddha at Gaya in the dark half or bright half of the month would sanctify seven of bis generations. Gaya Mahatmya observes: “Whoever offers a palmful of here, cooked rice would reach the abode of eternity. Whoever takes an oath on a sami leaf and offers rice balls, will have his one hundred and one descendants emancipated.”

Jabali argues with Rama 2.108.1-end

One is born alone and dies alone. No relationship is permanent on this planet earth. Worry not about them.

People have taken to the performance of shraddha especially on the seventh, eighth and ninth days of the dark fortnights of lunar months of Pausha, Magha and Phalguna under the impression that they gratify the manes. It is a wanton waste of food. Does a dead man ever eat? If the food eaten by one man here reaches the body of another in the other world, one might as well offer pinda to those travelling from home. No provisions for journey would be necessary then for them.’

On the futility of the performance of rituals for the dead 2.108.1-18

Atheists maintain that the injunctions of the Vedasare against dharma. Father is only a minor cause of birth. The major cause is the semen received by the mother during gestation. The semen enters the ovum and mingles with the mother’s blood. Th e combination of sukla and sonita is the cause of birth. The king who is dead has gone into those elements where he had to merge, that is, he has disappeared into the natural elements. The relation between father and son is unreal. Those that indulge in earning dharma and artha do so without actually getting any pleasure.

Jabali tells Rama, “I do not lament on those that indulge in experiencing and enjoying worldly pleasures”. He cites the reason why he is sorry about those that earn and have only a lot of sorrow here and even after death they have only disaster. Engaging in rituals of feeding the dead at the annual ceremony is only waste of food. A dead person does not eat food. If the food eaten by one could reach another then people would perform shradda for the travellers so that the food eaten by others would become the travellers food.

“Intelligent people who want to make money at the cost of others perform worship of gods. There is no other world and accept what is perceived” argues Jabali from the atheist point of view.

Rama’s refutation of Jabali’s arguments 2.109.1-37

"TO Rama, either gods or manes receive the offerings made by a person whose promises are untrue, Dharma is perceived in one’s own soul. He says be was prepared to give up the kshatriya dharma in which adharma is predominant and dharma is only partially present.

Vasistha’s advice to Rama 2.111.1-7

One should always adhere to the words of the guru. “Anushasanaparva” states: whatever instruction is given by the father, mother, guru or acharya, whether it is deemed good or not, should be carried out-. One should never violate the words of the guru, for as Manu writes, the sin of disobedience to the parents cannot be redeemed even after hundred years.

Bharata and Rama are declared correct in their arguments 2.111.13-15

“A Prayopavesha is permitted only to a brahmin. Kshatriyas who are sprinkled with holy water on their head on the occasion of their consecration as kings are not permitted by spiritual texts to sit at the door of any one under Prayopavesha. Hence get up; return speedily to Ayodhya and rule the Kingdom”, said Rama

Bharata seeks the sandals of Rama as his representatives 2.112.1-6

Sincerity of purpose and resolute attachment to truthfulness as well as righteousness were the hallmark of their dialogue.

Chaos in Ayodhya 2.114.18

There was a great conflict between gods and demons. The gods lost ground and Rahu threw down the Sun-god. This resulted in chaos in the universe, as there was no division of days and nights. The gods approached the creator, Brahma, who appointed sage Atri to officiate as Sun-god for a week. One of these days of chaos is referred to here as a day without the Sun.

Anasuya’s power 2.117.1-13

Sage Mandavya once cursed a hermitess, Sandili by name, who was a friend of Anasuya that she would be widowed one morning within the next ten days. The hermitess pronounced a counter-curse saying that there should be no dawn any more. Alarmed at this, the gods approached Anasuya who, by the power of penance, converted ten nights into a single night and averted the death of the hermit.

Anasuya blesses Sita 2.117.1

Anasuya embraced Sita, kissed her in the forehead and told her to follow Rama and sleep with him which proves that during night times, a wife should sleep with her husband. Bodhayana states right from the night till dawn a wife should sleep with the husband. To Manu, drinking, bad company, isolation from the husband, traveling, day dreaming, living in the house of strangers are the defects of a woman.

2.119.18-22

“Anushasanaparva” states, demons could be perceived everywhere in the forest. They are there to harm people and hence should be slaked.

**Prof. P. Geervani**

Born in Tiruttani on 15thNovember, 1936 in a traditional family devoted to Sri Rama, completed B.Sc in 1955, M.Sc in 1960 and Ph.d in Foods and Nutrition in 1977 from Madras University.

Started career as lecturer in Sri Padmavathi Women’s College in 1957, moved to the post of dietitian in 1960, and to Andhra Pradesh Agricultural University in 1968 as Associate Professor. Held position of Professor and Dean in Andhra Pradesh Agricultural University, Hyderabad till 1994. Took up the position of Vice-Chancellor at Sri Padmavathi Mahila University, from 1994 and retired in 1997.

Received International prize for research on ‘Technology for Child Nutrition’. Published over a hundred scientific papers in addition to few chapters in books. Selected as a Fellow of United Nations University, Tokyo, in 1986, as Fulbright Scholar in 1987, as FAO consultant in 1991-94, and as Fellow of National Academy of Agriculture Science in 1999.

Inspired by the teachings of H. H. Swamy Chinmayananda, studied Bhagavat Gita and Upanishads and participated in discussions at spiritual camps of Chinmaya Mission. Awakened to the beauty of epics by the enlightening discourses on Ramayana and Bhagavatam of H. H. Swamy Tejomayananda, Global head at Chinmaya Mission, decided to study Ramayana of Valmiki in detail. Motivated by the wonderful presentation of Human values and Philosophy in the epic, decided to undertake translation of Valmiki Ramayana in 2000 and monitor the project ‘Valmiki Ramayana’ undertaken by Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, Tirupati, A.P.

Dr. Nayak chaired two sessions in the European Association of Commonwealth Language and Literature Studies, Austria in 1993. **Message**

It is gratifying to learn that the Rashtriya Sanskrit University, Tirupati is shortly bringing out a critical edition of the Valmiki Ramayana along with its translation and transliteration in English. The Project intends to incorporate canto-wise summary and commentary by distinguished scholars of the 16thand 17thcentury India like Siromani, Amrtakataka, Tilaka, Dharmakuta etc.

The Ramayana is the world’s most ancient epic depicting the victory of truth and righteousness over devilry and falsehood. It teaches us the ideal code of conduct that one should adopt in life. This is fully illustrated in the life of Shri Rama who is perfection personified and therefore called Maryada Purushottama.

The story of Ramayana has spread all over the world, particularly in the countries of South East Asia. It has shaped their society, their civilization and culture. It has left its deep imprint over their literature, dance, drama, music, sculpture, art and craft. No other gift of India to the world is as precious as the Ramayana. In these disturbing times the appeal of the story of Ramayana is as relevant as before. Plain living and high thinking is what the world needs and not gross materialism and insatiable consumerism..

I congratulate the Vice-Chancellor of the University and wish the scholars of this project all success.  
Satyameva Jayate, Nanrutam.  
(Janaki Ballav Patnaik)

**Foreword**

Ramayana is the oldest epic in world literature. It is a treasure house of knowledge and an inexhaustible mine for later poets and has a special place in Indian culture as well as Sanskrit literature. It is translated into all Indian languages and to several European languages along with English. It is also rendered with variations in many South and South-east countries since several centuries and they have adopted the epic in their music, dance, ballet, art and architecture.

It is believed that Valmiki Ramayana was put to writing around 500 AD. It was told and retold since several centuries orally in and around India. Maharshi Valmiki is confident of its circulation among people until mountains stay erect on the earth.

Ramayana is known as a treatise of dharma. The four Purusharthas - values of life.viz., dharma, artha, kama, and moksha are dealt here with utmost care. Kalidas the famous Sanskrit poet summarizes the values of life upheld by the kings of Ikshvaku dynasty as narrated by Valmiki. The Ramayana epic is strewn with exposition of values of life from great sages. The concept of dharma is depicted well through the conduct of various characters and more so by Rama. He deals with difficult situations with the ardent devotion to dharma. It gives a clear message that dharma will be victorious in the end. But those who want to stand by dharma may have to pay the price in order to achieve benefit for the entire society. The path of dharma is open for fearless and noble people.

It is an arduous and yet rewarding experience for academicians and scholars working under ‘Ramayana Project’ to give comprehensive view of the entire epic along with its five commentaries. The idea of our attempt is to present translation of the text of Valmiki Ramayanam with word order and meaning of each verse followed by translation of verse in English. It is our intention to introduce through electronic and print media Valimiki Ramayana and its commentaries in English to the modem youth interested in ancient scriptures, who have missed the traditional learning and Sanskrit language.

Although Valmiki Ramayana is in vogue all over the country three well-known versions namely the Northwest, East and Southern versions are more popular. The Southern recensionhas been selected for the present translation. The best of the commentaries of Valmiki Ramayana being written in Sanskrit is not to the understanding of many readers. Moreover the influence of English on the present generation handicaps one to understand the Sanskrit commentaries.

Considering the importance of highlighting the philosophical thoughts, values and social ideals internalized in the commentaries of Ramayana, it is also attempted to translate selected commentaries into English (though there are some more important commentaries). Several authors have written commentaries on Valmiki Ramayana which are difficult to understand for all. The authors represent different Schools of Philosophy. These commentaries enriched Indian philosophy. The commentaries selected for translation for the present are Amrithakataka, Dhramakutam, Tattvadipika, Tilaka and Siromani. The English translation of commentaries has been given for important subjects on which commentary is given.

Indian literary tradition holds Valmiki as the first poet (Adikavi) and Ramayana as the first epic, Adikavya. Valmiki is the first path maker for the sweet expressions of poetry. He provided inspiration for all classical poets and his influence is seen in Sanskrit literature in Poems Plays and Kavyas. Even though Valmiki Ramayana has been composed in classical Sanskrit and not intelligible to the unlettered yet due to the efforts made by oral expounders it was made understandable to the masses in rural India. Lava and Kusa are the first expounders of Ramayana and great Valmiki himself trained them. This practice of popular exposition of Ramayana continued through centuries making illiteracy no bar for reading Ramayana. Keeping in view the melody of Ramayana an attempt is made for audio rendering of the verses to make the reader experience the melody of the poems. There is a practice of reading Ramayana or part of Ramayana daily, particularly Sundara Kanda so that not only professional exponents of the epic but also large number of people know Valmiki Ramayana by heart. Many people know to repeat off-hand Sundara Kanda, thus the text is retained in its original form in India.

If a poem has contributed substantially to keeping in Indian culture alive it is Ramayana Rama the warrior prince is a hero a likeable pleasing god-man later came to be looked upon as god more particularly with the Vedic gods receding into the back ground. Rama became a by word. The social ideals, family relationships introduced by Valmiki made it popular over other stories of the past such as Savitri-Satyavan, Nala-Damyanti, Tapti-Samvarana and Vasavadatta-Udayana. The description of human relationship in royal households of Ayodhya, Kishkinda and Lanka is unique. Ramayana is a book of dharma and Rama is an embodiment of dharma and a paradigm of an ideal man. Ramayana clearly illustrates that artha and kama can be enjoyed with in the legitimate bounds of dharma.

The story of Rama and Sita, the dharma by which they lived and the adharma they shunned express a value system basic to much education in India. Hope this presentation produces firmer devotion to Rama and commitment to dharma which each of us is called on to practice.

The Rashtriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, Tirupati has already brought out the Balakanda of the Ramayana as part of a major project planned for preparation and publication of this great ancient Indian epic in all its six volumes with selected commentaries so that its purport goes home through its rare and reliable expositions. In response to its wide appreciation by readers and researchers, the Vidyapeetha now presents the second in the line, Ayodhyakanda, divided in two parts for the convenience of scholars: Part I (1 to 53 sargas) and Part II (54 to 119 sargas). The commentaries selected are by the same distinguished authors as in Balakanda. The running translation of 4316 verses and the summary of each sarga in English have been designed to draw the attention of the readers across the globe. Ayodhyakanda begins with the preparation for Sri Rama’s coronation and ends with his exile in the company of Sita and Lakshmana.

While conveying my profound thanks to the scholars including the coordinator of the project but for whom the edition could not have seen the light of day, I hope the volume will earn the same warm response for its message of universal brotherhood the great sage-poet of India, Valmiki, preaches from page to page.

(Prof. Harekrishna Satapathy)

Vice-Chancellor

**Preface**

Valmiki Ramayana is an ancient epic of India, highly valued for its contribution to human values since centuries and has universal relevance. It consists of 24000 verses in seven Kandas, namely Bala Kanda, Ayodhya Kanda, Aranya Kanda, Kishikindha Kanda, Sundara Kanda, Yuddha Kanda followed by Uttara Kanda. Each Kanda is further subdivided into Sargas (sections) and each Sarga is composed of few Slokas (Verses).

Late Sri V.V. Subba Rao, Former General Manger, IDBI initiated the project, with Prof. P.Geervani, Former Vice-Chancellor, Sri Padmavathi Mahila Vrswavidyalayam Tirupati, to bring out translation of Valmiki Ramayana into English. Even though a few translations are available, this project is undertaken to give the word order and meaning in English and also Summary of the sarga so that readers appreciate the literary and poetic beauty of Sanskrit in Ramayana. To keep up with the present times, it is presented through electronic media. It is hoped that readers will develop interest in Sanskrit language and appreciate literary beauty of the Verses.

**Objectives**

- • To bring out a translation of the original text of Ramayana of Sri Valmiki through Electronic and print media.
- • To bring out translation of selected Sanskrit commentaries on Valmiki Ramayana.
- • To propagate the text and commentaries all over the world through Electronic media in English and as many Indian languages as possible.
- • To protect and preserve the ancient literary works on Ramayana in Sanskrit.
- • To bring in cultural awareness and universal brotherhood among international community.
- • To bring in behavioral change towards establishing creedless and broadminded society.
- • To develop ability to appreciate the essence of Ramayana at cognitive and co native levels.
- • To prepare glossary of Ramayana in English Language.

There are several commentaries on Valmiki Ramayana. The authors have looked at the epic from various angles like lyrical beauty, grammar, dharma, Culture and Cultural practices that were prevailing during their time. Many commentaries still remain unpublished. A few of them that are published also do not carry translations in any language. We thought it is necessary to give a broader perspective of the epic Ramayana through these commentaries to our wide range of readers. We have selected five of the commentaries written during the period from 16thto 19thcentury for translation. The selected commentaries and the names of the translators are as follows.

- • Shree Madhava Yogi Pranita Amritakataka
- • Dharmakuta of Tryambakamakhi
- • Shiva Sahaya Pranita Ramayana Siromani
- • Rama Pranita Ramayana Tilaka
- • Tatvadipika of Maheswara Tirtha

In order to ensure good translation and edition of slokas and summary in English, the following committee was constituted:
