Thus ends the thirtysecond sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 32

Sugriva was puzzled at Lakshmana’s anger. He asked his ministers why they were not aware of the reason. He wondered aloud, ‘To find a friend is easy but to keep friendship is not. My only fear is may not be able to repay all that Rama has done for me”.

Trying to clear Sugriva’s confusion, Hanuman said. The pain of separation from Sita must have prompted Rama to send Lakshmana. Unmindful of your promise, you let the time that you had set for Sita search, to pass. Autumn is here, the skies are clear and rivers flow gently. Yet you seem unaware of it all, and that is the reason Lakshmana is here! Appease the prince, Sugriva, I see no other way out. Rama can vanquish the entire world consisting of the devatas, danavas and gandharvas. It does not, therefore, augur well to vex him. Go now! Assure Lakshmana you will honour your commitment”.

**Summary**

Sarga 33

Guarded by mighty vanaras, Lakshmana walked into the kingdom of Kishkinda where mansions were encrusted with gems, gardens were lush and temple bells pealed. The citizens who were children of the gods and gandharvas were beautiful, bejewelled and lavishly robed. Thoroughfares were spotless, the air was filled with the fragrance of sandalwood and the aroma of brewing liquors. Homes were captivating, granaries were full and wealth overflowed in that city where charming women lent their dazzle to enhance an ambience of splendour.

Standing at the golden threshold of the palace Lakshmana hesitated to intrude into its privacy when Sugriva felt the presence of his visitor with a start! Alarmed and afraid of facing him, Sugriva wanted Tara to mediate, as he believed noble men would never harm women!

Freeing herself from Sugriva’s embrace, Tara came out. Lakshmana did not seem to notice her disarray as he stood with his head bent and anger subdued. Tara quietly asked, “What made you so angry?” And Lakshmana said “Neglecting his duties and ignoring us who are shrouded in misery, Sugriva spends all his time in the pursuit of pleasures. Immersed in these luxuries, he has lost sight of his duties, his goals and his dharma ”

Tara gently replied, “Lakshmana! It does not befit a noble prince like you to berate a friend. How can you, so disciplined, yield to a paltry passion like anger? It is true that Sugriva after years of hardship and deprivation indulges in pleasures in excess, perhaps. Please forgive him, for his intentions are honourable, though he has erred!

“Even great men whose powers of penance defy description and who are steeped in dharma have fallen for such passions. Why then blame a fickle-minded vanara ? Despite his indulgence Sugriva has not forgotten Rama. His indomitable armies of vanaras from across the world have been ordered to gather here and many have already arrived. Calm down Lakshmana and come in! you may demur to enter the ladies chambers, but it is not indecorous to behold wives of friends”.

When Lakshmana went in, there on a magnificent throne of gold sat the Lord of vanaras, whose golden hue rivalled the sheen of his throne. An Indra in the land of the gods surrounded by a bevy of beautiful women. His robes and jewels were magnificent, his garlands exquisite and his radiance stunning!

Beholding him who was the cause of Rama’s grief, Lakshmana was overcome by a boundless rage. His fury made him look like the very god of death. Sitting on the throne with his queen Ruma, Sugriva saw Lakshmana.

Thus ends the thirty-fourth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 34

When Lakshmana strode into the palace, Sugriva leapt from his throne and stood with folded hands. As they confronted each other, the prince was shaking with anger and the monkey king was stricken with fear. Looking at Sugriva who was still bleary-eyed and still in a stupor, Lakshmana lashed out at him. “A king who is bom noble, who has conquered his senses, who is truthful and compassionate earns great renown. There is nothing more wretched for a king than forgetting help rendered. Brahma himself has declared that every sin has atonement, except the sin of ingratitude.

“You abandoned Rama the moment he got you back your kingdom. If you still remember his kindness and if you are still grateful, start the search for Sita. You are like a treacherous snake that croaks to attract its prey, the frog. If ever Rama’s grace deserts you, you will go the way Vali has gone. If only you were aware of the power of Rama’s deadly arrows that fly off his bow, you would not be dallying so fearlessly. Oblivious of your commitment, you dishonor the sacred oath of friendship”.

Thusends the thirtyfifth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 35

Seething with anger and blazing like fire, Lakshmana stood facing Sugriva. Trying to pacify him and defend Sugriva, Tara said that it was unfair to be harsh to a dear friend. “Enticed by Menaka and deluded by her charms the great sage Viswamitra had once lost all sense of time. Engrossed in sensual pleasures he had spent ten thousand years, but like a day. If such a sage could fall victim to his senses, what then of a mere vanam?

“Never will Sugriva stray from the path of truth, nor tread the forbidden path of cruelty and cunning nor forget the debt he owes Rama. I implore you Lakshmana, give up this fury and forgive Sugriva! Trust me. He will renounce his queen, his kingdom and his wealth for Rama’s happiness. He will destroy Ravavna and unite Rama and Sita. Countless are rakshasas in Lanka and to vanquish those legions who can change their form at will is not easy. Sugriva is aware of Ravana’s might and of the fearful evil that rakshsa hordes are capable of. The vanam armies Ordered back home arrive in the thousands every day from all comers of the earth. The day they all congregate, Sugriva will embark on his mission.

Thus ends the thirtysix sarga of Kishkindakanda of the holy Ramayana, the first epic composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 36

Tara’s gentle, persuasive words had their effect and Lakshmana fell silent. In the quiet of that moment encouraged by Lakshmana’s silence Sugriva shed his fear. He tore at his garlands, even as the soft petals of the flowers dropped to the ground. It seemed symbolic of the end of that phase in his life spent in pursuit of pleasure and passion.

Standing before Lakshmana in all humility, Sugriva told him he owed his kingdom and his fame to Rama whose debt would be impossible to repay. “Rama can destroy Ravana with his own might. My presence there will be the only help I can render him. How can anyone rival him who with a single arrow had cleaved seven sala trees, a mountain and the earth? When the mere twang of his golden bow can strike terror and make the earth with its mountains quake, of what need is other’s help to Rama?

“Forgive me for my lapses, Lakshmana. There are none in the world free from mistakes. I may have exceeded my limits and lost my credibility. But I have not lost my integrity, my reverence for Rama!” Pleased with Sugriva, Lakshmana said, “You deserve your kingdom and the pleasures it offers. In a world where the greatest among men loathe admitting their faults, you not only confessed but also regret them! In many ways you are an equal of Rama. The gods themselves have sent you to our rescue. Let us now go to Rama who grieves for Sita. Holding you responsible for Rama’s sorrow, I lost my temper. Do not mind!”

**Summary**

Sarga 37

Sugriva asked Hanuman to take charge of the monkey warriors scattered across the far comers of the earth. Their habitats ranged from the white peaks of mount Mandara to the fearful groves of Padmatala and along the endless miles of the blue-tinged seacoast. The coal- black monkeys of mount Anjana, the golden- hued ones of the western caves, the white maned from mount Kailash and those bands who inhabit the Aruna mountains were all to reach Kishkinda as soon as they could. “Those who do not reach here ten days from now shall face death for disobeying the king’s command” warned Sugriva.

Soaring high, following the path of the stars and birds, the vanara messengers left. From then on countless bands of mighty monkeys of different sizes, forms and colours started pouring into Kishkinda. They came not only from the rivers, caves, forests, hills and valleys but from the tops of mountain peaks. Their advent almost blocked out the rays of the sun. Those who had gone to herald the royal mandate came back equally fast, bearing gifts of fruits and rare herbs for their king.

Thus ends of thirtyeighth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana, composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 38

Sugriva was happy that preparations for the quest of Sita were under way. At Lakshmana’s suggestion they left Kishkinda to meet Rama. Borne on a palanquin of gold, protected by a shimmering white canopy, surrounded by fierce vanaras bearing arms, Sugriva travelled in all majesty. Amidst the boom of kettledrums and the blowing of conch shells followed the rest of the army that seemed to cover the entire surface of the earth.

Arriving at mount Prasravana, Sugriva got off the palanquin and stood with folded hands before Rama. Behind him stood the rest of the vanam hordes who resembled a lotus- filled lake as they stood with their palms joined above their heads. Sugriva prostrated and Rama, thrilled at seeing his dear friend embraced him with great affection, saying, “A king who divides his time equally between dharma, artha and kama is a fit king! But the one who, neglecting his duties, spends all his time in the pleasures of life, is like he who sleeps on the branch of a tree to wake up only when he falls. Eliminating enemies, helping friends and protecting dharma, a king earns great renown. The time now is for war. Plan your strategy and prepare for it, Sugriva!”

Sugriva knew that he owed his freedom, his fame and his crown to Rama. With a deep sense of gratitude Sugriva was more than happy to embark on Rama’s mission, assuring him that indomitable legions of vanaras were gathering every day by thousands. They would go to war against Ravana to destroy him, his sons, his brothers and his kith and kin, along with his magnificent island kingdom of Lanka.

Relieved and happy at Sugriva’s efforts, Rama’s face beamed.

Thus ends the thirtyninth sarga of Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 39

Pleased with Sugriva’s response, Rama praised him saying, “Just as to the Sun its radiance, to vanara rain and to the Moon its coolness is natural, so is your magnanimity to your friends”. Even as Rama was speaking, there arose a cloud on the horizon veiling the Sun in a haze and obscuring the directions. As the earth and its mountains shuddered, out of that dust emerged the mightiest of monkeys whose mountainous bodies and countless numbers seemed to cover every inch of the earth. They came leaping, jumping and roaring to surround their master.

Many were their leaders like Susena, father of Tara, Kesari, father of Hnuman as well as Ruma’s father. The list of leaders and their followers seemed, endless and their staggering numbers swelled. Surveying, them Sugriva asked his generals to make their troops comfortable and ready them for being reviewed.

Thus ends the fortieth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 40

When the last of the monkey armies had reached Kishkinda, Sugriva presented them to Rama, saying, they were no ordinary monkeys but were feared for their might, respected for their courage, famed for their strength. They were achievers of the impossible. They were loyal and devoted. Holding Sugriva affectionately, Rama said that it was not for him or Lakshmana to command but it was for Sugriva to achieve the mission, as he was brave and knowledgeable. Rama’s well-wisher, he alone was capable of the task.

Sugriva deputed Vinata, the vanara leader to travel eastward in search of Sita on the banks of the rivers like Sarayu, Kausiki, Yamuna and the mountains of their origin. He was also to look in kingdoms and oceans where horrifying human forms lived. They were to look even on the peaks of the Jatarupasila and Udaya mountains in the ocean of milk. “On the highest peaks of these mountains rests the serpent Adisheshu. The tallest of the Udaya mountain peaks supported Lord Visnu’s foot as he took the first step in his incarnation as the dwarf, vamana. What lies ahead is not known. Come back in a month with news of Sita or face death” was Sugriva’s ultimatum to his troops!

**Комментарий:**

Note: The Vindhya range and the several rivers mentioned here are not south of Kishkinda. The inconsistency is irreconcilable. Candidly speaking the geographical description is not at all factual. Some interpolator in the north (Kurukshetra as central region) has committed several anachronous inconsistencies betraying his ignorance of geography.

*ityarse srimadramayane valmikiya adikavye kiskindakande ekacatvarimsassargah..*

Thus ends the fortyfirst sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 41

In the next contingent under Nila’s command were Hanuman, Jambavan and other stalwarts who were in charge of the southern direction from the Vindhyas to the winding rivers of Krishna, Godavari and the snake- infested Narmada. They were to carefully look for Ravana’s home either in the jungles of Dandaka or in the regions of the Andhra, Pundra, Chola, Pandya and in numerous other towns and cities that dotted the south. Pushing further south, they were to cross the Tamraparni. It was here that its gushing waters mingled with the foaming, white waves of the sea.

Deeper south would get them to the edge of the ocean in the middle of which was an island inhabited by the demoness Angaraka who attacks her prey, first by grabbing at its shadow. Their travel would also take them to the city of Bhogavati, home to fearful serpents ruled by Vasuki, their king. Behind all these were the paths which led to the land of realized souls, a heaven from which there was no return. Further on, was the land of the ancestors ruled by Yama, the Lord of Death, which is ever shrouded in impenetrable darkness. “Go now,” said Sugriva, “he who brings news of Sita shall get half my wealth and be my best friend! Dearer than my very life will he be, even if he were my enemy in the past.”

Thus ends the fortysecond Sarga in the Kishkinda Kanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 42

Sugriva delegated the quest for Sita in the west to Susena, Tara’s father. He was to search the towns, villages and groves in the region where the river Sindhu infested with deadly crocodiles and gigantic fishes merged with the ocean. It was also the region where winged lions lived feasting on large aquatic animals. The huge elephants roamed the Hemagiri hills, “You will also behold the Varaha Mountain shot up into the sky in all its splendour. Their lofty peaks are pure gold and on its summit rests the city of Pragjyotishya. There lives Narakasura. Search every inch of its broad slopes and its deep, dark caves.

Varaha past, comes mount Meru where the gods worship the Sun and where the Sun dips behind its peaks, plunging the world in darkness. Beyond that neither the rising Sun nor the setting Sun is visible, and profound darkness prevails. Go now and come back with news of Sita and of the abode of Ravana so that Rama’s debt can be repaid. Those who do not return thirty days from now shall face death”!

**Summary**

Sarga 43

The regions of the north towards the Himalayas were entrusted to the powerful vanara chief, Satavali. Sugriva who knew every inch of the earth instructed his generals to search the land of the Kurus, the Bahlikas and Kambhoja in the spectacular ranges of the lofty

Himalayas with their verdant forests, rippling streams and eternally snow-capped mountains, forever veiled by the swirling mists. “From there go to Somasrama, playground of the gods and gandharvas. Between there and mount Kailas lies nothing but barren wasteland. On the plateaus of mount Kailas lives Kubera in his golden mansion created by Visvakarma. After that comes the Krauncha Mountain with its forbidding caves which are hard to access. Be sure to look there for Sita. In those caves live sages who are worshipped even by the gods and whose effulgence rivals that of the sun. Scour its peaks, its slopes and its streams. The pinnacle of this mountain known as Kamarupa, devoid of trees, is home to a myriad birds. Seek then in the regions of the Manasa, an indomitable land inaccessible not only to ordinary beings but also to the very gods, and demons. Scrutinize every inch of that land whether it is high or low or impenetrable.

Beyond this comes mount Mainaka, home of the asura, Maya. It is also the land of kinnera women. Do not forget combing it for Rama’s consort. This passed, you will arrive in that part of the world where the holy hermitages of the Vaikhanas and Valakhiyas are situated. Honour and worship them, for their austerities have rendered them pure and many are their unfathomable magical powers. Ask them for news of Sita. It is also there that the Diggaja Sarvabhauma, Kubera’s mount, roams with his herd.

Far from these lies the land with neither beginning nor end where neither the Sun nor Moon shines, where no star twinkles and where no sound is heard. In that silence and stillness where no cloud is seen floating the skies, the only light comes from the luminance of the god like sages that live in eternal bliss. The glow of their dazzling brilliance brings light to the entire region which would otherwise be shrouded in endless darkness.

Your travel will next bring you to the river Sailoda where the regions around are rampant with bubbling streams and lotus ponds with their million blooms sporting their myriad hues. Along that riverbank glint the most perfect rounds of pearls, and flawless gems dazzle and wink at the Sun. In that celestial ambience rise golden mountains surrounded by endless fields of lilies. Fruits and flowers that adorn the branches are divine. Even to touch them is to experience heaven. The trees not only produce what is expected but also give the unexpected, like priceless robes studded with pearls and richly embellished conches. In this breathtakingly beautiful land gandharvas, kinneras, Siddhas and nagas revel forever. Beyond, comes the northern ocean out of which rise the golden mountain of Somagiri, abode of Brahma”.

Sugriva in his enthusiasm and in his reverence for Rama never seemed to tire of instructing and impressing upon his troops the importance of their mission: “You who are as fierce as the flames of fire and fast as racing winds should accomplish your goal with the greatest speed after which you can roam the world at your will and without care!”

**Summary**

Sarga 44

Sugriva’s final instructions were to Hanuman, the indomitable son of Vayu, who could attain the unattainable and to whom the word, failure, had no meaning. Sugriva was convinced that Hanuman among all the monkeys would be the real achiever and the one most likely to succeed. To him he said, “You, who can traverse the earth, the heaven and the oceans are the fittest to look for Sita”.

The entire responsibility of the search now rested on Hanuman. Rama was happy that the mission was entrusted to some one so capable and who had inspired so much confidence in Sugriva. He gave his ring to Hanuman saying that Sita would then be sure that it was Rama who had sent him. Bowing to Rama worshipfully, Hanuman rose into the skies along with the most powerful of vanara armies. Even as he was leaving, Rama said, “Hanuman, I am counting on your valour and your strength to bring back Sita!”

**Summary**

Sarga 45

The Vanara armies were gone and Rama once again settled down on mount Prasravana to wait for that time when Sita was to be brought back. He watched the generals lead their troops away. Satavali went north towards the Himalayas, Vinata travelled east, Hanuman and Angada went south and Susena towards the western horizon into which the sun dipped at the end of the day. Chafing for war, eager to find Sita and raring to destroy Ravana, the raucous armies left, stomping, roaring and bragging. “I can slay Ravana all by myself’ said one, while the other declared, “I can kill him faster and deliver the terror- struck, trembling princess Sita to Rama”. Still anther boasted, “I can seek her out even if she were in the very core of the earth!” and so went on the challenges of the monkey bands in the service of their king and their god, Rama.

**Summary**

Sarga 46

In the aftermath of the commotion caused by the vanara legions, silence once again returned to mount Prasravana. In the quiet of that moment Rama asked, “Sugriva, how do you know so much of the earth with its countless hills, rivers, mountains and oceans?” And Sugriva replied, “Listen to my story, Rama: “Many years ago Dundubhi, the demon, came up to the gates of Kishkinda and challenged Vali to battle. But even before Vali could confront him the terror- struck monster vanished into a cave. Bidding me to wait outside, Vali went after his enemy. Days, weeks and months passed but of Vali there was no sign. Then one day streams of blood came gushing out of the mountain cave, followed by cries of agony. Deeming my brother dead, grieving for him, I went back to Kishkinda.

“As I settled down to ruling the vanara kingdom, Vali came back! For it was not he who had died but Dundhubhi. Though I immediately returned the kingdom to him with all respect, Vali would neither believe me nor forgive me, but tried to kill me.

Trying to save myself, I fled Kishkinda with my ministers. Leaping across rivers and ravines, over hills and through countless cities I ran. But there seemed to be no escape. It was then that Hanuman reminded me that sage Matanga had cursed Vali with death, if he ever entered his grove. So after having run all over the world, that is where we found refuge and that is how I know every nook and comer of the earth.”

**Summary**

Sarga 47

The swarming monkey bands led by their leaders went in search of Sita in the various directions commanded by their king. Their days were spent scouring rivers, forests and mountains and at sunset after countless miles of travel they rested in the cool shade of fruit- laden groves.

Those who had gone towards the North, East and West searched in vain. Though they had given up hope of finding Sita, they were confident that the path Hanuman had taken would certainly yield better results.

**Summary**

Sarga 48

Even as the other warriors were going back, Hanuman and Angada too abandoned hope. They had battled against all odds in the most inaccessible regions of the Vindhyas and through intimidating countries where rivers were dry and groves dead. Trees stood stark and leafless. Lotus ponds held neither water nor lotus. Nothing moved in that endless barren expanse, as no man, bird or beast seemed to inhabit it.

Sage Kandu’s curse was the cause for such desolation. Except that they had to face and slay a fierce rakshasa whom they mistook for Ravana, their search was uneventful. Sita remained elusive and the vanaras remained unhappy! Tired and disappointed, they threw themselves on to the ground in frustration.

**Summary**

Sarga 49

Looking at his exhausted and dejected troops, Angada said, “Inaccessible caves and indomitable jungles have revealed no signs of Sita or of her abductor Ravana and we have no choice but to continue our quest. We have to obey Sugriva’s orders with fear, for he is a hard task-master and we had to fulfil Rama’s wishes with love, for he is a noble prince.” Prodded by Angada, the monkeys resumed the search ignoring their fatigue and their disappointment

**Summary**

Sarga 50

Even as Hanuman, Angada, Mainda, Jambavan, Gandamadana fought their way into the hostile depths of the forests of Vindhya, the time allotted to them for the search had almost ended.

One day their wanderings brought them to a cave whose entrance was choked with vine and thickets. Flying out of that almost impenetrable veil were birds with their bodies dripping wet and their feathers tinged red with the pollen of lotus. Encouraged by the sight, the thirsty armies pushed their way into the opening. Not only did they not find water, but had plunged into a terrible darkness where they groped for days. Losing all sense of time and direction, overpowered by hunger, thirst and exhaustion, they finally saw a glimmer of light following which they came out and what met their disbelieving eyes was a stunning expanse of the most exotic display! Momentarily forgetting their woes, the denizens of Kishkinda stood mesmerized. The lakes they beheld were pristine, the lotuses in them were golden and the homes that dotted the land had floors of silver and gold! Windows were festooned with pearls. Mounds of silver, gold, jewels along with the best of finery, food and drink seemed plenty.

As they stood bewildered, an emaciated, old woman, clad in bark and glowing with the power of penance, approached them. Hanuman asked her humbly to whom belonged the cave and the treasures in it.

**Summary**

Sarga 51

Hanuman explained to the ascetic lady that looking for water they had strayed into the cave where they had been lost for days and had just found their way out.

The pious lady told Hanuman that in the days past the golden grove belonged to the asura called Maya who had created that wonder with the power of his magic. “One day”, she said, “Indra was angry at Maya’s dalliance with the celestial nymph Hema who had slain him. Brahma later gifted all this to Hema, who in turn left it to me. I am Svayarnprabha, caretaker of this grove. How did you get here and what do you seek? But eat and rest before you narrate your story.

**Summary**

Sarga 52

Hanuman told Svayamprabha the reason for their presence in the golden grove: “Rama, lord of the earth and son of Dasaratha, king of Kosala, had come to live in Dandaka with his consort Sita and brother Lakshmana. One day Ravana, king of Lanka, abducted her. Commanded by our king Sugriva, ruler of the vanaras and friend of Rama, we are here in quest of Sita. No caves, crevices, forests or rivers are yet to reveal any sign of success. Having gone for days without water or food, we came looking for them”.

Grateful for her hospitality, Hanuman told her that if it were not for her kindness they would have all perished. He humbly asked how they could repay her. But the gracious lady turned down his offer, saying that she had no need of anything in the world and her hospitality was her pleasure.

Thus ends the fifty-third sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 53

Hanuman pleaded with Svayamprabha to help them get out of the cave as the time given them to search for Sita had ended while they were lost still groping in the cave. We live in fear of Sugriva who might punish us with death for having no news of Sita” lamented Hanuman. Though it was not possible for anyone entering the cave to leave it alive, Svayamprabha in her kindness led them out and sent them on their way with her blessings.

Out of the cave, the vanaras saw what the ascetic had said was the great ocean Mahodadhi. They gazed at the endless expanse of water that seemed to reach the end of the earth. Mighty waves rose to awesome heights and crashed with a deafening roar terrified the monkeys. Unsure of what lay beyond and intimidated with what they now saw, the baffled bands sat huddled.

Seeing his troops swaying between fear and anxiety, Angada said: “Of Sita there is no news but of Sugriva’s fury at our failure there is no doubt. His cruelty will never permit forgiveness. It is better that we die here than be put to death at Kishkinda where it will cause pain to our families and friends”. Though Angada’s words saddened the army, they agreed with him. “Yes, Sugriva is merciless and Rama pines for Sita of whom we have no information. So death for us is imminent at Kishkinda. We either find Sita or die here. It is unwise for the errant to ever meet their king.”

As an easy solution to all their troubles, Susena said, “Let us all hide in the magical cave without fear of either Indra, Sugriva or Rama” And the vanaras seemed to agree with him.

Thus ends the fiftyfourth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 54

Hanuman silently watched the troops and their leaders voice their fears about their fate and felt that the very kingship of Sugriva was threatened. Though Angada was like Brihaspathi in wisdom and in valour like his father Vali, his loyalty towards Sugriva seemed to waver. And that alarmed Hanuman. Ever a loyal servant, master politician and a skilled diplomat, he sprang into action. Creating dissension among the vanaras was his first ploy and when they dispersed, chattering and arguing, Hanuman cornered Angada. With intention to intimidate,

he said “Angada, you too can rule as well as your father but will the vanaras, fickle-minded by nature, ever settle here without their wives and children?

“Let me also make it clear now that neither Jambavan, Nila, Suhotra nor I will join you. No bribe or threat will ever sway our allegiance to our king. Banking on the safety of this cave do not for a moment think that it is impregnable and beyond destruction. In your foolishness you have not thought of Lakshmana’s arrows which can pulverize mountains. Leading a life of denial and regretting their decision, the monkey bands will soon desert you. With no company and support you will languish in this wilderness as hapless as a blade of grass tossed by the winds. You are also abandoning the search for Sita which will amount to treason and felony the price of which will be the wrath of Lakshmana”.

**Summary**

Sarga 55

Angada was not only unimpressed with Hanuman’s ardent admiration for his king and his qualities, but denied them with great vehemence, “Sugriva is devoid of purity, compassion, courage and dignity. Impervious to morality, how did he dare to live with his elder brother’s wife who is like his mother, while that brother still lived? What made him entomb Vali while he was battling for his life? Why did he choose to ignore his promise to Rama with whose help he got his kingdom? Even the search that he has now ordered is to protect him self? Was it the fear of blame for being ungrateful and unrighteous that Sugriva sent his troops or was it the dread of Lakshmana’s wrath? Fear and not dharma dictated his decision.

“How can I trust him who is so treacherous? Why will he crown me, son of his enemy? It is better to die here rather than be put to death in Kishkinda. Leave me, go back home, pay my obeisance to Rama, Lakshmana, Sugriva, to all the elders, my aunt Ruma and to my dear mother Tara who may even die grieving for me!”

Angada then lay him self on a bed of reeds to starve himself to death. Sorrowing for Angada, abusing Sugriva and praising Vali, the swarming monkeys decided to die with their prince. They bathed in the sea and lay facing East along, the Northern shores of the great ocean. The mountains with their caves echoed back the wailing and the thunderous noises created by the immensely large-bodied legions from Kishkinda.

**Summary**

Sarga 56

As the vanara warriors lay on the sands of the Southern ocean, the ancient bird Sampati, brother of Jatayu, came out of his cave in the Vindhya Mountains. A majestic bird which was to live forever and whom death would never touch was once famed for strength and valour, but was now feeble with age.

From his perch on the rocky summits of his home, he saw countless monkeys dotting the shores below. The sight pleased him and he said “God in his mercy sustains all creatures according to their karma. It is perhaps destiny that has at last sent me food in the form of these monkeys.” It was Sampati’s moment of delight and Angada’s moment of despair as he said, “Hanuman! our mission is incomplete, the king’s mandate remains unfulfilled and now we face this peril and probable destruction.”

“We have all heard of Jatayu who fought and died for Rama’s cause. He is lucky to be dead and in heaven and not living in fear of Sugriva. When all creatures, even the lowliest among them, are ready to die for Rama, we who are here for the explicit purpose of finding his consort are ready to kill ourselves”. Angada also blamed the many events from Kaikey’s boons to Sita’s abduction that had come to pass, as reasons for their present predicament. Listening to Angada, Sampati grew sad.

**Summary**

Sarga 57

Sampati, the sharp-beaked, woke up with a start and called out stridently, “Who is it that talks of the death of my dear brother Jatayu? Those words like the clanging of fearful bells send tremors through my being. Tell me of the war between him and Ravana and tell me how Jatayu died”. He then asked the vanaras to help him down, as he could not fly. Though he looked weak and his voice was feeble, the monkeys were wary as they had heard his earlier plan to devour them. But Angada said there would be no harm in bringing Sampati down and they might as well be food for him, instead of starving themselves to death. “This way we will die faster and go to heaven”, observed Angada ruefully.

**Summary**

Sarga 58

The pitiful tale that Angada had to tell saddened Sampati. Wiping his tears he said, “Even after hearing about my brother I am unable to avenge his death for I no longer have the strength to fight. Once in our childhood, Jatayu and I raced towards the Sun in order to test our speed. As we drew closer I tried to protect my brother from the scorching heat of the Sun’s rays by spreading my wings over him. But my wings soon got burnt and I fell onto the Vindhyas where I have stayed as I could no longer fly”.

Angada asked Sampati if he knew where Ravana lived and the bird said, “I have seen many worlds, many wars, the churning of the ocean for amrita and I have seen the beautiful consort of Rama being carried away. I assume she was Sita for she kept calling Rama’s name. She is now in the island kingdom of Lanka built by Visvakarma and ruled by Ravana. A captive in that enchanting city she is guarded by fierce rakshasas. My divine powers enable me to see up to a hundred yojanas and I can see Sita and Ravana too. You will surely find her. Rama will slay the sinful rakshasas and Jatayu’s death shall be avenged”.

**Summary**

Sarga 59

When they heard Sita’s whereabouts, the vanaras who were about to kill themselves rather than face Sugriva were ecstatic. They milled around Sampati raining questions and pestering him for more information. And he told them of what he knew: “From the day I fell on these mountains, I have lived and grown old here. As I cannot hunt for my food, my son Suparshva came with some every day. Intense is passion to the gandharvas anger to the serpents fear to the animals and hunger to the birds! So when one day Suparsva came not only late but empty handed, I was furious. Suparshva explained that while he was trying to procure my meal, he was disturbed by the appearance of some one dusky and large travelling at great speed. He had in his grip a beautiful woman who glowed with the radiance of the sun. Suparsva had later learnt that the man was Ravana and the lady being carried away, Sita.

“Though I heard of this evil what could I, a wingless bird, do?” Though Sampati bewailed his helplessness he soon rallied around saying that he could still help them who.

**Summary**

Sarga 60

Having offered libations to his brother Jatayu, Sampati sat surrounded by the vanaras and resumed his narration “I remained unconscious for days after I landed on the mountain. Coming back to my senses on the sixth day, I slowly recognized the sea below to the southern ocean and the Vindhyas mountain. The only inhabitants here at that time were the great ascetic Nishakara and I. Revered by even the gods, the sage lived in a cave of this mountain, while I dwelt on its peaks. He lives no more but I have been here for eight thousand years.

One day I got down painfully to meet the holy one who had known Jatayu and me as children. Full of concern for my plight, he asked me the cause of my disfigurement and said he was sorry as he could hardly recognize me”.

**Summary**

Sarga 61

Sampati went on to tell his vanara audience what he said to Nishakara, “Pride and foolishness have done this to me. Once Jatayu and I had made a wager in the presence of sages on mount Kailas that we would follow the Sun right up to Asthagiri.

Beholding lofty mountains, meandering rivers and lush green groves we flew higher and higher towards the Sun. Soon losing our sense of direction, exhausted and thirsty, Jatayu started plummeting to the ground. I went after him swiftly shielding him with my wings, but my wings got burnt and Jatayu fell down. He must have landed somewhere in Janasthana, while I had fallen unconscious on this mountain, badly charred and wingless. I who had soared in the skies following the path of the Sun, wandered in the Himalayas, touched the peaks of mount Meru and the summits of Kailas with its pristine lakes plugged down to earth to remain here fore ever! Bereft of my brother, my strength and my kingdom I too wish to die.”

**Summary**

Sarga 62

Sampati went on to say that even as he bewailed his fate, Nishakara coming slowly out of his profound silence and prayerful meditation said that one day Sampati ’s wings, vision and strength would return: “A great event is about to take place and the time for your redemption is close” was his prediction, as he continued, “Rama, the noble son of Dasaratha, king of Kosala will soon come to Dandaka with his consort Sita whom Ravana will abduct and Rama will come looking for her. Even before that the vanara armies sent by Rama in search of Sita would be here. You will have to remain on this mountain until then to give them information of Sita. Rama’s task is not only important to him and you, but to all brahmins, devas, and rishis. I too would have liked to see Rama, but I have no desire to live that long”.

**Summary**

Sarga 63

Assured by Nishakara, Sampati had crawled back home on the Vindhyas to await the arrival of the vanara legions. “It has been a hundred years since the holy ascetic passed away, years that have been full of agony and anguish for me. There were times when I almost wished to die, but memory of Nishakara’s words has sustained me”.

Even as Sampati sat talking to the monkey congregation, his wings started growing back. Sampati’s joy and his gratitude to his master were boundless. “Rendered youthful and strong by the grace of Nishakara, I can once again take on any enemy, trounce him and get back Sita!” wagered the once feeble bundle of woe, now bouncing with vigour and vitality.

**Summary**

Sarga 64

Excited about their imminent descent on Lanka, the blustering bands from Kishkinda surged towards the southern shores of the ocean. Standing at the water’s edge, they beheld the turbulent blue expanse which turned their joy into horror. Towering waves rose and fell with untiring zest. Fearful sea creatures with their mouths wide open and the asura living on the ocean bed terrified the vanaras who only moments ago were chafing for war.

Seeing their terror and timidity Angada said, “Do not ever yield to fear, for it can kill as easily as a serpent can kill a sleeping child. Which among you can jump over the yojanas of sea to reach Lanka? Whose might and valour will achieve our mission, rid us of Sugriva’s anger and take us back home? Let him who can do so speak now!” But Angada’s requests met with a stony silence!

**Summary**

Sarga 65

Not one among the vanaras volunteered even to attempt crossing the heaving, crashing menace before them. Finally their leader Angada and stalwarts like Gaja, Sarabha, Mainda and Jambavan demonstrated how far they could leap. Jambavan the oldest among them was the only one who could clear the longest span, but it was limited to ninety yojanas. Angada said that he could easily land in Lanka, but may not have the strength to come back.

Jambavan put a stop to Angada’s plans saying that as king, he could only command, but not go with them. When Jambavan told him that he could only depute or deploy, Angada said, “Since I cannot go and no one else can, should we try to starve ourselves once again? Disobeying the king’s orders, exceeding the time permitted for our return, how can we hope to live when we reach Kishkinda? It was then that Jambavan saw Hanuman sitting happily by himself. Telling Angada that he had found the achiever, he went to prod Hanuman into action.

Thus ends the sixtysixth sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 66

Hopeful of convincing Hanuman to take the leap across the sea, Jambavan said, “Why do you sit so quietly, Hanuman? Knowledgeable, valiant and well-versed in all shastras, you are an equal to Rama and Lakshmana. Mightier than the mightiest in intelligence, courage and strength, why are you not aware of this. You are the son of Vayu, the god of wind and Anjana the most beautiful of apsaras. Strong and indomitable even as a child, you mistook the sun for a fruit and chasing after it, flew to such heights that Indra fearing harm to the world sent his vajra after you. Struck, you were thrown on a mountain the impact of which broke your chin. And it is also the reason you are known as Hanuman, the one with the broken chin. Your father, Vayu, witnessing your fall, was furious and stopped blowing over all the three worlds. Alarmed at this and trying to appease your father, Brahma granted you a boon rendering you inviolable to all weapons of war.

As for Indra he was so relieved to see you smiling even after your injury that he gave you the best boon of all, declaring, “Your death will be of your own choosing.” So, Hanuman, as swift as Garuda and as powerful as Vayu you alone can save us!”

Inspired by Jambavan and elated at the cheering of the monkeys who eagerly a waited to witness the almost impossible feat, Hanuman was galvanized into action. Waving his tail gleefully, he grew his body to incredible proportions in preparation for the flight into Lanka, to the joy of the watching vanaras!

Thus ends the sixtyseventh sarga in Kishkindakanda of the first epic, the holy Ramayana composed by sage Valmiki.

**Summary**

Sarga 67

Just as the creatures had gazed in awe at the incarnation of Lord Narayana as Trivikrama, so did the monkeys marvelled at Hanuman’s expanding form. The more the vanaras cheered, the taller and heftier he grew.As he stood among the happy, clamouring army of monkeys, Hanuman’s magnificent form glowed with the radiance of a blazing fire. Paying homage to venerable elders, he said to all those congregated, “Vayu, friend to Agni and mighty traveller of the skies who can shatter lofty mountain peaks is the god of wind and I, Hanuman, am his son! There is no one who can span this sea or go round mount Meru a thousand times like me. Churning the seas with my bare hand, I can flood the earth and leaping across ten thousand yojanas, I can make it quake. I can race with the sun, starting from the east to travel to Asthagiri and back without touching the ground. I will land in Lanka with the speed of lightning, I will see Sita and can uproot the very city of Lanka. So give up your sorrow and be happy”.Impressed by his confidence and moved by his zeal, Jambavan blessed Hanuman with success, saying, “Our fives depend on you, Hanuman!” And son of Maruti reached the summit of mount Mahendra to spare the earth of the impact of his incredible leap which could shatter it. As he readied for his leap, even gigantic boulders were dislodged, water from caves and crevices gushed out and serpents stuck out their hoods, making the slopes look like fields of swaying pennants. Rishis and animals fled their homes startled at the sudden chaos that seemed to threaten their very existence. The mountain stood mute and forlorn, like a traveller deserted by his companions.

As for Hanuman, his exhilaration was boundless. Though he was still poised on the mountain peak, his mind and spirit were already in Lanka.

Amrithakataka, Rama’s agony 4.1.3-113

The sight of the enchanting environs of the lovely Pampa Lake makes Rama’s pangs of separation from Sita, more intense, as the lotuses, lilies and the fishes resembled respectively, the face, the eyes and the long side-glances of his beloved Sita.

Kalidasa says, ‘On seeing charming objects (scenes) and hearing sweet sounds even a happy person becomes lovingly anxious’. How much more it should be in the case of Rama whose pangs of separation were intense?

Tattvadipika, Rama’s wailings 4.1.5-113

Rama was extremely disturbed on account of separation from Sira and the sight of the delightful lake Pampa enhanced it further.

Tilaka,4.1.55-56

‘Kataka interprets the reading ‘Paksi Pranaditas tatha' and ‘Vihagah Pritiharakah’ as Rama thought this bird had chirped so very pleasantly while flying earlier when Sita was with him. But now it is a cry of distress when Sita was not there. Then he refers to the omen saying that the joyful crowing indicates that Sita is not suffering and it sounds as though it carries Rama to her.

4.1.115

When admonished thus by Lakshmana, Rama whose understanding was just clouded by excess of grief regained his firmness of mind and sallied forth in arch of Sita.

Mahatmanam 4.1.123

The commentator refers to ‘Mahatmanam as one whose mind is not polluted by rajas and tamas and who is gifted with infinite valour and courage. Krtathmanam is one whose self is trained by preceptors in Srutis and Smrtis. The commentator adds that though Lord Rama was sorrowful, these emotions were not true as they were a result of maya (illusion).

Dharmakutam, 4.2.1

A king should be suspicious of all. As said in Raj adharma ‘one must always doubt even the undoubted, doubt the doubtful. For, the fear caused by the undoubted cuts asunder roots even’. As elsewhere — ‘Oh. King ! One should always run the government apprehensively when enemies are there. Sugriva feared whether those mighty-looking two (Rama and Lakshmana) had been sent by the arrogant Vali.

4.2.4-5

It is indicated that the present calamity of his should be reported to friends. As also in Udyoga says Vidura — ‘A king who consults the old in age, knowledge, intelligence or righteousness (dharma) and one’s relative after worshipping and propitiating them over what should or should not be done will never feel bewildered.’

4.2.8

It is suggested here that a king should not be forsaken in times of peril. As in Rajadharma - ‘the learned, who are truthful, noble, of unchanging demeanour, upright in conduct, loyal and have attained the object will not desert the king. And in Kamandaka - ‘A servant must not leave the master (protector) during distress though he be devoid of virtues by the one who stands by in times of calamity. There is no better sacrifice or worship.

Sugriva’s dilemma 4.2.8

If the reading is ekayanagatah, it means Sugriva , leader of the herd of monkeys was fleeing all alone’. Or it could be, for the monkeys, ,Sugrivas happiness was their happiness and his sorrow was their sorrow. So they approached him and stood around him.

4.2.18

Even under distress, it is suggested, a king possessed with intelligence and divested of delusion shall be worthy of prosperity. As in Kamandaka — ‘A king endowed with intelligence, energy and regal power will be an excellent receptacle of wealth like the great ocean of Maya (Laxmi) guarded by intelligence like the lotus by abundance of water’. Vidura too in Udyogaparva says- ‘O, king! one who is not deluded in distress and one who checks impetuosity born of anger and joy becomes worthy of wealth.

4.2.21

By this it is conveyed that kings with many friends must not be trusted. As in Raj adharma - ‘Wise men say that those who attend on kings will have fear from those kings who have many friends as also from those who have many enemies. O, the best of kings! one may prove to be trustworthy to others or one may trust only one. However, trust in one’s own sons is not commendable. O, sinless one! I have told you the purport of the sastras. It is said that distrust of kings by men is the highest secret.’ ‘And also: when a person who serves an enemy with or without a purpose, a person who is one’s own but separated or a person endowed with weapons approaches, his movements must be closely watched’.

Why did Hanuman go in the form of mendicant 4.2.22-24

By this is indicated that the nature of enemies must be considered covertly incognito: Rajadharma

In Kamandaka - ‘The spies of a king disguised as ascetics, traders or artisans must loiter around drinking in (as if) the people’s minds. For this reason the monkey in the guise of an ascetic went to meet Rama and Lakshmana.

Judging strangers 4.2.25-28

Intention of strangers whether good or bad is to be known through appearances, signs, movements and manner of talks. As Manu puts it-‘Intention in actions should be known through forms, gestures and movements. From external signs the internal thought or feeling of men can be interpreted or ascertained. The inner mind is grasped by the tone (svara — such as choking, tarring etc.), colour or countenance (varna — showing pleasantness, indifference etc.), movement of sensory organs (ingita — such as looking straight, looking elsewhere etc.), insurants (akara — such as sweating, shivering etc.), movement of motor organs (cesta — such as stretching hands, biting fingers etc.), modification in face or eyes, speech and strides (involuntary or reflexive actions) of the organs.

In Rajadharma, Indra addressing Brhaspati says, the wicked speak of demerits behind and envy merits. If extolled by others, they remain mute or turn away. The cause of silence is divulged through constant heaving, biting lips, shaking the head, speaking coherently or incoherently, doing differently when unseen, keeping silent when seen and eating separately. The feelings are observed specially in sitting, sleeping and travelling. Rejoicing in love and suffering in pain, in affliction is the characteristic of a friend. Its opposite is the characteristic of an enemy’.

An amiable master seeing the servant becomes pleased; respects his words, offers him seat nearby and enquires about his well-being.

The master does not suspect him seeing in isolated places or confiding a secret. This apart, he listens attentively to his account or affairs. He praises him in matters to be praised; feels pleased when he is praised; remembers him in other events or contexts; being pleased himself, he enumerates his qualities. He sisters to his palatable utterances; does not mind or puts up with his censure; respects or acts upon his words. He rejoices in his prosperity; suffers pain in his calamity.

On the other hand, a bad master treats his servant with indifference even when he has done wonderful services, speaks of the work actually carried out by him as done by someone else. He incites his servant’s enemies; neglects him in his ruin; encourages him in his task but once accomplished remains passive. The master sees a cruel import behind his sweet language and in his praise smells only abuse.

Even when there is no cause for anger, he gets angry; though pleased does not reward him; laughs at him, leaves abruptly and casts hard glances. While being apprised of professional matters, the master suddenly gets up and goes; hits at the vulnerable points and does not highlight his good qualities. The master labours his demerits; deprives him of the means of livelihood and mistakes the words rightly said. If displeased, the master breaks the conversation in the middle, though entreated while lying on bed, he simulates sleep; even if carefully solicited, behaves like one in a dream.

Sugriva’s instruction to Hanuman before meeting Rama and Lakshmana 4.2.25-26

When Rama and Lakshmana approach you and if they show pleasant feelings you may stand before them and instill confidence in them about me and ask them the purpose of their entering into Kishkinda or it may be read as ‘instill confidence in them about me standing before them as you do before me, praise them and ask why they have come. ’ The point is that Hanuman can speak very well before Rama and Lakshmana who are strangers.

Delivery of a message 4.3.2-3

It is indicated that a messenger must speak softly both to the sender of the message and to the person he reports. As said in Kamandaka, he must admire their greatness in lineage, or reputation or deeds.

Vyakarana 4.3.2

It is said Vyakarana is the study of the correct use of words. In the absence of corrupt word in the verbal transaction of Hanuman, it could be inferred that he had studied the Vyakarana. That the Vyakaranasastra enunciates the use of right words is established by sage Patanjali in Mahabhasya.

Hanuman approaches Rama and Lakshmana in mendicant’s robes 4.3.2-3

The objection here is: ‘it is improper for one who is in mendicant’s robes to bow before another". The objection can be overruled, because just at their sight Hanuman understood that Rama and Lakshmana were above the ordinary, They would be able to vanguish Sugrivas foes. The form itself revealed the prowess. Hanuman wanted to express his servitude to Rama. So he prostrated.

Since tbe signs of kings and gods were seen in Rama and Lakshmana, Hanuman thought that their arrival there was most improbable.

Rama’s comments on Hanuman’s wisdom 4.3.25-38

A question arises whether it was proper on the part of Hanuman who was in the guise of a mendicant to prostrate before the householders. This may become an ideal standard to follow by others also. Is it not inappropriate? Manu says, if a Yati given to Karma bows before one superior in wisdom it is not inappropriate. Some are of the opinion that on seeing the splendour and brilliance on the faces of the princes, Hanuman, for a while, forgot that he had assumed the guise of a mendicant and bowed instantaneously.

Rama instructed Lakshmana to reply to Hanuman, who was a minister of Sugriva. It was in order with the protocol. He did not directly reply to Hanuman.

Rigveda study expects a thorough knowledge of Samhita, Pada, Krama, Jata, Ghana Pathas (Prakruti and Vikruti Pathas). Yajurveda expects a lot of discretion. Samaveda has a thousand Pathas. It is very arduous to master these. But Hanuman has achieved that rare distinction. Hanuman had learnt grammar from Indra.

Study of Vedas essential 4.3.26-35

Here it is pointed out that without conversance with the Rgveda etc. it is not possible to speak with perspicuity and without faults, such as distortion of face or eyes. Not merely by the study of the Vedas can these be avoided since Siksa (phonetics) and Vedangas are also helpful in Vedic learning. It is said that the Vedas must be read and understood without any motive by a brahmana as dharma. Without any motive means regardless of obligatory rite (Nityakarma). Karana (motive) means fruit (phala) by which it is affected. Vedic study must be conducted with six subsidiary studies. It amounts to say that the reading and understanding of the Vedas with its auxiliaries is an obligatory rite (dharma) like worship of Gayatri (Sandhyopasana) etc. This is a Sruti (Vedic) injunction according to Haradatta while it is a Smrti statement according to Bhattacarya. Siksa and others constitute the auxiliary as they have been extolled so. It is said in Siksa, the face of the Vedas is Vyakarana (Grammar), eyes Jyotisa (Astrology), ears Nirukta (etymology), feet chandas (prosody), nose Siksa (phonetics) and hands kalpa (sacrificial lore).

Hanuman’s knowledge and wisdom 4.3.28-33

Hanuman was obedient and had learnt ‘Pratisakhya’ devotedly. He knew Yajurveda because it is easy to remember the anuvakas as each of them gets mixed up with other anuvakas. He knew Saamaveda because it is not possible to know singing without the knowledge of Samaveda. It is the interpretation of Tilaka.

In addition to Vedic knowledge Hanuman knew grammar by which the words, their meaning and formation can be known. This suggests his knowledge of language to be good. The voice of Hanuman was neither too high nor too low as it remained at the middle level. ‘Kanthagatam’ means produced from the hollow of the neck, the articulation of which reaches the hearer. The commentator refers to Hanuman as ‘Vakyapadiya’ meaning one who has the knowledge of the process of word and sentence formation and correct pronunciation of the syllables. His articulation that is neither short nor long delights the heart. His tone emerged from the lungs, the neck and head, meaning he is well-versed in the delivery of speech.

Rama’s assessment of Hanuman 4.3.29-40

On hearing Hanuman, Rama tells Lakshmana “If one has not studied the Rigveda, has not memorized the whole Yajurveda and has not mastered, Samaveda it is impossible to speak like this”. Kama’s idea is, Hanuman pronounced every syllable with proper svara very carefully, so he must have studied the Rigveda. Rama said that (Hanuman was an expert in Yajurveda because he did not mix up his statements in confusion. The study of Yajurveda requires such skill because the sentences of one anuvaka should not be mixed up with another. The difficulty in the understanding of various melodies called Uha and rahasya etc. is involved in the study of Samaveda. Hanuman had mastery in all the Vedas according to Rama.

Since Hanuman did not use even a single unchaste expression it is suggested that he spoke in chaste Sanskrit, Hanuman spoke in middle tone that was neither low nor high without elaboration. His speech was rich in erudition and delivered without any haste. it could please the mind of even an armed enemy because it was so attractive and was obviously emanating from the three places of articulation viz. chest, throat and head.

Facial expression of a messenger 4.3.30

Distortion of face, eyes etc. must be avoided at the time of pronunciation of letters. As said in Narada Siksa ‘A learned man should never shake the limbs of his body. Like a tortoise withdrawing its limbs he shall express his intention. Remaining calm and fearless he utters letters (well-accented) distinctly. These are six bad reciters, — he who sings, who is fat, who shakes his head, who reads what is written, who does not know the meaning and he who has a low voice.

Presentation by a messenger 4.3.31

Vistara is the presentation of a small (minimum) idea by manifold (maximum) words, absence of it (contrary to it) is Avistara, precise / accurate. Flaws like ambiguity etc. must be shunned. These are enumerated in Paniniyasiksa, Mahabhasya and Kaiyata's commentary: Doubtful, frightened, non-stop, indistinct, nasalized, harsh, high pitched, with displaced vocal organs, whispering, hurried, throwing about, delayed, choked, contracted, swallowing words/letters, piteous words, stuck, sputtering, (accompanied with saliva), blowing (lengthening the short vowels), shortening (the long vowels), closed mouth, shaking, are the kinds of wrong utterances.

In Naradasiksa chest, throat and head are places of origin of letters/sounds while in Taittiriyapratisakhya, chest, throat, head, lips and nose are said to be so. In Pratisakhya different places of speech, seven in number, viz., upamsu, dhvana, nimada, upasabdimat, mandra, madhya and tara are enumerated.

Qualities of an envoy 4.3.34-35

Puranasara states, ‘Envoy is a messenger who is learned, eloquent, wise, studies others minds, composed and truthful’. He is of three types — one who gives up or cares little for what is asked, one who does meticulously what is asked; and one who accomplishes by his ability what is good for the king, asked or unasked. Kamandaka says, ‘A messenger is of three types — ‘one who does what he is entrusted with, one who speaks with caution, and one who carries the order.

Again a messenger is described as of two types, Prakasa and Aprakasa. Udyogaparva says, ‘one who is endowed with eight qualities, namely, nassuming., strong-minded, un-procrastinating, compassionate, upright, not to be swept away by others, healthy and elegant in speech is a messenger.

Rajadharma specifies seven qualities for a messenger, one who is of noble descent, endowed with good character, an orator, dexterous, sweet-spoken, reports accurately and bright/resplendent.

To Manu, a messenger is of two types, prasasta (good) and aprasasta (bad). ‘A king’s envoy who is devoted, pure (honest), industrious, having good memory (discrete), knows place and time, handsome, intrepid (fearless) and an orator is prasasta. According to Puranasara, a bad envoy is one who is illiterate has not studied even in dream, has not smelt a little of either the Vedas or Sastras, has not touched the province of poetry/drama and who is unmindful’. In front, he is modest, behind, he is harsh, inclined to be badly motivated, greedy (desirous of stealing) even when plentiful’ — such a bad envoy is obtained as a result of bad deed.

Nrsimhapurana says, ‘Envoys who are averse to truth, deceitful, who have given up the evening prayers, who are deeply engaged in preaching moral lessons in low and discordant voice, who are searching for loopholes, disposed to bribery, treacherous by nature, tormentors of pious people, who are plunderers of their masters’ wealth and keen on deceiving corrupt a king’.

‘A king must acquire a good envoy, observes Manu, who is conversant in all sciences, who can discern the intention, form and gestures, and who is clean, dexterous and of noble descent’.

In Kamandaka one who is illustrious, has a good memory, an orator, conversant in weaponry and science and has work experience is eligible to become an envoy of a king. Without disclosing his identity he must neither enter the kingdom nor the assembly of an enemy.

He must know the enemy, his differences with his friends and relatives, his fort, treasury, army.

A king must attract the enemy through the envoy and know the moves of the enemy’s envoy on his own side. An envoy must be learned and of unassailable valour. He should be tolerant of hardship and suffering and dexterous.

Manu says, Danda (scepter) rests with the minister (Commander in Chief). In Danda rests the rules of discipline, compliance, propriety, modesty. With the king rests the treasury and kingdom and with the envoy, conciliation and dissention. It is only an envoy who makes peace (reconciles with the enemies) and who divides the united.

Thus, endowed with all these qualities of an envoy, Hanuman is rightly an accomplisher of the object. It is posited in Sundarakanda (5.2.39-40) that though unasked he accomplished what was good to his master. In Yuddhakanda (6.1.7-11) Rama enumerates the characteristic features of the best, the mediocre and the worst envoy To him Hanuman is the best envoy.

4.4.2.

Acquisition of good adherents is essential for an accomplisher. So says Vidura in Udyogaparva, ‘one must gather conformable adherents. Difficult things are achieved through allies. Objectives depend upon allies and allies are formed through the objectives. The two are interdependent.

Great men speak kind words 4.4.20-21

In times of action great men must speak kind words. About the despised men too is suggested here. As in Kamandaka — ‘a knower of time, because of the heaviness of work enumerates the qualities though non-existing concealing the existing draw backs.

In Dronaparva addressing Satyaki are the words of the king Yudhistira -‘oh, Varsneya you endowed with prowess equal to Krishna are always devoted to the Pandavas like Kesava. I entrust the responsibility to you who are capable of bearing it. In the terrible war you who are brave, devoted to truth, un-dreadful to the allies support your friend and elder brother Arjuna. In a different context Krishna requests Ghatothkacha — ‘The time of (displaying) bravery of yours, none else has come; may you become the raft to the sinking Pandavas in the battle. These Pancalas take to heels troubled by Kama’s shower of arrows like the tormented deer by the lion. In this war that has ensued against Kama none else but you can with stand. There is no one equal to you in fighting in war’.

Hanuman also says ‘thereafter, Sugriva too will be your succor’.

Signs of speaker of truth 4.4.31-32

It is suggested that pleasant countenance etc. proves the absence of untruth. Hanuman exhibited pleasant countenance as an envoy. So says Yajnavalkya, ‘In case one who moves from place to place, who touches the corner of the mouth with the tip of his tongue, whose forehead sweats and whose face becomes pallid, who stammer, who contradicts too much; who evades reply or avoids meeting the eye, who curls up the mouth and who is naturally crooked by mind, speech and action is considered capable.

Hanuman’s announcement of Rama’s arrival 4.5.1-9

Sugriva assumed human form after he heard Hanuman’s announcement of Kama’s arrival. It must be understood that Hanuman stationed Karna and Lakshmana in another place and went in to report about them to Sugriva.

4.5.11-16

In Uttara Ramayana also the friendship between Vali and Ravana was solemnized only in front of fire.

4.5.15-33

Trobbing of left eye is considered good for women (Sita in the present context) and not for men (Ravana and Valin in the present context).

Qualities of a friend 4.5.17-18

Kamandaka says, ‘Purity, sacrifice, prowess, equal sharing of pain and pleasure, affection, dexterity and honesty are the qualities of a friend’.

Characteristics of friendship 4.5.21-22

In Vamanapurana it is said that friendship is (demonstrated) through help alone, though an enemy but who does good (salutary) is a relative; though a relative but who is hostile is an enemy. Disease produced in the body is hurtful, though medicine which is of the forest is wholesome. Elsewhere it is stated ‘Like two hands to the body, like two eye lashes to the eyes, one who does good without announcing it is called a friend’.

Kamandaka says, ‘he who always stands by in times of peril or injury out of regard is a relative’. One, whether affectionate or not, who offers help is a friend. Draupadi in Vanaparva says, ‘O, Madhusudana, I tell you about my grief out of love for you’.

Padmapurana: ‘When grief is communicated to a friend it is felt reduced, like the load on the shoulders when shifted to a load-bearer’.

According to the science of omens, the throbbing of the left eye, shoulder etc, is said to be auspicious for a woman and inauspicious for a man.

**Sugriva’s ignorance of Rama’s dwelling 4.7.2-3**

**Sugriva says having committed such a despicable act he might not stay at the capital. ‘I do not know Ravana’s palace of dwelling where he walks with his long feet’. He should be a demon says Sugriva and this does not contradict Sugriva’s statement while sending Hanuman in search of Sita.**

4.7.12-13

It is indicated that the object of resolute men who have given up sorrow is accomplished. Dronaparva: ‘O, king! sin of a sorrowful person only increases Therefore, a wise man relinquishing sorrow must strive for final beatitude. Knowing thus and becoming steady, kill the enemies’.

In Moksadharma Bhisma said to Yudhistira — ‘Fortitude is felicitous. It brings happiness to a person estranged from sons, wives, pleasures and wealth and drowned in deep misery’.

Friendship with great men 4.8.3-4

In Adiparva, Vidura tells Dhrtarashtra that the Pandavas got back the kingdom and respectability amongst relatives on account of the support of great men like Krishna, Drupada and others. ‘O king! who will not want to enjoy lost wealth, with Drupada as a warrior friend, Balarama as an ally, Janardana as a counsellor, Satyaki as an adherent and Dhrstadyumna and others as brothers-in-law etc?’

Kamandaka says, ‘the winner of many battles will quickly subdue his enemies by the prowess of one, with whom the former enters into an alliance.’

The wealth of the good belongs to the common folk.

King’s duty is to protect 4.8.17-19

These words manifest Sugriva’s helplessness. It is Rama’s duty to lend protection to Sugriva. A king’s highest duty is to protect the afflicted.

As in Kamandaka — ‘Pleasing, and truthful speech, compassion, charity, protection of the afflicted, association with pious men and giving good counsels — these are virtues of good men. These good men are equal to, if not greater than, those who lift up men plunged in the mire of suffering. A king, taking pity, should wipe the tears of those who are oppressed and helpless. Non-injury is the highest virtue of all beings and a king, therefore, must protect with compassion the miserable’.

Karnaparva: ‘one who helps a person in distress is a friend and a kinsman.’

Not giving protection to the afflicted when one is capable is a sin. When a person with power knows the evil but does not remove it is affected by the very evil itself, says Adiparva. A person who does not protect one who seeks shelter, chased by the enemy goes to hell, says Harivamsa.

King’s duty is to keep his promise 4.8.21-25

Gadaparva: It is the duty of a kshatriya to keep his promise.’ See also Yudhakanda.

As in Suresvara Vartika, An act, though prohibitory, may be performed to accomplish a task found to be impossible.’ Bhima in Gadaaparva struck Duryodhana’s thighs with his mace though the Sastras prohibit striking the part below the navel. Balarama was enraged at this improper act. However, Lord Krishna tells Balarama that in order to fulfil a vow a small act, though forbidden, will not amount to any sin. ‘Know it to be the duty of a kshatriya to abide by what is sworn. I shall smash Duryodhana’s thighs in the great battle was the vow by Bhima.

In Karnaparva Arjuna took the sword to kill Yudhistira who asked him to hand over his Gandiva to Krishna since Kama can never be killed in his hands. Arjuna had taken the vow to cut off the head of a person who decisively says to him to give his Gandiva to some other warrior. Arjuna tells Krishna that ‘he had, therefore, taken up the sword to keep his word by killing Yudhishtira’.

Similarly Rama had vowed to kill Vali that day. Killing from behind, therefore, was not wrong. Had he openly challenged him, he might not have confronted him out of fear. He might have carried Rama to some other country, or he might have sought the help of Ravana. He might have surrendered before Rama. Or he might have confronted Sugriva with the entire monkey army. In the first three alternatives, the killing may be accomplished in course of time. But he had vowed to kill him that very day. This would have amounted to transgression of time. Even transgression of time is a sin. In Mahaprasthanikaparva, Arjuna had said, ‘I shall burn the enemies in a day’. But did not do so and thus he fell down’.

And with regard to the fourth alternative, whether the surrendered Vali can be killed or not is the question. Certainly not, because killing of one who has taken shelter is prohibited. It is echoed in Taittiriya Upanisad.

In Anusasanikaparva, it is said that ‘one who kills a man who has sought asylum is a sinner on par with one who approaches the bed of Guru’s wife, who destroys the foetus and who drinks liquor.

Rama had sworn to give security to each being who has surrendered to him. Thus, having vowed, Ramabhadra left uninjured Jayanta who had wronged his queen because he had surrendered. Thus it would go against his nature to kill Vali if he gave in.

‘If he is not killed’, ‘I shall kill him today’ etc, -these statements run contradictory. Rajadharma says, an enemy well-equipped has to be fought in abattle with support only. Had Rama invited Sugriva to battle with the support of the entire monkey army the monkeys who were also his subjects as vowed by Rama before Bharata (‘I am also the king of forest dwellers and animals’) would have been killed. This would have been unlawful because it is the primary duty of a king to protect people in preference to self-protection’.

Kamandaka: The physical body of a king is the internal kingdom, his external body is his own country. The two are mutually dependent. The physical body of a king is to be protected in order that the welfare of the world is ensured. Dharma is truly accomplished through the physical body’.

Manu: Kings committed to the protection of people go to heaven, their oppression of people results in hell. Rajadharma: ‘A king who relinquishes administration of justice and causes affliction to the people (indiscriminately) enters Kali (vice personified) then. He must live in hell for many years’.

Thus, the killing of such a person from whom violence is apprehended islawful.

Kamandaka: ‘Sages like kings take to lawful violence. They are not tainted with sin by killing the wicked for the sake of dharma. A king committed to safeguard dharma may kill those who torment people. The act, which noble men who know the Vedas praise is dharma and the one they censure is adharma. A king who knows both dharma and adharma and obeys the instruction of the good must protect people and kill their adversary. These thieves, tormentors of the world and offenders of dharma must be subdued. Punishment is of two types — manifest (open) and unmanifest (secret), The enemies and the tormentors of the world are to be given open punishment. Danda should be inflicted through poison, weapon and philosophical teaching so that it is not visible to others. The king by his danda (sceptre of justice) must quickly in manifest or unmanifest form finish those offenders of the world. A king may like to meet the culpable in secret. Men with hidden weapons and identity may follow him.

The Mahabharata: ‘If, one who does not kill a servant who is ambitious, who is equally competent and exerting and one who devours half the kingdom, is killed in turn’? Here the killing of a person of equal competence out of fear that he may rob half the kingdom is justified. Rama too does not act where there is people’s dissent. In the Uttara Ramayana (7.83.4-19) Rama avoided performing Rajasuya sacrifice though it is the foremost dharma.

Rama to Lakshmana who sets about killing all demons in order to kill Indrajit who had disappeared, says ‘For the sake of one individual it does not behove you to kill all the demons on the earth’. Thus, it is indeed unimaginable that Rama is inclined to kill the entire monkey folk in order to kill Vali. And also when open fight ensues, keeping up the promise, ‘I shall kill him (Vali) today and I shall hand over Ruma and Rajya back to you’ may become difficult, and there may be opposition by many also. After thinking in this way Rama took recourse to secret killing that was admittedly just. By reflecting upon the words of Mahabharata that one who has gone astray from dharmic norms should be killed by fraudulent means also is what is arrived at by Rama. Thus everything is in place.

Though the killing of Vali is lawful in the aforesaid manner, the public scandal was that Rama killed Vali by unfair means lingered. In Dronaparva, Arjuna tells Dharmaputra that ‘Infamy lives for long in the three worlds of movables and immovables’, Rama’s act of killing Vali, is like the fall of Drona, reminds us of this. And in the Uttarakanda of the Ramayana, Rama observes: ‘A person whose infamy is sung in the world sinks as lastingly in the nether worlds’. Vanaparva says, as long as a person’s infamy lasts he does not reach heaven. Thus, is the sin due to infamy unavoidable? No. For, when a thing is accomplished, the sin on that account is not caused here, but in a different place. Infamy is of two types — one, due to the performance of prohibited action out of desire, anger etc., another, due to the performance of action prohibited by the Sastras in order to preserve dharma. Of these two, only the first one is the cause of sin. Therefore, in the Mahabharata, Dharmaputra out of greed for the kingdom uttered untruthful words — ‘Aswathama was killed’ and suffered ill-reputation. For this reason only, his chariot that was moving in the sky (four inches above the ground) fell down instantaneously and touched the ground in this world and in the other world, he had to visit hell as in Dronaparva and in Svargarohanaparva.

The second type of infamy, on the other hand, does not result in sin. Therefore in Gadaparva it is said that Bhima’s smashing of Duryodhana’s thighs though prohibited is carried out to fulfil the vow. It did not cause any sin.

Safeguarding the vow is a primary dharma. ‘You will earn fame having kept the promise made’ are the words of Krishna. Thus the fame as a result of fulfilled promise is stronger than the infamy produced by secret killing; in which case the infamy shall lead to sin.

The ignominy of Dasaratha as understood in Lakshmana’ words should have caused sin. But not so. On the other hand, we like to see Rama free from debt to his father and Dasaratha too went to heaven being relieved of his debt to Kaikeyi. As in the words of a sage in Ayodhyakanda and in the words of Mahesvara to Rama in Yuddhakanda his father went to Indraloka. Thus as a consequence of stronger reputation produced by keeping the promise Dasaratha’s attainment of heaven is indeed conveyed. While the infamy caused by untruthful words on the part of Yudhistira due to his greed for the kingdom was sinful the ill reputation of Rama produced out of Vali’s killing in order to fulfil the vow does not lead to any sin. In short, the killing of Vali is not censurable in the light of Rams’s fulfillment of the vow.

Yet it may be argued that the killing of Vali by Rama was sinful because Rama with the desire to get back Sita courted friendship with Sugriva as advised by Hanuman. But it is not so. Courting friendship with Sugriva may be adduced as the cause. However, in killing Vali there is no motive. By the abduction of Sita, Rama’s heart was greatly afflicted. Not finding any means to obtain her, Rama, having come to know from Kabandha that the procurement of Sita was possible only through friendship with Sugriva who did not ask for any help in return. Afterwards, when his friend Sugriva narrated to him his sorrow depressingly, only then did Rama take the vow that he shall kill Vali that very day considering it to be his duty (dharma) to protect his friend and uplift the depressed. In order tofulfil it Vali’s killing took place. Here, the desire to get back Sita is not the motive. Had there been this desire at the root of Vali vadha, then during the time of befriending Sugriva there should have been a pact that he shall kill Vali and Sugriva shall find him Sita’.

On the other hand, Sugriva’s friendship with Rama was preceded by the act of surrender. Had there been any expectation of help in return, the act of surrender would have no meaning. Therefore, killing of Vali is not motivated by the desire for friendship. In fact, behind befriending Sugriva and killing of Vali and Ravana with the desire of getting back Sita was the determination to erase the stain of ignominy on himself and his family.

Therefore, in Uttarakanda (7.45.3-17) it is posited that Rama deserted Sita out of fear for scandal though procured back with difficulty by killing Ravana and having confirmed the purity of Sita through the fire-god.
